<meta>This page is the editor's preface to William Gilbert’s posthumous work. It follows the title page, where the editor (the author’s brother) and the source of the manuscript (Sir William Boswell) were introduced.</meta>

# WILLIAM GILBERT
### of Melford,
## Brother of the Author of this New Philosophy,
### TO THE READER.

I found these papers and small codices <note>original: *codicillos* — small notebooks or manuscripts.</note> in a state of disorder—or rather, scattered about—through my searching; once found, I arranged them to the best of my ability. I have done so not in a manner fully equal to the weight of the subject, nor to the merit of the Author; and perhaps not even according to his own wish had he lived, for he certainly would have more successfully adorned the truth he discovered with his own genius. Yet I hesitated in my mind, fearing that by suppressing a subject of such great weight, I might do an injustice to those minds inclined toward great things. The hope of being of service overcame my fear, as did the desire to challenge others, through the means of that devotion <note>original: *pietate* — here meaning familial duty and affection.</note> which demands of me the highest duty toward a brother who loved me with more than brotherly love. I wish nothing to be attributed to me except the care and performance of my duty; but for him, and for this, his unfinished <note>original: *immaturo* — literally "unripe," referring to the work being left incomplete at the author's death.</note> work, I greatly desire trust and remembrance. You, indeed, Reader, whoever you are, who shall have toiled more over this subject, or who shall have labored more fittingly on this work for his sake, will have done me a great favor.

### NOTE.

*The reader will perhaps marvel that both brothers are named William. But those skilled in English affairs know that this sometimes happens among the English—not without reason relating to domestic arrangements <note>original: *rationes oeconomicas* — this refers to a historical practice, sometimes seen in the 16th century, of giving the same name to multiple children to ensure a name survived or for specific inheritance purposes.</note>, and even among those who are not of the lowest rank of the people. My authority for this is G.B. <note>Presumably Sir William Boswell, mentioned on the title page as the source of the manuscript.</note>, a man most worthy of a longer life, who recently joined the many <note>original: *concessit ad plures* — a classical Latin idiom meaning he passed away.</note>.*

<summary>A preface by the author's brother, William Gilbert of Melford, explaining how he collected and organized his late brother's scattered notes for publication out of a sense of fraternal duty. It includes a curious note explaining why both brothers shared the same first name.</summary>
<keywords>William Gilbert, preface, posthumous publication, fraternal duty, naming conventions, Long Melford, editing process, scientific manuscripts</keywords>

### *To the Most Illustrious and Learned Man,*

# ANTHONY VIVIAN

### Lord of Bovino,

->Sends Greetings.<-

## ISAAC GRUTER.

This book was contemplating its journey into the light of the world, seeking to undergo the scrutiny of the scientific <note>original: *Physiologici* — in this period, "physiology" referred broadly to natural philosophy or the study of the physical world</note> audience, whose tastes are now refined by the most rigorous application of deep curiosity. It required the companionship of a guardian spirit to win favor in the public eye and to be fortified against the biting malice of an envy that leaves nothing unprovoked. To be sure, the author’s own renowned reputation shines upon this posthumous offspring—he who is most highly celebrated for his successful experimental investigation of the Magnet <note>original: *Magnetici scrutinni* — a reference to William Gilbert's landmark 1600 work, *De Magnete*, which established the study of magnetism</note>. Yet, I foresee the clouds which [are gathered] against the writings of the Fa- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword *rente* suggests the full word is *Parentis*, or "the Father/Author."</note>

<summary>In this formal dedication, editor Isaac Gruter presents William Gilbert’s posthumous work to Anthony Vivian, seeking protection for the text against critics by invoking the author's existing fame as a pioneer of magnetic science.</summary>

[of its] parent, the foul unfairness of the times easily breathes out [malice], which must be overcome by properly invoking the power of a designated Patron. Nor was that patron to be sought from afar, since it was not the recklessness of fortune that offered you to us—snatching at whatever is nearby for help—but rather reason that chose you from a selection. You have shown such great affection toward me and toward all writings of exquisite skill that it would be an act of ingratitude if I were to direct my hopes for goodwill and for a defender against this age of petulant Criticism <note>original: *Criticâ*</note> to anyone else. You will look more kindly upon whatever fortune has allowed here that requires excuse—in books which, by an unlucky fate, did not experience the final polishing <note>original: *limam* — literally "the file," a common metaphor for the final editing and refinement of a manuscript</note> of their Author.

For an effort in such difficult subject matter—one which expects progress from all future generations—must not be cheated of its rightful praise, even if it has occasionally fallen into error. This author suffered from the unfortunate hand of copyists <note>original: *librariorum* — refers to the scribes or clerks who transcribed the original manuscript, often introducing errors</note>, from whom the best works often emerge in a most corrupted state; furthermore, while bringing noble daring and a praiseworthy self-confidence to these arduous tasks, he was unable to enjoy the further progress of a longer life. Indeed, the labor of every age will find—if it does not allow itself to be squeezed into the narrow constraints of an intellectual Dictatorship <note>original: *Dictaturæ* — likely a reference to the rigid "dictatorship" of Aristotelian philosophy, which Gilbert and other early modern scientists were working to overturn</note> that clips the wings of great geniuses attempting great things—in

# TO THE READER, GREETINGS.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter G within a square frame, embellished with scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
The great glory of **William Boswell**, <note>Sir William Boswell (died 1650) was an English politician and diplomat who served as the resident ambassador at The Hague. He was a polymath and a patron of the sciences.</note> earned through his just merits, was well known among the learned of our time. Born of an ancient and most noble family in **Yorkshire**, <note>original: *Eboracenses*</note> he brought the studies of both gentle and more rigorous literature—happily cultivated in the shadows of the Academy <note>Referring to the university environment</note>—into the light of the Royal Court. He maintained a capacity for majestic business, free from the harshness of envious splendor, combined with a tempered serenity of the highest kindness. Just as he proved his loyalty to the **Scepter** <note>The English monarchy</note> and showed a skillfully versatile industry in conducting affairs—having served for a long time as the Ambassador <note>original: *Orator*</note> of the late most Serene **King of England** <note>Charles I</note> to the **United Netherlands** <note>original: *fœderatos Belgas*</note>—so too did he shine as a most kind and faithful protector to the **Muses** and to the students of every kind of learning. He sought to shield them from the injustices of the age and, as far as possible, to guide them into a harbor away from the storms of an ill-favored fate. But I do not weave a barren eulogy for a man who can never be praised enough—a man who, even amidst the greatest misfortunes of the time which dismally disturbed English affairs and Boswell's own private fortunes, will surely have heralds worthy of his rare virtues. For my part, as I wish to say a few words by way of preface to this **Physiology**, <note>original: *Physiologiæ* — In the 17th century, "physiology" referred broadly to "natural philosophy" or the study of the laws of nature, rather than just the human body.</note> I felt it necessary to touch upon these things; I had to compress into a short speech a subject matter open to ample praise, so that I might honorably boast of such...

<summary>The editor begins his address to the reader by praising the late Sir William Boswell, a diplomat and scholar who protected intellectual works during the chaos of the English Civil War.</summary>
<keywords>William Boswell, Yorkshire, Ambassador, Netherlands, King of England, patronage, natural philosophy, physiology, English Civil War</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the address "To the Reader" from the previous page, shifting from the praise of Sir William Boswell to the technical difficulties the editor faced in reconciling the manuscript sources for William Gilbert’s work.</meta>

...through his illustrious friendship, I should acknowledge the gift of the two manuscript copies <note>original: *gemini MS. codicis*</note> from which this polished edition has been prepared for you, Reader. However, the labor involved was immense. This project was a most vexing undertaking, where troublesome difficulties nearly choked any hope of success. Both manuscript copies suffered from the hands of the worst scribes—men who did not even know Latin. They were filled with "monsters of errors" scattered everywhere, casting a thick shroud of darkness over the original meaning. 

My attention had to be constantly fixed as I struggled against frustrations that were almost too much to stomach. I had to persist stubbornly through diligent reading and comparison <term>collation: the process of comparing different copies of a text to identify variations and errors</term>, which, after being repeated accurately several times, finally brought the work into the light. Thus, the mind of **Gilbert** gradually revealed itself from the midst of that dark and corrupted Latin into which the ignorance of the copyists had forced him. He was a sagacious **Philosopher** and a pioneer in **Physics** <note>original: *novaturientem*, literally "desiring to innovate," referring to Gilbert's revolutionary approach to experimental science</note> who is usually his own best interpreter when he is not hindered by external errors. 

Yet, I did not indulge in rash corrections or wanton conjectures—even though I felt I understood the Author's genius from his books **On the Magnet** <note>William Gilbert's most famous work, *De Magnete* (1600), which established the study of magnetism</note>. I have conducted myself with such care that, although the text is now intelligible to readers, I have left a significant "gleaning" <note>original: *spicilegium*; a metaphor for the remaining work or insights to be gathered by future scholars</note> for the skill of those who will follow. They will see the exhaustion we felt in "breaking the ice" and clearing away the obstacles that would have surely exhausted the patience of anyone trying to avoid such mental torments <note>original: *cruces ingenii*, literally "crosses of the intellect"</note>. Regarding the mathematical diagrams, the other

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor's preface, detailing the specific challenges faced when comparing the two manuscript copies of William Gilbert’s work. It addresses the discrepancies in chapter order and the editor's decision to prioritize a complete text over a perfectly reorganized one.</meta>

# TO THE READER.

...one copy alone had readings that were sufficiently clear and accurate, while the other had either very confused ones or was entirely lacking them. The sequence of chapters did not match in both, and there were chapters present in one—though very few—which you would have sought in the other in vain. In the midst of such confusion, I believed I was permitted some discretion, as I preferred the work to come forth enlarged rather than truncated. 

In examining the **Method** <term>Method: In the 17th century, this referred to the logical structure and organizational framework of a scientific treatise</term>, I was far more lenient. I saw that a correction would have to be extended quite widely if I were to undertake a total reformation—which, though currently lacking a protector, needed to be done according to the standard of the art (which I found had been violated). That standard organizes individual points according to the clarity of nature, proceeding from more general to more specific things, and weaves the explanations of qualities and properties distinctly into their proper places. However, among Critics <note>original: *Arbitros*, referring to scholarly judges or editors</note>, such sweeping changes to another person's work are, quite rightly, not permitted.

Therefore, a Reader who is keenly fastidious and of a censorious brow will easily stumble upon small offenses against either the sense or a more exact elegance, which I suspect escaped my attention and will not be lacking in number. But let such a reader remember to acknowledge that these errors belong to men, knowing that they are **a slippery thing** <note>original Greek: *ὀλισθηρόν τι πρᾶγμα* (olisthēron ti prāgma), a philosophical idiom suggesting that human nature is prone to error or instability</note>. 

Let him also know that this **Physiology** <term>Physiology: Here, the term refers to "Natural Philosophy" or the study of the laws of nature, rather than the modern biological sense</term> lacked the **Author's** final hand. He surely would have corrected his own work had he survived his first attempts—which are like so many bursts of meditation not yet severely examined. We preferred that it exist in this state, neither perfected by him nor fully polished and refined <note>original: *exasciatam*, a woodworking metaphor meaning "hewn into shape with an axe"</note> by us, rather than...

<meta>catchword: mind</meta>

<summary>The editor explains his decision-making process in reconciling two inconsistent manuscripts, choosing to preserve Gilbert's original (if unpolished) structure rather than over-editing it. He notes that the author died before he could provide a final revision of this work on natural philosophy.</summary>

<keywords>manuscript collation, editorial method, William Gilbert, Physiology, natural philosophy, scholarly criticism, posthumous publication</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, moving from the admission of potential errors in the transcription to a discussion of the work’s chronological relationship to Gilbert’s famous book on the magnet. It notes that the current text may have been derived from a superior, now-lost manuscript that was once circulated among famous scholars.</meta>

# TO THE READER.

...to defraud the industry of the mind of a posterity that, having followed through so many aids of a later age, will have more successfully performed those things where **Gilbert’s** labor—chaste indeed, but perhaps not everywhere reaching its goal (as we are a race prone to slip, especially in things confidently <unclear>p</unclear> risked <note>original Greek: *ἀποκεκινδυνωμένοις*, referring to bold or hazardous intellectual ventures</note>)—might have failed. I raise one doubt which I do not untangle, and if it is of such great importance, I leave it to be unraveled by more fortunate conjecturers, and by those more instructed by that reading of **Gilbert** by which he has long been public: namely, whether this **Physiology** <term>Physiology: In this period, the term referred generally to "natural philosophy" or the study of the physical world and its laws, rather than just biology</term>, or his books **On the Magnet** (which won unanimous approval <note>original: *omne punctum*, a Latin idiom for "every vote"</note> among men of the most refined judgment, such as **Galileo** and others) were composed first. I seem to have gathered no slight evidence for these discussions about nature which might suggest the former, yet I also have reason to be more inclined toward the other side; thus, with my assent suspended, since I am permitted to determine nothing, I am forced to withhold judgment <term>to withhold judgment: The editor uses the Greek term *ἐπέχειν* (epéchein), a core concept in Skeptic philosophy regarding the suspension of belief when evidence is balanced</term>. 

But leaving those matters aside, let my discourse return to its purpose. Although I do not interpose my own judgment on the physical treatise <note>original Greek: *πραγματείᾳ*</note> which we now provide—deferring instead to the one who will engage in these speculations and who greedily and candidly studies nature <note>original Greek: *φυσιολογοῦντι*</note>—nevertheless, I do not wish to hide this fact: this work was formerly read in manuscript by great men of most celebrated fame, who do not deign to spend their literary leisure on worthless writings. It was, unless I am mistaken, read from a more correct copy than those which have reached us, since [to read the current ones would] fatigue the patience and tor[ture] the wit...

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, specifically discussing the reception of the work by those skilled in natural philosophy and the editor's commitment to preserving the legacy of the manuscripts' previous owners, Sir William Boswell and William Gilbert.</meta>

# TO THE READER.

...they would otherwise not have been willing to apply the seed <note>The Latin *sementum* suggests the sowing of ideas or the initial groundwork of an argument.</note>. Those men, endowed with a sharp intellect, especially in Physics <term>Physics: In this era, the term referred to "natural philosophy," the study of the physical world and the laws of nature</term>, have given testimony of labor not to be regretted in unrolling this work; for they are considered to have examined it in its entirety, and they cite here and there certain things that differ from common opinions, having confirmed them by their own calculation. Perhaps others who philosophize freely, and are not slaves to the Peripatus <term>Peripatus: A reference to the followers of Aristotle, known as Peripatetics, who were often criticized by 17th-century scientists for adhering too strictly to ancient dogma</term>, will find that it has set a value on the reading and—as is fitting with paradoxes—on careful meditation.

For me, it will be enough to have made this offering to the spirit <term>spirit: The original uses *Manibus*, or the "Manes," a Roman term for the souls of deceased loved ones</term> of the most noble **Boswell** with the diligence of this careful edition, so that I might not offend those spirits of **Gilbert** by the publishing of a writing which his brother <note>William Gilbert of Melford, who published his brother’s posthumous work *De Mundo* in 1651</note> dared to bring into the Royal Library, dedicating it to the Prince, after collecting it from scattered papers and arranging it into a system of art, by a method (as I said) not to be approved by all. 

Farewell, and expect from me shortly—God willing <note>original Greek: *θεῷ διδόντι* (theō didonti)</note>—several unpublished works of **Verulam** <term>Verulam: Francis Bacon, Baron Verulam, whose manuscripts were also handled by Boswell</term> of various subject matter and style in Latin, which, having been transferred to me from the paper chests of **Boswell’s** kindness in manuscript form, currently exist only in English. Farewell.

### CHAPTER ONE.

->*How, and by whom, Philosophy concerning nature and the principles of things began.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter Q featuring floral and leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>Those who believe that an exact knowledge of all things and sciences, or refined arts and sciences, were infused from above into the first humans in nature, seem to be foolish indeed—falling into a manifest error (though an honorable one, full of a certain piety, as they seek to honor the fame and memory of the first Fathers all the more). Moses, venerable by the very antiquity of his writings, shows that Jubal, after ten generations on earth, was the founder and master of Music; and Tubal-cain <note>Tubal-cain is a biblical figure from Genesis 4:22, traditionally credited as the first blacksmith.</note> the smith and craftsman of metalwork: (a highly necessary art;) while Music is most pleasant through the allurements of its melodies and harmony. Yet Natural Philosophy, the science of the stars <note>original: siderum scientia; i.e., astronomy</note>, and the other Mathematical arts still lay hidden; the earth was rough with forests, and sterile sand lay in the fields; men were naked, untaught, and wandering. At last, when a certain people was brought under control through governance—though with very few laws—and through the virtue and command of certain heroes, and as minds came together, inquiries began into speech, letters, and writings. And from such beginnings, when [they advanced] toward greater [things]...

progress, the art of Arithmetic came into the light, and at the same time the foundations of Geometry were laid: a little later, methods for keeping time <note>original: temporum habitae rationes; refers to the development of calendars</note> were established, and several observations of Astronomy were initiated. Much later, however, the principles of things were debated and disputed in various ways through the kingdoms of the Assyrians, Persians, and Egyptians—lands favored by a certain exceptional fertility and by the very convenient access provided by their rivers and ports. As soon as that ancient and perverse liberty (which nowadays we observe in certain untamed indigenous peoples <note>The author is likely referring to the "New World" indigenous populations being encountered by Europeans at the time of writing.</note>) was suppressed by the tyranny of strong men and the conquest of peoples, those empires were indeed established in which the arts necessary for cultivating civil life began to be investigated. And so, from here and there, wisdom grew among mortals as if by steps, and honor was established for the wise who inquired into the causes of divine and human things; such as the Magi among the Persians, the Chaldeans among the Babylonians and Assyrians, the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks for Indian ascetics and yogis</note> among the Indians, the Priests among the Egyptians, the Prophets among the Jews, the Druids among the Britons and Gauls, and the Philosophers among the Greeks. Finally, their minds began to be gripped by various cares and reflections—once they had noticed that the whole nature of things, situated upon the globe of the earth, was destined for perpetual mutations—concerning by what principles, or by what causes, the world (perpetually propagated through its individual members) would never entirely grow old, but instead, day by day, new faces of things would succeed the old, and the whole would be adorned by a continuous succession.

We are incited to live; but to violate life is impious, and to attack it by word or deed is the mark of a dissolute and backwards man. > *The Father himself did not wish the way of cultivation to be*
> *easy, sharpening mortal hearts with cares.*
> <note>original: "Haud facilem voluit pater ipse colendi / Esse viam, curis acuens mortalia corda." A quote from Virgil’s *Georgics* (Book 1, lines 121-123), suggesting that God/nature makes life difficult to force humans to innovate.</note>

Anyone who desires to gaze upon the face of an earlier age as if in a mirror—to see its way of life, arts, and customs—should sail to the West Indies <note>original: "Indos occidentales"; here referring to the indigenous peoples of the Americas as understood in the late Renaissance.</note>, specifically to those who live in the innermost inland parts and have learned neither the yoke of others nor the refined arts. Such were the Britons—though they were somewhat skilled in the art of war—during the war with Julius Caesar "the Briton" <note>original: "Iulio Cæsare Britannico"; likely referring to Caesar's campaigns in Britain.</note>; so too were the Germans, Gauls, Spaniards, and Italians before Rome flourished. Even Greece, which once called all others "Barbarians," recognized its own original barbarism; thus *times change, and we change with them.* <note>original: "tempora mutantur & nos mutamur in illis."</note> For in the principal cities of old, although they were quite large and vast with many houses, few of the more refined or <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>practical skills or engineering</note> were invented; truly, none were perfected or complete. They recognized almost no system of agriculture <note>original: "rem rusticam"</note>, except for what the forests provided of their own accord and what the livestock gave in the pastures. Nor did the fame of Heroes or Gods grow, nor their number increase, nor honors and worship be decreed for them, any more than what the discoveries and early principles of certain hidden individuals—born of such simplicity and need—unlocked for the common benefit of mankind.

The fame of Apollo is revered and renowned because he was the first to reveal the art of Medicine, which was previously unknown; as was the fame of Asclepius and Hippocrates. Cadmus invented the smelting of metals <note>original: "metallorum conflaturam"; the origin of metallurgy</note>; Ceres taught the cultivation of the earth and grain; Minerva gave the olive; Mercury, the lyre.

<header>METEOROLOGY</header>

## CHAPTER III.

### *Who first devised the fable of the elements, and how this opinion has endured until the present day.*

The Chaldeans, and the Magi who were their neighbors—the first of all in the disciplines of learning—had as their greatest desires the worship of the Supreme Deity and the understanding of the motions and influences of the heavens. But the Egyptians labored to learn more clearly the parts of this misty sky and the mortal world, along with their inherent causes and laws. Therefore, a certain matter was the beginning of things, and from it the four elements were then separated and many living beings were perfected. Manetho <note>original: "Manethus"; an Egyptian priest and historian (c. 3rd century BCE) often cited in antiquity as a source on Egyptian religion and history.</note> is the authority for this in his *Epitome of Natural History*, as is Hecataeus <note>original: "Hecatæus"; likely Hecataeus of Abdera, a Greek historian who wrote extensively about Egyptian philosophy and culture.</note> in his first book on *Egyptian Philosophy*. They claim that the Sun and the Moon were gods, called Osiris and Isis respectively, and that the Egyptians represented them through the scarab, the dragon <note>original: "draconem"; in this context, it refers to a serpent or a symbolic lizard-like creature common in ancient iconography.</note>, the hawk, and other animals. 

The Greeks, having been taught by these peoples, largely embraced this way of philosophizing, as did Anaxagoras and Empedocles. Finally, Aristotle—though he wrote much and indeed with a better method than anyone else (even if he said very little concerning such a vast foundation of the whole of natural philosophy, and that only in passing)—through the authority of the man and the learning of his books, which is by no means to be looked down upon, confirmed the opinion concerning the number, position, and qualities of the four elements. What was previously only a conceived opinion, he established in the minds of all as if it were implanted and innate, and it has remained so to this day, such that no one has ever wished or been able to uproot it; although there have always been some who deserted it to join the Academics <note>A school of philosophy that practiced skepticism, often questioning the definitive claims made by "dogmatic" schools like the Aristotelians.</note>. Eventually, however, at the urging of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician (c. 129–216 CE) whose theories on the four humors and elements dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> and the physicians who followed him, this entire earthly world <note>original: "inferior mundus"; literally "lower world," referring to the sublunary sphere or Earth, as opposed to the celestial spheres.</note> was seen, through a marvelous transformation, to be arranged into four elements in a far different manner than in the previous age. At that point, everyone [began to swear] by these

<header>BOOK I.</header>

...[Aristotle's] words had to be sworn by; thus, the form of teaching and debating was reduced to a religious standard. It was even commanded that these trifles be offered to the youth, and a decree entered every school of liberal arts: *"He himself said so,"* <note>original: "ipse dixit"; a phrase used to denote an unproven statement that rests solely on the authority of the speaker.</note> *"Aristotle said so,"* *"Galen says."* The student left instructed in what to say, but remained plainly ignorant and unaware of what to do. 

Hippocrates, the father of Medicine, acknowledged that philosophy of earth, water, air, and fire—which was debated in various ways by so many—yet he judged that it should not be greatly insisted upon. For instance, in his book *On the Nature of Man*, after he had recounted certain opinions, he noted that it was enough that these theories, handled with a certain "paltry Greek" <note>original: "græcula"; a diminutive, often pejorative term used to characterize the Greek style of intellectualizing as trivial or overly talkative.</note> chatter among the common people, tortured men's minds without producing any fruit. He argued that one should no longer search for the causes and principles of things, but rather every effort should be given so that those things handed down by our Ancestors might be properly understood and perceived. 

From this arose so many Interpreters, Commentators, and expositors, who for the most part composed entire volumes from the smallest and most absurd points. They seemed to have performed something remarkable in philosophy, and appeared to report a victory, if they could reconcile certain contradictions—which the philosopher [Aristotle] had mixed into his writings through error or ignorance—by using the veils of certain words and the disguises of distinctions, as if they were entirely consistent and perfect in every way. 

Therefore, through so many such defenders, this opinion was spread and grew daily in the minds of men, because it was easy and convenient, manifest even to common women, the bleary-eyed, and barbers. <note>The author uses a classical idiom—*lippis et tonsoribus*—meaning something is so obvious that even the half-blind and the town gossips in the barbershop know it.</note> For who, once they had grasped the four elements and the predominating qualities in each, and then their harmonies with one another, did not immediately claim to know everything? Who did not contend that they could probe the causes of things and had clearly explored the natures of diseases, medicines, plants, shrubs, and animals? But how feebly, how childishly, how arrogantly! The plague derived from these sources not only [invaded] the whole...

<header>METEOROLOGY</header>

This theory corrupted philosophy and the better-known science of the natural world, but by ascending high into the heavens, it also brought no small disaster to the laws of the stars. For astrologers, acting with more madness than mere poor judgment, assign elementary qualities to their Trigons <term>Trigons: Also known as "Triplicities," these are groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</term> and establish four categories to match the four elements. Many such fictions were invented by unlearned fortune-tellers within Astrology—once considered the queen of sciences. 

Furthermore, this philosophical madness has trickled down to even more foolish Alchemists. To better deceive people, they claim they can break down compounds and use fire to divide them, arrogantly and foolishly boasting that they can extract the four elements individually from these substances. 

This "elemental river" has likewise flooded the fields and gardens of all physicians—Greek, Arabic, and Latin alike—as well as every subterranean substance from which metals are mined. The situation has reached a point where no medicine can be put to use without its properties being defined by these elements. 

This is far different from the approach of the great Hippocrates, who never chased after the empty fantasies of these "primary elements" when trying to reveal hidden or doubtful truths. He would have rejected the constant appeals to the terms "hot," "cold," "moist," and "dry" <note>In Galenic medicine, these four "qualities" were believed to be the root of all health and disease.</note> if he had foreseen the errors, foolishness, and ruin that would later be introduced into the medical profession because of them. 

The same can be said of the illustrious Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician whose work on herbal medicine remained authoritative for over a millennium.</note>, who through great effort excellently recorded the powers of simples <term>Simples: Medicinal herbs or medicines consisting of only one ingredient.</term> for future generations, without any of this empty elemental arrogance. Yet, when Galen copied an entire book from him regarding the properties of simple medicines, he believed he had done something magnificent simply by inserting "elemental causes" into the descriptions.

Thus, these two patrons of philosophy, Aristotle and Galen, are now worshipped like gods and rule over all the schools. Aristotle (who, by some twist of fate, holds the same rank among philosophers as his pupil Alexander the Great held among the world's monarchs...)

To such an extent was this true that, with all others driven out, many of his monuments alone, or the dogmas of his followers and imitators, are now publicly viewed in all schools as trophies of great virtue. Nor was any "robed master" <term>purpuratus magister: Literally a teacher wearing purple, referring to high-ranking university professors or those holding prestigious chairs.</term> ever found who did not stubbornly defend every single conclusion or at least sweat to reconcile them and protect them from criticism.

For in the time of our ancestors, especially during the shipwreck of the liberal arts, the opinions of the elders so prevailed that one was allowed to know nothing except what the "fathers" judged to be true—unless one wished to be considered publicly insane. For this reason, from the "flood of the Goths" <note>A common Renaissance trope referring to the intellectual "darkness" following the fall of Rome to Germanic tribes.</note>, when everything shuddered with insane barbarity, until the time of our grandfathers, when literature and genius began to emerge again, nothing was discovered, almost nothing observed; everything lay hidden, obscured by mist and darkness. 

But this later age, having driven out the "barbarians," has taken care to restore the Greek and Latin authors to their former beauty and dignity. It remains that if those ancients wrote with less than total truth, and if our own **Sages** <note>original: *Sophi*</note> have been able to produce only minor or less famous results, they should be restored to health all the more diligently through better and more fruitful principles. These principles should not be despised for their novelty—for nothing that is true is truly new, but is perfect from eternity, though unheard of by wretched mortals—so that **Philosophy** might finally bear fruit. This is necessary so that philosophers are no longer judged by "barbarians," by the bold rabble-rousers of the **Paracelsians** <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), who rejected traditional Greek medicine in favor of alchemy and chemical remedies. ### CHAPTER IV.

#### *That the World from the Moon’s orbit to the center of the Earth is not filled with the four elements.*

Concerning the heights and the regions of the upper world, the sacred and venerable doctrine received from God—which marvelously examines the secrets of eternity far removed from our senses—teaches of a splendor and a magnificent essence of the Heavens that transcends the workings of nature. It speaks of the blessedness of the inhabitants of heaven and the happiness so greatly desired by weary mortals; it also proves that it is foolish for Philosophers to divide the World into the "celestial" and the "elementary" <note>In traditional Aristotelian thought, the "elementary" region (Earth) was made of four corruptible elements, while the "celestial" region (the stars) was made of a perfect fifth element.</note>. For this reason, more recent Philosophers also contend sharply regarding those bodies further away from us—the Moon, the Sun, the wandering stars <note>The planets</note>, and the fixed stars—claiming that they consist of a <term>fifth essence: Also known as the "quintessence" or "aether," this was believed to be an immutable, eternal substance distinct from the four earthly elements.</term> that is more noble. They do this all the more because all the <term>Peripatetics: Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle, who famously walked about while teaching.</term> establish that the nature of those heavenly bodies is simple and unchangeable, while they claim our own region, placed below the Moon, is inconstant, filthier, more infamous, and subject to perpetual changes, even if certain simple bodies might exist within it.

There has also been added a very serious error derived from the ingenuity and inventions of Mathematicians and Astronomers, though they were originally well-intended. While those scholars had proposed certain paths of lines and circles—by which the stars are carried within their limits—merely for the purpose of calculating their movements, certain idle pseudo-scholars <note>original: "scioli"</note>, always establishing their own distorted laws based on the labors and foundations of others, introduced physical, circular, concave, and convex spheres of wonderful craftsmanship. These are all the more "wonderful" because they can hardly be imagined as material objects without marvelous absurdities. We know, however, that these circles were rightly invented according to the hypotheses of the Ancients; and while those men demonstrated that the distant bodies were moved by these paths and lines...

Therefore, would anyone be right to divide the entire world into "the fruitful globe" and "these unfortunate islands"?

### CHAPTER V.

->*That there are not four elements.*<-

After it had been accepted by all that there are certain "elements"—though they are neither pure nor entirely simple—the Greek philosophers fought marvelous battles over the number and ownership of these elements. (This was either due to the simplicity of the human mind at the time, or because men who were competitive in the world of letters wanted to show off their new ideas to the public). Heraclitus championed only fire; but Thales of Miletus, taking the opposite view, admitted only water. Others established air as the primary element. Anaximander, however, proposed a certain middle substance between fire and air—denser than fire but thinner than air. These thinkers were quite stingy and strict, granting mortals only one element instead of four. Others, however, increased the number in various ways, such as fire and earth; while still others...

# ON METEOROLOGY

...fire, earth, and water; others, fire, earth, and air; Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, often associated with natural philosophy in Renaissance texts.</note> [proposed] air, water, and earth; Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who famously proposed the theory of the four classical elements.</note> [proposed] fire, air, water, and earth, from which bodies were thought to arise through condensation and separation. The Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</term> established those four elements, in which an inseparable matter exists that is subject to contrary qualities; from these, in turn, fire, air, water, and earth are transformed and altered. The differences between these are the primary qualities <term>primary qualities: the fundamental building blocks of matter in ancient physics—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</term>, which are perceived through touch. For they [the Peripatetics] do not wish the elements to be defined by whiteness or blackness, sweetness or bitterness, nor by any of the other contrary qualities that fall under the senses. Rather, because they have the power both to act upon one another and to be acted upon—for they mix together and turn into one another through their qualities—they are distinguished by heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, with the former two being active and the latter two being passive. 

And these are the four rules of qualities established by Aristotle; who says that since there are only four, and they sustain only four pairings (for the same thing cannot be both hot and cold, nor both moist and dry), there will certainly be four combinations of elements: heat and dryness, heat and moisture, and again, cold and dryness, cold and moisture. Thus, the number of elements will be four. For fire is hot and dry, air is hot and moist, water is cold and moist, and earth is cold and dry. He established the four-fold number of elements based on the combination of four qualities in each, through the dominance <note>original: "excellentiam"</note> of one; such as by the predominance of heat in fire, moisture in air, cold in water, and dryness in earth. But he could also have established four other elements in this way: where dryness prevails over a milder heat; where intense heat is paired with mild moisture; where moisture conquers a weaker cold; and where cold is quite rigid with less dryness. But as for the globe of the earth, with [all these things] flowing together in it...

However, what those qualities commonly called "elementary" are, how they are to be understood, how they are changed, or how they exist in mixtures, must be discussed in another place. 

Now we must inquire concerning the subjects of the elements themselves: how they exist, and whether they truly exist in nature. Since the number and condition of the elements has been determined, they further insist that four elements exist in their own seats within the sublunary world <term>sublunary world: the region of the universe below the moon, which ancient science believed was the only place subject to change, decay, and the mixing of elements.</term> as exact masses of simple bodies, by which that entire space is filled through certain spheres and regions, as it were. 

Yet all parts of the earth, even those dug out from the deepest places, show a nature other than that of a "simple body" of earth; this is true in every region, in every zone—whether southern or northern—and in islands as well as the continent. Their "pure water" also seems to exist nowhere; for we perceive through taste that all water is affected by some flavor. But every flavor is produced by some admixture of another nature, different from a simple moisture. Indeed, all seas are salty; certain lakes and springs gush from the earth both salty and bitter; some contain the taste of vitriol <term>vitriol: a historical term for sulfate minerals, often recognized by their metallic or sour taste.</term>, alum, sulfur, bitumen <note>original: "bituminis"; a naturally occurring petroleum substance like asphalt.</note>, or nitre <term>nitre: also known as saltpeter, a mineral used in gunpowder and fertilizers.</term>; even those waters which are called "sweet" have a flavor borrowed from the earth. Therefore, all water is a mixture, not a simple element. 

Air is the least simple of all, and is not constant in its own nature; for it participates in infinite mixtures, whether you look at the lower atmosphere or the upper. That there are no more than four elements...

## CHAPTER VI.

->*That Simple Aristotelian Elements Do Not Exist in Our World.*<-

They <note>Referring to the Aristotelian philosophers.</note> profess that the elements are the principles and "mothers" of things, that they produce and nourish those concrete bodies, and that their closer and neighboring parts are mixed among themselves in mutual substances. Yet they claim that each element retains its whole and pure dignity, and is not corrupted in its entirety or even for the most part; they assert that earth is preserved uncorrupted, and likewise water, air, and fire. 

Since they were never able to dig out these "forms" of things or bring them down from the heavens so that they could be known by the eyes and senses—even though they insisted the entire region below the moon <term>sublunary region: according to ancient science, the area between the Earth and the Moon where all change and decay occurs</term> was so filled with these elements that they contended not even the smallest bit of void or a tiny portion of foreign substance could be found—each philosopher nonetheless fashions flimsy and feigned descriptions according to his own feeling. They lie about nature as if it were known and understood by them. 

Earth—if indeed it is an element like any other—is thought to be simple and firm because of its stability and coherence, and because it is not corrupted by any harms from its neighboring "concave" <note>In Aristotelian cosmology, elements were arranged in concentric spheres; the "concave" refers to the inner surface of the surrounding element's sphere (the air), while the "convex" refers to the Earth's outer surface.</note> but only suffers change on its outer surface. Yet, earth has never yielded even the slightest portion of such a "simple" mass. This provides a wonderful opportunity for thinking that its entire nature has always been variously mixed, and was never genuine and simple in the past, just as it is not now. Therefore, since they do not know where else to seek this element, nor can they even imagine another place for it (for it was no longer permitted to tell fables or lie), they admit with great embarrassment that the bed of the sea is the location of the watery element; yet they do so timidly and hesitantly, lest their madness should become known by their own evidence.

# CHAPTER VII.

## On Fire.

First, we must indeed consider the nature of fire: whether it is that body extending across a vast distance from the circle of the Moon down to the air. We begin with that "fiery fable" <note>original: "ignita fabula"; the author is being skeptical of the traditional scientific model of his time.</note> which claims that the highest and first part of our elemental world is a sphere of fire. This was the opinion held by Ocellus Lucanus (a student of Pythagoras), Hippocrates, and Aristotle. However, Aristotle was more uncertain, sometimes identifying the highest region as air, sometimes as the *fuel for fire* <term>hypekkauma: a Greek term used by Aristotle to describe the upper atmosphere which, though not fire itself, is so hot and dry that it is ready to burst into flame</term>, and sometimes not as fire at all.

Those ancient opinions were originally formed regarding the fiery substance of the heavens and the stars. Because of the effects the heavens have on us, and because of the burning flames and "fiery impressions" <note>Meaning phenomena like meteors, comets, or lightning.</note> darting about in the heights, the ancients concluded that fire must exist as a distinct element. This happened after the "fiery force" was rejected <note>original: "explosa," literally "hissed off stage" or driven out; the author suggests fire was removed from the definition of the eternal heavens and relegated to a lower, elemental sphere.</note> from the celestial orbits in the views of certain philosophers. Indeed, all of antiquity easily believed—with some philosophers even encouraging the idea—that the entire upper world remained boiling and hot, simply because heat seemed to flow down to us from the Sun and the stars.

*Ether* <note>original: "Æther"</note>, in fact, is an ancient name that means the same thing as fire. Anaxagoras thought the highest place was full of fire and that the force found there should be called ether. On this point, all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, known for walking while teaching.</note> tell a sort of lie regarding their version of fire. They imagine that this element, composed of extremely thin and boiling parts, fills the entire upper space all the way to the sphere of the Moon. Yet they claim it is not so harmful to the other elements that the entire lower world would catch fire—which would seem the likely result. They invent a "pure and peaceful" nature for it, as if heat would not affect a body it is touching, and as if the whole lower world, enclosed within this structure, would not grow hot when touched by fire. But even those wise men...

<header>BOOK I.</header>

...the fire-bringers <note>original: *flammiferi*; likely referring to those philosophers who argue for the existence of a celestial sphere of fire</note> say, the highest region of the air grows hot due to the proximity of fire, and glows with perpetual little sparks and fiery "impressions" <note>The term "impressions" was used in Renaissance science to describe transient atmospheric phenomena like meteors, comets, or lightning.</note>. How contradictory these claims are! For it seems probable that the remaining elements would have been ignited; since fire—whose source and fuel are not consumed—if it ignited or heated the closer things in any way, would not be contained by certain limits. It would be restrained by no natural laws from progressing further and spreading like a wildfire.

Therefore, it would necessarily have raged further and more distantly through the air. Furthermore, the proportion of the elemental form is always more suitable to be overcome by a dominant quality. For larger spheres overcome smaller ones, as the smaller ones yield more to a narrow space and are constrained. I do not wish to introduce arguments—though they are suitable enough—from the likeness of other bodies which, when they are long enveloped on all sides by a dominant heat, grow hot in every part down to the very center.

Let us pass to the convex surface of the fire, adjacent to the sky. What kind of compatibility is there between a boiling and burning body and the "incorruptible and divine essence" of the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, so named because they walked about (*peripatos*) while discussing philosophy</term>? How can an active and instigating force agree with one that is peaceful? Or a pressing force with that which nowhere gives way? Or something breaking in where entry is not allowed?

Nor indeed, as some desire, does fire seem "scarcely foreign" to the substance of heaven. It is even less true that it contains the principles of light within itself, since above the air no light exists, nor does it flow there from some other source. Nor will it be enough to solve the problem by saying it is not an "enemy" to the heaven because it cannot harm it with any force. In that case, it would have been arranged by nature either in vain, or imprudently, or shamefully: that an active force of the greatest magnitude and efficiency (in the view of the Peripatetics) should be joined to the immutable heaven to no purpose.

All these things are grasped speculatively <note>original: *phantastice*; meaning based on imagination or abstract theory rather than physical evidence</note> without any certain evidence—such as the idea that a fiery nature is always the hottest and rarest, even without a solid container or supporting fuel. Now indeed, when exhalations are raised from the earth into the heights, to which we also notice moisture is joined, and from which—according to their opinion <note>the opinion of the Aristotelians</note>—burnings and fiery "impressions" <note>original: *impressiones*; a Renaissance term for transient atmospheric phenomena like meteors or lightning</note> are generated: these conglomerations of vapors, I say, cross and pass through the region destined for the element of fire, and they mostly hold their seat and place within it.

As we have observed more often—both in the earlier years of 1572 and 1577 <note>These dates refer to two major celestial events: the Supernova of 1572 in Cassiopeia and the Great Comet of 1577. These observations were revolutionary because they proved these objects were further away than the Moon, contradicting Aristotle.</note>—that splendid one and this "tailed" impression <note>The comet</note> penetrated far above the aforementioned highest region of the air. It would be necessary for these to be thinned, dissipated, or set on fire over such a long time and such a long journey by the very rare dissolutions and the penetrating, burning forces of that region. But it is most absurd to claim that meteors and comets remain there, or are gathered, generated, and moved, before they catch fire and become known to men by their own lights. 

But the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking about the *peripatos* (walkway) of the Lyceum in Athens</term> must be pardoned; they observed the heights and locations of comets less accurately, and being inexperienced, they brought forth a wavering and uncertain judgment about remote things. They relied more on the probable deceits of words and suppositions than on the things themselves. Furthermore, if fiery matters—whether flaming, or heating without flame, or only elementary and material <note>original: *hylææ*, from the Greek *hyle*, meaning matter or substance</note> substances—remained there, the depth from the lunar orb to the upper air would be so great, and would have such a profound and opaque material force across a height of so many miles, that it surely would have removed all appearance of the stars from our sight: as would be easy to demonstrate.

But no mind can even conceive how that thinnest substance—through that insane and fictional rapid daily revolution of the first mover <note>original: *primi mobilis*; in the old geocentric model, this was the outermost sphere that moved all others</note>, since they claim everything is drawn around by force—would not collide under that violent impetus, be disturbed, and be mixed with the essence of heaven, which (as they claim) is most subtle and thin. This is particularly problematic since all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note>, taught by the movement of Comets and fiery "impressions" <note>original: *impressionum ignearum*; transient atmospheric phenomena</note> which are incited according to the rule of the first mover, contend that not only the summit of the fire, but its entire mass and all the upper air, are snatched into a circle every single day.

Why then, moreover, should the motion of fire not coincide with the sphere of the Moon? For the progressions of these impressions do not align with the Moon’s velocity toward the east—neither in the fire nor in the air—but rather with the motion of the first mover toward the west. Those who place fire in the upper region act poorly when they claim that comets are formed there and that vapors are ignited by the element of fire. For they are ignorant of both the generation and the locations of comets; moreover, fire would consume the entire air just as it would ignite the material of comets, or it would dissipate the comets' solid form. 

Those who believe the daily revolution belongs to the first mover, and not to the Earth, dream up heat in the element of fire because of the velocity of circular motion. # BOOK I.

...is introduced? Can the element of fire—separated from the other elements by its physical position, located in the higher regions next to the heavens—truly be called an element of mixed bodies? For just as it is distant and separated from those bodies by the intervening air, it is placed there in vain. Fire cannot be called an element because it requires fuel <note>original: *pabulo*; literally "food" or "fodder," here meaning the material consumed by combustion</note>, nor does it persist or endure by itself in the nature of things. All fire is nothing other than intense heat, violently devouring moisture. When a vapor <note>original: *halitus*; a breath or exhalation</note> is ignited, it becomes a flame. This flame does not ascend to the higher regions as if seeking a "fiery home" <note>Aristotle argued that elements have a "natural place," with fire's place being the highest sphere</note>, but rather it is carried away from the matter remaining below by an expansive motion and the release of moisture; it is driven in the opposite direction and lifted up by the thicker air. 

Furthermore, this "element" remains idle, even though it is supposedly the most active of all elements. It generates nothing and alters nothing; it merely fills space and presses against the heavens because it does not look down toward lower things, nor is it turned toward them. It cannot even protect the air around the poles from perpetual freezing—so much so that those who inhabit the cold zones have no reason to fear the air catching fire. 

In fact, the tip of a flame rises more strongly and steadily toward the heights in cloudy and thick air than it does in thinner air or during the most extreme cold of winter. Just like a flame, no fire exists in our world that is constant and certain; instead, it is born through a perpetual generation of successions. It perishes when the moisture is gone, or as the fire dissipates, the heat and everything else vanishes. 

Indeed, when bodies containing moisture are heated more violently, they emit smoke from the dissolving of that moisture, which is quite hot at the very moment it exits; eventually, as it heats up more and more, it is called a flame. This appears nowhere more clearly than in a small iron rod, which first grows hot from the fire and has the temperature of rising smoke, but afterward appears ignited and glows. In the former case <note>the smoke/flame</note>, there is the burning of a dissolved body; in the latter <note>the iron</note>, the burning of a firm and compact body that is not easily dissipated. Therefore, a flame also moves because it consists of fluid and wandering matter, and it does not remain unless...

But in what way, or by what paths, does it descend? Or how can something be called down across such long distances when it stubbornly flies upward and strives to remain in the highest seats? For things which are moved toward the heights by their nature come to rest in those heights. 

Furthermore, if fire were torn away or driven down from on high, a vacuum would necessarily be left behind. # BOOK I.

...in certain places clouds and hail fall, and there is perpetual cold on the highest mountains, while there is less cold on the lower ones, which are nevertheless colder than the plains; and the plains and valleys are colder than the interior parts of the earth, in which there is neither ice nor frost, but warmth, heat, and even fires. For the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who believed the universe was organized into concentric spheres of elements</note> themselves establish fire in the upper region as its own proper seat because flame tends toward higher things. Yet this is false and poorly understood, since flame in the upper air is poured out in every direction, and sometimes extends itself sideways and sometimes downward. Therefore, just as such a vast ignited body—the **element of fire**—appears nowhere and is of no use in the nature of things, and is wrongly accepted as a "body" rather than a "quality," so it is most foolishly assigned to such a vast space. This will be understood more clearly when we speak about heat. **Moses**, in **Genesis** and the account of the creation of the world, does not acknowledge it, nor does he explain anything of the sort from the doctrine of the Ancients (in which he was most well-versed), nor from sacred understanding or revelation. Thus, it is foolishly and impiously imagined by many philosophers, based on certain trifles of reasoning, that such a thing hangs over us or occupies the heavens.

**Fire** is the intensity of heat. **Flame** is the intensity of heat in a thinner moisture <note>original: *humido rariori*; refers to vapors or gasses</note> when the vapor heats up more vehemently. And in a thick, compact, and dense thing, such as a glowing coal or glowing iron, fire does not destroy the physical property <note>OCR reads "politatem," likely a misspelling or misreading of "qualitatem" (quality) or "soliditatem" (solidity)</note> while the body remains unharmed; but the acquired property is changed through fire, since glowing iron, as it returns to its normal state, conceives another property from the earth.

Those who established that heat is produced in the upper region from the **celestial rotation** <note>The friction supposedly caused by the spinning of the heavenly spheres</note> thought that fire was made from the air only by that whirling and, as it were, friction; they doubted whether fire naturally existed there. ## CHAPTER VIII.

->On the Air.<-

**A**ir seems to be accepted into the number of the elements not without cause, as it is necessary for every animal and highly desired for living; this is even acknowledged by those who have rejected fire from the nature of things. But now, we must further investigate whether air is truly endowed with those qualities which the entire school of the **Peripatetics** <note>Aristotle's followers</note> claims it possesses; and whether it exists in such a way that it fills the vast space above us. They propose that air is a certain body arranged in a middle position between fire and the waters, being naturally hot and "most moist." For them, it was not enough to say the air is merely moist; it had to be "most moist" so that it might have its own predominant and "conquering" quality <note>The Aristotelian system assigned two qualities to each element, one being "dominant": Earth (cold/dry), Water (cold/moist), Air (hot/moist), and Fire (hot/dry)</note>. Just as they established heat in fire, cold in water, and dryness in earth, so they decided that moisture must excel in the air. One might wonder where on earth the inventors of this long-accepted "aerial philosophy" actually lived; if they lived in hot and drier regions, they would have denied moisture; if in cold regions, they would have undoubtedly denied heat.

But it appears that they were Greeks <note>The author suggests that early philosophical theories were influenced by the specific Mediterranean environment of the Greek thinkers</note>, people of the sea or islands, living in humid and warm regions. But now let us see, not what the fourth or fifth climate <term>clima</term> <note>In ancient and medieval geography, a "clima" was a latitudinal zone of the Earth characterized by the length of its longest day</note> shows in certain places due to the more moderate light of the Sun, or from their situation and position near seas and rivers; rather, it will be helpful to contemplate the entire globe of the lands, so that this aerial, all-encompassing, spherical element may be understood. However, it is not found to be so scorched everywhere as the simplicity of the Ancients long ago led us to believe <note>Ancient geographers often claimed the equatorial "Torrid Zone" was a wasteland of fire where no one could survive, a view corrected by Age of Discovery explorers</note>. In the regions nearby, however, there is a more proper balance of temperature, more favorable for sustaining the life of animals and plants, as they are further removed from the summit of heaven (the giver of daily light), and the rays descend at less of a right angle at midday. 

But in the extreme **Northern** <note>original: *Boreali*</note> and likewise the **Southern** <note>original: *Australi*</note> Zone, all things are frozen and stiff, and they shudder with continuous snows, especially in winter, amidst the horrendous silence of the nights. For this reason, **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath who argued that air was naturally cold</note> wished for the element of air to be considered the coldest of all. Either, therefore, some unknown and hidden force exists which, in those furthest Zones, changes so vast an element and all the air—which is otherwise of a warm and benign nature—into something coldest beyond all excess and hostile to mortals; or, by some great occasion, heat has receded from those parts, so that the form of so great a spherical element is now defective and unequal; or this must be a "fifth element," or something else vehemently contrary to air. For neither the opposing face of heaven, nor the northern stars, nor any celestial bodies in the Southern Zone, nor hidden planets, nor any occult causes could possess so great a power over the air...

# BOOK I.

...extended for a thousand paces, it is stained black at one end for only half a foot, though the rope was otherwise white.

But it is a wonder how **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose system of physics dominated European thought until the Scientific Revolution</note> deformed the machinery of the element of air with his opinions. In its upper part, he wants it to be dry: <note>original: οὐκ ἐστὶν ἀὴρ μόνον, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον πῦρ</note> *it is not only air, but rather fire*; therefore, it is not "hot and moist" <note>In the Aristotelian system, every element is defined by two qualities; air was traditionally hot and moist</note>. He also wants the lower region to be moist from rising vapors, and he established the middle region as cold. Thus, the whole element—that vast primordial source of nature—perishes and undergoes a total change: the upper air is transformed by fire, the lower by the earth, and the middle by some phantom of an opinion. 

But our **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, so named because they supposedly walked about while teaching</note>, having understood from certain signs and from the meteorological formations born of cold that the air slightly further up is violently frigid, fabricated a certain **Antiperistasis** <term>Antiperistasis</term> <note>A term in late-medieval and Renaissance physics describing the supposed intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite (e.g., heat being "pushed" inward by surrounding cold)</note>. This was more than childish, imagining a surrounding pressure of opposites, whereby cold is supposedly squeezed and intensified from all sides by the heat above and below. From this, they claim, comes the immense and perennial cold of the middle region of the air, even in hot seasons; from this come hail and icy rains, and raindrops that are larger in summer than in winter. No greater disgrace than this has ever been committed to writing in the name of **Philosophy**, nor ever admitted. 

And from this, it easily appears what madness and wretched reasoning one must resort to so that such an absurd fable might stick in the minds of men. For that cold could not have been increased in any way by nearby heat. For although heat trapped within solid bodies may be set further ablaze by a surrounding cold (if all vents are closed and there is fuel), so that bodies often burn more fiercely through antiperistasis; nevertheless, it does not follow that a cold or less-hot body—even a solid one, and much less one that is fluid and thin <note>Referring to the "thin" or "tenuous" nature of air compared to solids</note>—is cooled further by a surrounding heat, or that it intensifies its internal cold. But neither are the parts of the air so...

What? Should the simple, pure, and uncorrupted element of air suffer such a great, contrary, and troublesome force in its very depths, and as if in its middle bowels, unjustly through antiperistasis? 

But it is now known and perceived for certain that the higher places and cloud-bearing mountains, such as the higher **Alps**, shudder with intolerable cold no more in summer than in winter. In the higher place dedicated to air, nothing of the sort exists—or rather, no "airy qualities" exist there. The highest mountains of *Sweden, Norway, Scythia, Lapland, and Greenland* are inaccessible due to snow; and all those to the north which are high like the Alps have even their lowest valleys covered in snow and ice, with the bottommost air being extremely frozen. Does the upper air there shudder with cold because of antiperistasis and the surrounding of opposites? Moreover, how could the heat of the lower region, rising to a height of two or three miles in only the warmer climates of the world, increase the immense cold of such a vast space—indeed, confirm it everywhere throughout the entire internal vastness of the air from pole to pole? They want the air to be hot and very moist, so that it predominates...

### BOOK I.

...of the [governing] qualities, one should be granted to each element. Does moisture, then, become more moist because of fire? For it must come either from fire or from water. But water cannot give more than what is already in itself; fire, on the other hand, would sooner induce dryness. But these phantasms and the sordid dross <note>original: "sordes & scoriæ"—literally the "filth and slag" or waste products of a smelting process</note> of errors are not worthy of any refutation. By heat, water is dissolved into air; how, then, is water to be forced out of air? Perhaps through cold? If this were true, the entire force of the northern air would turn into water because of the cold, and it would rain perpetually among the **Northern peoples**, the **Swedes**, the **Muscovites**, and the **Scythians** <note>Scythians was a term often used by early modern writers to refer to the nomadic peoples of Central Asia or Great Tartary</note>. Yet, throughout the entire winter, there are no rains there; the air, perpetually frozen, remains clear. Everywhere in the world, air is only with difficulty converted into water, or even imbued with the qualities of water. 

Dry animal bladders, distended by air and submerged with a sufficient weight in a spring for an entire month, emerge still full of air; the air is not changed at all by the power of the water. This is also true when a vessel with a wide opening, full of air, is held under water with its mouth turned downward. What, therefore, is the material of rains? It is not air, but **vapor**, which is hot and thick, and which thickens into a cloud through accumulation and the agitation of contrary winds, and is then dissolved into water. Sometimes, the thinner air, having been weakened by those vapors, returns to a watery nature. 

Thin and pure air is not thickened by cold, nor does it return to vapor or water; the thinnest air is always penetrating and subtle, even in the greatest frosts. The force of this thinner air is very often absorbed by the earth, in whose bowels it thickens when mixed with vapors. For just as every airy force exhales from the water and the earth, so too are certain parts of it called back into the earth, as we shall demonstrate at some point. For the most part, the innate spirit is carried to and fro above the exterior parts and nearby spaces of the entire globe. Air, therefore, arises from water through heat, and water from air; but first, that air must be converted into a thicker vapor. Thin air is made from water,

...just as water thins into vapor, and vapor into air; so must air first be converted into vapor before it is reduced back into water. This conversion is not caused by cold, but by the moisture within the air; for it arises from air that is vapid, thick, and misty when heat is withdrawn—heat which, having been driven further away by a stronger heat, strikes against the thick vapor, as is seen in **distilling vessels** <note>original: "vasis stillatoriis"—the glass or metal apparatus used in early chemistry and alchemy to condense steam into liquid</note>. Otherwise, intense cold would produce continuous rains across the entire globe and sea, since all air in the upper regions is chilled and gradually passes into the deepest cold, both in the **Middle Zone** <note>The Torrid Zone or the tropics</note> and in the temperate and extreme Zones. But in the Middle Zone, there are droughts, which arise from the heat greatly thinning the lower regions, and the intense cold above does not condense these thin substances. In the **farthest Zones** <note>The Arctic and Antarctic circles</note>, there are perpetual colds in winter, so that no abundant vapors arise, nor is the air obscured by thick rain clouds. Therefore, it is manifest that water arises when, as the heat lets up, vapor thickens into water and is driven together by a flowing; but in no way is water constricted out of air by cold when pure, thinned air has lost its innate heat.

# BOOK I.

...to all things whole, in a form absolute and perennial. For they <note>likely referring to the philosophers or "physiologists" mentioned previously</note> constitute a full and whole bodily nature from the elements extending from the circle of the Moon to the center of the earth. But concerning the opinion conceived above regarding the element of fire, it has been discussed previously. Now we must speak of the air, which, since it is nothing other than **moisture** <note>original: "humor"</note>, thinned into **spirit** <term>spirit (spiritum): in early science, this referred to a highly refined, vaporous, or gas-like state of matter</term> by heat, does not truly and primarily exist by itself in the nature of things like the earth does; rather, it is only an **effluvium** <term>effluvium: an invisible "outflow" or discharge of vapors from a solid body</term> of the earth—moisture extended into a broader nature and a poured-out substance. For when heat drives moisture, or when the lights of the stars—especially the Sun—strike this globe of ours, vapors rise up, and that body (which is rare among us) grows by powerful causes that breathe out and extend the moisture.

The Sun, on account of various movements in nature, illuminates everything from all sides—either by its daily revolution or its annual course—and ignites heat with its light, raising up airy matter throughout the entire world: in the **Middle Zone** <note>The Tropics</note>, as well as in more temperate places, and in the extreme regions or under the poles themselves. For these regions, which by themselves would all shiver in perpetual frost at their edges and find a certain warmth only through internal spirits conceived from the earth, actually grow warm from more vehement rays of light. This happens either because of a more direct overhead position, as within the Tropics; or because they are not far off, as in temperate places; or in the furthest regions, because of the lingering and long duration of light above the horizon, as usually happens during their longest days of four, five, or six months. In these cases, the moisture, driven by light, exalts itself. Therefore, air is chiefly generated by the Sun, which, as the principal author of all spirits, creates a varying system of air according to its annual motion.

## CHAPTER X.
->*On what Air is.*<-

Air, called "ether" by the ancient poets, and called *aithēr* <note>original Greek: αἰθήρ</note> by Zoroaster as well as Orpheus, constitutes an element along with fire, water, and earth. But those who distinguish air from ether believe they differ greatly from each other. They maintain that ether is superior in its location, its nature, and its excellence; they designate nothing else by the term "ether" than the spread-out substance of the heavens or the celestial spheres, which they contend is more perfect, incorruptible, and almost **impassible** <term>impassible: a philosophical term meaning incapable of being changed or affected by external forces</term>. There are some who take it to be the element of fire, among whom is Anaxagoras, and they think it is named from the word "to burn" <note>original Greek: αἴθειν (aithein)</note>; others say it comes from "to run always" <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ θέειν (aei theein)</note> due to its perpetual motion. For this reason, Apuleius <note>a 2nd-century Roman author and philosopher</note> says that by the name "ether," the heaven itself, the stars, and the entire starry framework are understood—not, as some think, because it is fiery and burning, but because it is rotated in rapid courses, although the word *aitho* <note>original Greek: αἴθω</note> also signifies heat or burning. Thus, certain controversies of no real importance exist regarding these words, since ether is often used for air, and sometimes for a more sublime material, while air designates the matter poured closely around us.

But we shall dispute not about words or the names given by others, but about the things themselves: what it is that nature has placed in the highest location. There are those who think that the ether in the heights and the air below do not differ in their basic matter, but only in their form, which was granted to each part by the creator of all matter; they argue that the matter of both is a **primary flow** <note>original: primarium fluorem</note>. However, because we have truly admitted the existence of a separate **vacuum** <term>vacuum: empty space; the author is likely arguing against the contemporary "plenist" view that the universe is entirely filled with matter</term>, we shall declare that the whole world is not filled by any such perpetual flow. For the sources and heaps of materials are the planetary globes themselves, and the "flows" <note>original: fluores</note> are poured around them or sometimes called forth further away; these are what we call **effluvia** <term>effluvia: invisible "outflows" or emissions of vaporous matter from a solid body</term>.
