# C H A P T E R XI.

## On the Motion of Air.

When discussing the motion of air, we must speak not of that straight-line elemental movement described by the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who were known for walking about while teaching</term>, which proceeds from heaviness and lightness. That is truly nothing more than simple motion—either a displacement into wider spaces or a return to its own starting point. Rather, we must investigate the causes of other impulses that occur within this fluid nature due to various circumstances. First, we must address its circular motion, by which it is thought to be carried from east to west in accordance with the motion of the *primum mobile* <term>primum mobile: the "first moved" sphere in ancient astronomy, believed to drive the rotation of all other celestial spheres</term>. For since comets, or other luminous phenomena which were thought to reside in the air, appeared to take a course from east to west along with the revolution of the heavens, it seemed likely that those "meteors" <note>original: "meteora." In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including comets and lightning</note> were carried along by the rotation of the air. Indeed, such a motion seems common to them as it is to the "wandering stars" <note>the planets</note> and the fixed stars, even if they appear to lean toward other regions of the sky due to their own specific impulses. <margin>Chapter 7 of this book.</margin> But we have taught elsewhere that neither the thin celestial spheres nor the air—which of all bodies around us is the least capable of being led—can be gripped in its entirety, led, or dragged by celestial causes. It can, however, be poured out, agitated, or disturbed; it cannot be rolled and carried around fixed poles while its consistency remains intact and its entire substance stays continuous. Furthermore, its own specific motion—the force of its speed, its spreading out, and its shifting—does not occur because of its distance from the earth. For since comets—even those located above the Moon—progress sometimes faster and sometimes slower against the daily rotation at both greater and lesser distances, they do not derive the speed or slowness of their motion from their distance or from the sphere in which they wander. For it has been observed that in a higher region, or one more remote from the globe of the Earth, they sometimes move faster than in a lower region, and sometimes slower. As for the fact that more often above the Moo—

For if the *primum mobile* <term>primum mobile: the "first moved" sphere in ancient astronomy, believed to drive the rotation of all other celestial spheres</term> were to give motion to the globe of air above the poles of the world, the sphere of the Moon, being more closely connected to it, would roll the air around its own poles—yet this has never appeared in any of the observations of comets. Therefore, it is more credible that comets are not driven by the daily revolution of the air, if they were to exist below the Moon; nor did nature divide bodies in such a way that those above the Moon were of another, more excellent nature—composed of vaults and spheres—since in both spaces, similar things occur, rising and setting. It remains, therefore, that they be left in their own places where they originated (where, in these empty spaces, there is no carrying or drawing along, and no resistance, because there is no real force, and the entire matter together with all its outflows is far distant from the transit <note>or "passing by"</note> of the Earth). Thus, they only *appear* to be carried toward the west, like the rest of the celestial bodies. However, when they are driven by the rays of the Sun—the actor of the world’s motion—they proceed as if by a certain innate and peculiar process.

Therefore, there is no reason for the air to be rotated by a daily turning. We must see, then, what other motions there are, and by what forces they are impelled. Air of itself has no constant or certain motion; however, it is moved when moisture, dissolved by heat, is converted into air—or rather, into a more rarefied moisture, for all air is moisture <note>The author adheres to the traditional view that air is a form of evaporated or "thinned" water</note>. When water is dissolved into air more violently and abundantly, that air is moved, taking its beginning from its origin, and the newly born air pushes the air closest to it. In this way, the steam from boiling pots, or the "spirit" <note>original: "spiritus," here meaning air or steam</note> in the instrument from Hero's *Pneumatics* <term>Hero's Pneumatics: *Spiritalia*, a famous work by Hero of Alexandria (1st century AD) describing steam-powered inventions and the properties of air</term>, breaks out with a very powerful force as the moisture inside grows hot, much like the action of strongly compressed bellows. ...in a fireplace of coals, smoke is stirred up, pushing against nearby objects and driving rotating instruments <note>This likely refers to "smoke jacks," which were vanes in chimneys turned by rising heat to rotate roasting spits</note>. From the Sun, the earth and sea grow warm, and from there, vapors rise up; the earth also, within, dissolves moisture by its implanted heat. After these are carried into the air and the force of their expansion <note>original: "fusionis," meaning the spreading out or melting into a fluid state</note> toward the higher regions ceases, that filled region discharges itself into the next, and so it proceeds until it contains itself within the limits of the outflows with equal abundance, or until the motion of the dissolving moisture settles. Winds are stirred up from the earth itself, from the light of the Sun (which pushes most of all), from the lights and peculiar forms of the planets and stars, and also from the Moon—not so much from its borrowed light as from the effort of its unique power and <term>synentelechia</term> <note>original: "synentelechia." A term derived from the Greek "entelechy," referring here to an internal driving force or the Moon's specific "vitalizing" influence over fluids</note>. For when the tide of the Ocean is moved by the Moon, the air is also pushed by that motion, since the spirit <note>original: "spiritus," referring to thin, energetic vapors or gasses</note> of the rising Ocean exhales into the air. In this way, spirits are summoned even from the firmer earth by the Moon. Regarding the annual winds, as well as why the wind might blow here now and elsewhere at another time from one region or another of the Horizon’s limit or point, and what the true cause of each individual wind is—matters which we place far differently than the common Astrologers and Philosophers—we shall clearly declare when we discuss Meteors.

For this reason, the force of the winds does not climb higher, and clouds in the upper region often seem to be at rest, while other clouds in the lower regions are driven most swiftly, and the air above the face of the earth is most violently pushed; this is the true cause of this lateral <note>sideways</note> motion.

[...that] bodies are simple, pure, and untainted by the mixture or decay of other bodies; pure water—clear, limpid, and infected by no odor or taste—would seem to be either the element itself, or to approach very closely to the nature of an element. But this pure water reveals itself in a smaller quantity than the massive scale of an element requires. In truth, other waters, which are thought to possess a certain mixture, prevail in the nature of things and dominate far and wide: such as the vast seas, which are perceived by our senses as salty and turbulent. For this reason, Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose "four elements" theory dominated science for centuries</note> placed the home of the element of water in the sea; yet he did so with a wavering and uncertain opinion. For the place we see the sea occupy is not the "place of the sea," but rather the place of water. It seems, however, to be the place of the sea because that which is salty remains at the bottom by reason of its weight; whereas that which is drinkable and sweet is accustomed to climb to the heights because of its thinness <note>original: "tenuitatem," referring to the lack of density in fresh water compared to salt water</note>. Therefore, we must first see what waters are, what salt waters are, and what sweet waters are, and what place they occupy.

This globe of ours—which consists of earth and water together with other out-flowings <note>original: "effluviis"</note>—is imbued with <term>magnetic forces</term> <note>the author refers to the emerging 17th-century theory that the Earth acts as a giant magnet, an idea championed by William Gilbert</note>, particularly in its solid and firmer primary part. Certain fluids wash against the high points of this globe and are driven here and there by various motions through the deeper places of the sea and through internal caverns and pipes in the upper part, from which springs erupt and rivers glide down into lower places. (Here also those men are deceived who judge subterranean waters to be the lowest, the seas to be in the middle, and rivers to be the highest. For although in some places water is found in wells as deep as two hundred <term>fathoms</term> <note>original: "orgyam," a unit of measurement roughly equal to 6 feet</note>, yet because the surface of those lands is much higher than the surface of the sea, and because the depth of the sea itself is greater, the sea settles in the deepest bottom of all waters.) But the vast and deeper mass of the more constant globe, which we call "the earth," even if...

<note>original: "ra," completing "terra" from the previous page</note> [the earth] appears resistant, firm, and almost dry, it is not, however, devoid of juice, parched, cold, and barren, as many philosophers, led by a vain opinion, believe. But just as its upper parts, though a chaotic mix of things being born and things decaying, nevertheless display an innate moisture to our senses (unless that moisture occasionally appears diminished when a more burning Sun has driven away the thin, absorbed liquid); so too the entire internal mass of the earth possesses an innate moisture, implanted from its first origin, which is its own. From its interior parts, thinned flows and <term>vapors</term> <note>original: "halitus," referring to exhalations or steamy breaths rising from the earth</note> emerge, and are again conceived and absorbed. From this motion and action of nature, the springs, rivers, and seas endure forever. Thus, the flows of water are those proceeding from the earth; in the higher parts of the lands, they are condensed into a sensible and more resistant liquid by the accumulation of vapors and the upward movement, followed by a cooling or release; this happens, however, according to a greater or lesser degree. For the seas are thicker and more resistant, while many springs (and the rivers that come from them) are thinner and more subtle. Truly, those waters which are "thick" are for the most part salty, and some are bitter. We do not speak here of muddy waters, which are rather the result of a confusion of different natures. Indeed, <term>salts</term> are juices condensed from the thicker vapors: for this reason the entire sea is salty, since on its floor—as soon as they are reached—the overflows of the lands which are washed by the sea either break out into the substance of the sea or pass into salts; thus, salty depths and the salty whole exist from a "salty generation." For we should not ask so much why the sea is salty, as why springs and rivers are sweet and drinkable. For the generation of springs is more subtle, since a thinner moist matter is produced either from vapor exalted into the higher reaches of the mountains, or when parts of the earth attract and soak up the exterior air and conceive it into their interior; these thinner waters arise from vapors sublimated far away from the dregs <note>original: "fæce," referring to the heavy, impure sediments or "dregs" of the elemental process</note>.

But just as salt waters endure in the sea, so the deeper parts of the earth—especially those distant from the surface by several <term>fathoms</term> <note>original: "orgyis," a Greek-derived unit of measurement roughly equal to the span of a man's outstretched arms, or about six feet.</note>—conceive salts. In <term>Pannonia</term> <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note> and <term>Sarmatia</term> <note>A vast ancient territory in Eastern Europe, including parts of modern Poland, Ukraine, and Russia.</note> there are salt mines, but they are quite deep, reaching 50, 60, or even 100 fathoms. In Africa and Asia, there are "fossil" salts <note>original: "sales fossiles," meaning salts that are dug out of the earth like minerals rather than evaporated from water.</note>, and in many places, much of the earth itself tastes of salt; this is especially true of decomposed earth, in which <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "halinitrum," also known as stone-salt.</note> abounds. There are also many nitrous clods; <term>blue vitriol</term> <note>original: "Chalcanthum," or copper sulfate.</note>, <term>copper-stone</term> <note>original: "Chalcitis."</note>, <term>sori</term>, <term>misy</term> <note>Sori and Misy are ancient terms for various metallic sulfates or vitriols used in medicine and metallurgy.</note>, <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, traditionally gathered from volcanic vents or organic matter.</note>, and <term>alums</term> are all juices that possess the nature of salt. Indeed, all veins of metals originate with salt, and all bodies burned among us reveal a salt residue. For wandering, thin, and overly fluid juices do not endure within bodies; therefore, thicker and firmer juices are required, such as those that display the quality of salt.

Consequently, the thicker <term>exhalations</term> <note>original: "halitus," referring to the steamy breaths or vapors rising from the interior of the earth.</note> emitted from the earth everywhere—those which never ascend high into the air—are the material of salty things. Those things which condense from thinner exhalations, however, such as clouds and rain, are rarely or never salty; for they thicken from thinner vapors into "sweet" <note>fresh</note> waters, and do not originate from thick and juicy sources. Therefore, all these things—the sea, springs, and rivers—are the <term>outflowings</term> <note>original: "effluvia."</note> of the earth, just as is all the surrounding air, as the appearance of the following figure shows.

The way that ancient and more recent authors define a fluid—as something not contained by its own boundary but by the container it sits in <note>original: "quod proprio termino non continetur, sed alieno." This is the classical Aristotelian definition: liquids take the shape of their vessel rather than having a fixed shape of their own.</note>—actually fails to show the true nature of moisture, nor is it correct. For just as a drop of water gathers itself into a sphere and finds its own boundary, so the vastest seas gather into themselves; they are convex, not flat. Indeed, if there were any primary sphere in nature, it would take its shape from water. 

But water flows across the earth into hollows and downward-sloping places, seeking a greater uniformity for the whole globe. For all rivers run to the sea as if to lower spaces, and also as if toward a certain general origin. Among us, there are three primary <term>fluids</term> <note>original: "fluores," literally "flows," used here to categorize moving substances like air and water.</note>: Air, which is <term>thin</term> <note>original: "rarus," meaning rarefied or of low density.</note>; rain, spring, and well water, which are denser; and sea water, which surpasses the others in density. These, having been drawn out from the earth onto its surface, move, flow, glide, and travel back and forth, driven by various causes.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### *Water is not generated from Cold.*

In <term>distillation vessels</term> <note>original: "stillatoriis vasis," referring to early laboratory equipment like alembics used to condense vapors.</note> water is generated, even though the upper parts are hot.

<margin>See chapter 8.</margin>
When the upper parts are cooled from the outside, water forms more quickly; not because of the cold itself, but because that upper body, by heating up, prevents <term>concretion</term> <note>original: "concretionem," the process of vapor thickening into liquid.</note>.

Air is in no way turned into water by cold; for if it were, it would always be raining in cold regions and during cold seasons.

Air is not changed into water through cold: for air in a bladder, submerged in cold water, does not turn into water at all, even over a long period of time.

Therefore, water is not generated by cold, but is rather consumed by it, as we see in extremely cold places where everything dries out.

But neither is it generated by moisture. For nothing is more moist than water itself. Nor does watery moisture change air that has been submerged within it.

<margin>In the same place, chapter 8.</margin>
It remains, therefore, that water is generated from air and dissolved vapor that thickens, either in naturally dark places, or in the bowels of the earth, or when it is driven together into some place...

### CHAPTER XIV.

->*On the Composition of the Elements.*<-

When elements were first admitted into Philosophy in a previous age, scholars anxiously sought to understand how those elements were composed. Plato (or perhaps it was the opinion of the <term>Pythagoreans</term> <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that the physical world was built upon mathematical and geometric foundations.</note>) thought that these elements were composed of surfaces; thus, by a poor method, he makes mathematical principles the basis of bodies consisting of nature. Anaxagoras, having considered that bodies of <term>similar parts</term> <note>original: "similarium partium," referring to the concept of "homoeomeries," where every part of a substance contains the same properties as the whole.</note> were the primary matter of all things, and seeing that everything is generated from these bodies which we are accustomed to call elements, believed that in these elements there are especially similar parts—and, as it were, the seeds of all things—from which all things can likewise be generated and arise. But Democritus, whom Epicurus followed, said that the matter of all things consisted of indivisible bodies (which he called <term>atoms</term> <note>original: "atomos," from the Greek word for "indivisible." In this era, atomism was often seen as a rival to the religious and Aristotelian view of nature.</note>) distinguished from one another by their shapes. They claim that all these elements are constituted from these atoms. But these opinions were finally—and not undeservedly—rejected, and it was confirmed by Aristotle above all, and by all his followers, that those elements are conceived to consist of <term>matter and form</term> <note>original: "materia & forma," the two core principles of Aristotelian physics; matter is the "stuff" of the world, while form is the specific identity or design that makes it a particular thing.</note>.

### CHAPTER XV.

->*That those elements, as they are poorly understood, do not arise from one another through their own qualities.*<-

<margin>
See chapter 8.
</margin>
This transformation seems to occur especially in the case of air and water. For since all the elements strive to arise here and there by the force of nature, air arises most easily from water. When heat pushes moisture more vehemently, it first becomes vapor, which then passes into air; this is easily accomplished. For this reason, some also maintain that air is converted back into water by means of cold; however, this can in no way be persuasively argued. If it were so, then their entire "middle region" of the air <note>In traditional natural philosophy, the atmosphere was divided into three regions; the "middle region" was thought to be perpetually cold and the source of clouds and rain.</note> would turn into water, and perpetual rains would exist around the poles in the cold regions; yet, in those Zones, the sky is actually less humid.

<margin>
In the same place.
</margin>
But let that theory also be refuted by experiment. Take a <term>bladder</term> <note>original: "vesica," likely a pig's bladder, commonly used in early science to contain gases or liquids.</note> distended with air, and submerge it with some weight in icy water for a whole week, a whole month, or even a year. When the bladder is pulled out, it is found to be full of air just as before, not at all thickened or congealed into water, and in no way changed; this remains true even though the air was surrounded on all sides by both suitable moisture and cold, being enclosed, contained, and incubated by the water itself. Therefore, air is not turned into water by cold or moisture. Furthermore, in the superior element of fire, what force of cold exists that could diminish it enough to overcome its heat? Or how could that fiery dryness ever depart into moisture? Could anyone produce water from earth by means of cold, when we see that all rigid things instead become harder, rougher, and drier over a longer period of time?

## CHAPTER XVI.

->*That the entire space between the earth and the Moon is not filled with elements, but only that certain emanations rise to a height of a few miles.*<-

Some <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who dominated university education in the medieval and early modern periods.</note> believe that the entire space between the earth and the Moon is filled with Elements; to ensure this space is filled more certainly, they believe that water, air, and fire increase by a certain proportion, and rise in volume by a ten-fold ratio. But through certain experiments, the seas are known to reach barely two miles in depth, and they cover only about half of the globe's surface; therefore, they are by no means to be compared with the mass of the earth, whose diameter is 6,875 of such miles. Thus, water is not ten times greater, but more than three hundred times smaller than the earth. 

But if the Elements maintained a continuous ten-fold proportion, the other Elements together would contain the earth 1,110 times. For 10, 100, and 1,000 make 1,110—which is utterly false. For if you observe the spaces lying between the earth and the Moon, they will be much larger than the earth—by 40,000 times. But if they want this ten-fold proportion to be understood regarding the *diameters* of the elements, and not regarding the volume of their bodies, that would be much more absurd. First, because it is false that the distance of the Moon from the earth contains 1,110 semi-diameters of the earth; it would follow from this that water is a thousand times larger than the earth, and that the entire sphere of the elements has a proportion to the earth like the number 1,000,000,000 to 1. This is ridiculous, as the learned <term>Clavius</term> <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit astronomer who was a leading authority on mathematics and the calendar.</note> correctly concludes, and he demonstrates at greater length that this "machine of the Elements" is an empty theory. For if the element of air—even being small in respect to such vastness—rises only to a height of 52 miles, according to the demonstrations of <term>Alhazen</term> <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), a pioneering mathematician and physicist known for his work on optics and the atmosphere.</note> and Vi-

## CHAPTER XVII.
### *On the proportions and quantities of the Elements among themselves.*

<margin>See chapter 16.</margin>
When the Philosophers had fashioned an excellent machine of the elements in the nature of things, they also desired there to be a proportion between those elements, as well as certain laws and a most balanced construction. Thus, some imagine that the proportion of quantities in the elements consists of a continuous ten-fold increase. This cannot happen unless the vastly larger part of the space between the Moon and the earth is empty. But let some bold fellow from the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of thought.</note> crowd imagine, according to his own sense, that the proportion of the spherical distance from the earth to the sphere of the Moon is 1,110 of the earth’s semi-diameters; if he then compares this with the mass of the earth, he will see how much that outermost body and the entire mass placed between them would exceed the earth. It is therefore ridiculous to say the earth is in any convenient and na-

However, the proportion between water and earth can be easily discerned; so much so that it seems Philosophers have been raving for many centuries, claiming that water is many times larger than the earth. The most skilled Spanish, English, and Dutch navigators—with whom we have frequently conversed, and many of whom have circumnavigated the globe—report that the vastest seas are rarely more than 500 paces deep <note>Roughly half a mile</note>, and very rarely 800; in most places, they hardly exceed 30, 40, or 50 **fathoms** <term>orgyas: a unit of depth based on the span of a man's outstretched arms, approximately six feet</term>. If, across the entire globe (removing the mountains), water stood 500 paces deep over the earth, and that entire sphere had a diameter of 3,500 miles, while the earth’s diameter was 3,000 miles, it would follow from this that the earth is more than 2,333 times larger than the water. But because the exposed surface of the earth is larger than—or not much smaller than—the surface of the waters, and the water in most places does not reach a depth of 50 paces, it follows of necessity that the earth is more than 5,000 times larger than the water. The earth would be larger than the water because there is more land on the surface, even if the water reached down in a pyramid shape to the very center of the globe, as anyone can easily demonstrate. Water is therefore not ten times larger than the earth <note>The author is attacking the "Decuple Theory," a medieval belief that each element was ten times larger in volume than the one "heavier" than it (e.g., water was 10x earth, air 10x water).</note>, since the earth is more than five thousand times larger than the water. Yet, through these follies born of poor foundations, all authentic Philosophy has long been delirious; the Schools ring with the most absurd doctrines, and the common people and the youth are infatuated with vanities and errors.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

### *That there are no mixtures of Elements, nor of qualities, when bodies are generated.*

<margin>See chapter 12.</margin>
Cooks, when they fashion small cakes from barley-meal <note>original: *polenta*</note> and brewers when they brew ale—even the pharmacist when he composes electuaries <note>A medicinal paste made of powder mixed with honey or syrup</note> and syrups—all create a single thing out of many components. Nature, however, is not so mechanical as to establish the forms of things through such "mixtures." Therefore, she constitutes bodies without the use of "elements," whether in composition or in mixture. The Earth is the common mother; she alone provides the matter, and within her lie hidden the seeds <note>original: *seminaria*, referring to the "seminal reasons" or tiny blueprints for life believed to exist in the soil</note> of all things. Once these have been conceived in a suitable place, they take their beginning of motion, growth, and fixed state from the action of moisture <note>original: *humoris*</note> within the boundaries of their specific form. Elements are not fetched from elsewhere: every single thing exists in its own appropriate essence. Those things that take root cling to the earth and draw from it the sap necessary for each specific form. This sap is drawn from the earth, which possesses this inherent and natural juice everywhere and throughout its entire mass.

As for those creatures that live in the waters, they move about within the more liquid "sap" of the earth and are preserved by the suitable warmth of the waters.

In the air, however—which is a more thinned-out fluid—the remaining animals live. They are refreshed by this spiritual fluid <note>Likely referring to *pneuma* or the life-giving quality of air</note> and sustain their lives by its warmth, taking in nourishment so that as moisture is acted upon and consumed, new growth may be added.

## CHAPTER XIX.

### *On the Motion of heavy and light things.*

After the "machine of the elements" <note>The traditional Aristotelian model of the universe where Earth and Water move down while Air and Fire move up</note> was devised and committed to writing, various opinions arose concerning the causes of those motions themselves. Some of the ancients said that the elements move because they are led to their own proper place by the places themselves, which possess an attractive force. More recent thinkers believe that the motions of the elements arise from generation <note>The process of coming into being or being "born"</note>. For while they are generated and corrupted <note>Decayed or broken down</note>, they become heavy or light, from which they tend upward or downward; this, they say, happens due to an external cause. Others believe that the elements are moved by their own "forms" <note>The essential nature or "soul" of an object in Scholastic philosophy</note>, and thus have an internal mover. The interpreters of Aristotle <note>The "Peripatetics" or Scholastic philosophers who dominated university learning</note> occupy themselves with these matters, and they fruitlessly clash with one another in various ways, each according to his own wit. For it must necessarily happen this way when they seek for reasons based on false principles.

It has been established by us previously that the elements do not exist in nature in such a way, nor do they reside in various places: motions upward and downward do not arise from contrary natures. <margin>See chapter 12.</margin> The entire nature of terrestrial things depends upon the globe of the earth itself, flows out from it, and flows back into it. The Earth does not remain in its place because of gravity <note>original: *gravitatem*. In this era, "gravity" referred to the inherent "heaviness" of an object rather than a universal force of attraction</note>, as we have taught before; likewise, bodies do not flow together toward the earth unless they have first gone out from it.

Exhalations go forth both from the heat enclosed within the bowels of the earth, and from the light of the Sun and the actual alliance <note>original: *confæderatione*, suggesting a shared physical influence or "conspiracy" of forces</note> of the Moon. Worn-down humors <note>Liquids or fluids</note>, both oily and watery, rise up through the motion of melting <note>original: *fusionis*</note>; they are elevated by the thicker, vaporous air, and seem to climb somewhat toward the higher regions. But that motion is immediately diminished, and the vapors wander with uncertain movements <note>original: *lationibus*, a technical term for the carrying or path of a physical body</note>. For these are outflows <note>original: *effluvia*</note> already risen from the earth, not far distant from it; when they have been raised up, they are not immediately thickened—as if "meteors" <note>In early modern science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, wind, and snow</note> were created by the "Peripatetic cold" <note>The Aristotelian theory that the upper atmosphere was cold enough to condense vapors into weather</note>—but rather when the vapors thicken together from the piling up of matter. Thus, if the South Wind <note>original: *auster*</note> should pass into the North Wind <note>original: *boream*</note>, it immediately snows; if the North Wind into the South, it brings rains. Thus nature gathers itself together again, and, having been recollected, returns to its original source. Therefore, the gravity of bodies is an inclination toward their own...

# CHAPTER XX.
## On the Separated Vacuum.

Aristotle rises against the concept of a separated vacuum <note>A "separated" vacuum refers to an empty space existing independently of matter, which Aristotle famously argued could not exist (*natura abhorret vacuum*)</note> with certain flawed little arguments, seeking them in his own fictitious Elements and the movements of their parts. He argues that if every simple body has a natural motion—such as fire moving upward, and earth moving downward toward the center—then it is clear that a vacuum cannot be the cause of that motion. For what, then, would a vacuum be the cause? It appears to be a cause of motion in respect to place, yet he claims it is not. 

We have already stated how and from where these straight motions of the elements arise (which are so often chanted by the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, known for teaching while walking in the shaded walkways, or *peripatoi*, of the Lyceum</note>). Furthermore, no sane person would say that a vacuum is the *cause* of motion; rather, bodies are moved *within* a separated vacuum. They are moved not by the vacuum, but by the bodies themselves, which emit their own actions. In a vacuum, the primary bodies are moved—the globes themselves, such as the planets, the earth, and even some fixed stars (if they should have a motion that cannot be discerned by us due to their great distance). Or, bodies may rest in a vacuum, such as the majority of the fixed stars,

Aristotle wishes to demonstrate that there is no vacuum in his "stuffed world" <note>original: *farcinato mundo*</note> composed of a mass of elements; this is ridiculous. *Furthermore,* he says, *if there is some place deprived of body—that is, a vacuum—to where will a body placed in it be moved? For it will not move in every direction.* <note>The author is quoting Aristotle’s *Physics*, Book IV, where Aristotle argues that in a void, there is no "up" or "down," so motion would be impossible.</note> That straight motion is simply the inclination of matter toward its principles, its sources, and its globes <note>The author views planets and the earth as "globes" or primary sources of attraction.</note>. When loosened parts rise a little from a globe, it happens due to extension and greater thinning <note>original: *attenuatione*</note>, and they join with the **effluvia** <term>effluvia: out-flowing vapors or invisible emissions that the author believes extend from a body like the earth or a magnet to interact with surrounding matter</term> of the globe. For **effluvia** are parts raised by thinning into a larger space.

<margin>See chapter 11 of this book.</margin>

When thicker and more compressed bodies are within these **effluvia**, they tend immediately toward their principle and like-substance—namely, toward the earth. But if thick matter should be separated far from the **effluvia** by some chance, it does not immediately slide down toward the earth, just as **electrical** <term>electrica: referring to the attractive properties of amber and other materials that exhibit what we now call static electricity</term> things do not attract bodies outside their own **effluvia**. Instead, **Comets** remain in the vacuum, unless that matter is driven and moved by the **form** <note>In this context, "form" refers to the internal organizing principle or "soul" of a celestial body that dictates its behavior.</note> of the planets or by light; like comets, which as soon as they appear, are driven only by **circular motion** until they vanish.

Aristotle thinks, moreover, that no cause can be assigned as to why a thing that is moved should rest here rather than there; therefore, he argues that everything which moves must either be naturally inclined to rest everywhere and be carried everywhere, or the vacuum must be discarded. Here is the truth of the matter: All things placed in a vacuum remain at rest; thus, many globes of the world are at rest. But some globes are driven around certain bodies both by their innate forces and by the action of other bodies—such as the planets around the **Sun**, or around the **earth**; the earth around its own axis toward the Sun; and the **Moon** around the earth and toward the Sun.

If the **Sun** rests in the middle, like **the Dog Star** <note>original: *Canis*, referring to Sirius</note>, like **Orion**, or like **Arcturus**, then both the planets and the earth are driven into an orbit by the Sun, their own **forms** agreeing to this for the good of the globes themselves. If, however, the **earth** rests in the middle (the annual motion of which is not to be debated in this place), then the other moving bodies are driven around it.

If the separated parts of the primary globes <note>The author refers to planets and the Earth as "globes."</note> were moved in a vacuum, it does not follow from Aristotle’s opinion that this would happen in an instant. For the parts of the earth move toward the earth faster or slower depending on the nature and arrangement of the medium; they move fastest in the thinnest medium, yet not without time. Thus, even in a vacuum, motion would occur successively <note>original: *successive*; meaning one moment after another, rather than all at once.</note>.

A separate vacuum is nowhere enclosed by a body, but a vacuum is like a single and, as it were, continuous space: it is not finite, because it is not a real physical thing; nor is it infinite, because it does not truly exist.

In a separate vacuum, there is an absolute deprivation of bodies and actions. The air closest to us, as well as the highest air, is an **effluvium** <term>effluvium: an invisible emission or vapor flowing out from a body like the Earth, which the author believes mediates forces like gravity and magnetism</term> of the earth; it is extremely cold, and it does not turn into water because of that cold, but exists in a very thin state with the smallest accumulation of matter.

<margin>See Book 3, chapter 3 and following.</margin>

Those who think that what moves through a vacuum moves in an instant say nothing of value. They dream much about "natural straight motions," which are not truly natural motions incited by nature itself, but arise from force and disturbance when bodies are placed outside their natural state and return to their own principles <note>By "principles," the author means the source or parent body from which a fragment was separated.</note>. However, the circular motion of the primary globes is a true natural impulse, and it occurs in a vacuum with no body resisting it. But those other supposed straight motions <note>i.e., falling or rising in a straight line.</note> do not occur through a vacuum. For if a part of the earth were located farther away, beyond the earth's **effluvia**, it would not fall back to the earth; just as **electrical** <term>electrica: referring to the attractive properties of amber (electrum) and similar materials; the root of our modern word "electricity"</term> things cannot attract bodies beyond their own **effluvia**. Here, the entire philosophy regarding the proportion of straight motion through a plenum <note>original: *plenum*; a space entirely filled with matter, the opposite of a vacuum.</note> and through a vacuum appears to vanish. It is manifest from **electrical** principles that the motion of the earth's parts occurs only through force. That force, moreover, is brought in by the light of some star, or by the action of "forms," as happens in the case of comets, which travel through the vacuum; regarding which I will speak more fully elsewhere. As for the arguments presented by Alhazen <term>Alhazen: Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), a pioneering scholar of optics whose work "Perspectiva" was foundational to European science</term> in his *Perspectives*, which prove that the heavens are rarer than air and fire, those same points more fittingly prove that there are empty and void spaces above the **effluvia** <term>effluvia: the vapors, magnetic forces, or "breath" emitted by the Earth</term> of the earth.

If the whole world were full and crammed with matter, the light of the fixed stars would reach our senses only after certain intervals of time once they had risen above the horizon, because the intervening body—spanning such vast distances—would offer resistance. But light is present to the bodies it strikes **instantly**, not over a period of time, when passing through a vacuum; yet light does pass through **transparent** <term>original: *diaphana*; referring to materials like glass or water that allow light to pass</term> bodies over a period of time. Therefore, there is a vacuum.

Bodies are affected by lights while the light is passing through them, and this occurs over time; however, through a vacuum, there is no such action. Therefore, light does not pass through a vacuum over a period of time, but is present from one body to another without the passage of time.

The Milky Way <note>original: *Lacteus circulus*; the "Milky Circle"</note> is real matter, spread out and persisting through the empty spaces of the world, yet distinct from the void itself.

The freest possible passage is open to light through a vacuum, but not in the same way through a transparent body.

No body is so transparent that there is not some resistance within it, and every resistance is an impediment and a **refraction** of light.

Light is an **act** <note>original: *actus*; in Aristotelian philosophy, an "act" or "actuality" is the fulfillment or operation of a potential</note>, but an act does not exist except in a body, and a vacuum does not "grasp" or contain light.

When a vacuum lies between them, light is present to the objects it strikes without passing through time: even though light passes through actual transparent bodies over time.

If there were no vacuum, the celestial bodies would appear much larger than they are. <note>The author suggests that if space were full of matter, it would act like a giant magnifying lens.</note>

In any region and at any time of year, the air—even if it were at its clearest and thinnest—would always produce **twilight**; for no air can be imagined so subtle that there would not be some resistance in it, and some refraction of the light proceeding from the Sun. # CHAPTER XXI.

->*On the commonly conceived Motion of the Elements, and on both weight and lightness.*<-

They <note>The "they" refers to traditional Aristotelian philosophers</note> say that some bodies are simple and others are composite; that simple motions belong to simple bodies, while mixed and imperfect motions belong to composite ones. They claim simple motion is either in a straight line or circular. They say the simple elements are carried in a straight line; while celestial bodies, being free from all solid material <note>original: *concretione*; the process of matter thickening or gathering together</note>, revolve in a circle. And these are "natural" motions; those contrary to them are "violent" <term>violent motion: in Aristotelian physics, any motion that goes against an object's "natural" inclination (like throwing a stone upward), usually requiring an external force</term>, as they are spurred against the inclination of nature. Fire is always light and seeks the heights; whereas earth and all earthy things are carried downward, toward the middle or the center. That is called "absolutely heavy" which lies beneath everything else; while that is "light" which stands out and rises above all. Yet, it is clear enough that such simple bodies are found nowhere among us. This makes their absurd classification even more intolerable, as they oppose a very small quantity of composite things to the immense power of simple bodies and the vastness of the whole world. ...simple bodies <note>original: *simplicia corpora*; the "cia" from the start of the page completes the word from the previous page</note> are the vast nature of all things; while composite bodies are hardened from certain outflows and mixtures of elements only around the periphery of the earth. Elements, then, when outside their natural place, are carried in a straight course toward that place; yet the elements themselves cannot be moved entirely from their original seats. But if their parts were torn away, those simple elements would have appeared to mortals at some point as a small fragment. Instead, it is claimed they are immediately altered and corrupted by neighboring bodies. If that were so—that they cannot be shown in any way, and if they entered the boundaries of others, they were corrupted—why do we assign motion to simple elements, when simple elements are never moved? They either rest perpetually, or lie hidden, or, being unfamiliar and forbidden, they never come out into the light. If "simple Earth" were moved, it would emerge beyond its highest surface: but that never appears; therefore, its motion is not simple. 

By these simple motions, the elements are distinguished and called either "heavy" or "light," because they are born to tend toward the center or away from the center. Earthly things torn from the earth are immediately carried downward by their nature. # BOOK I.

...are carried by the inciting nature of the world. Indeed, the opinion of those who say that if the Earth were moved into the orbit of the moon, its parts would not for that reason move toward it <note>Meaning the Earth itself.</note>—on the grounds that the world's center is similar to them—is false and irrational. They claim that if those parts were lifted from the center, they would fall back toward the center; they believe that wherever the "whole" must naturally be carried, it is necessary for the parts of that whole to be carried there as well. 

However, they grant immobility to the Earth, while granting mobility to its parts; they say the parts move toward the Earth's specific location and rest there. They argue that heavy things move toward the center, and therefore the Earth rests in the center. But rest is not proved by motion, nor does the body of the Earth—which is by nature always at rest—possess parts that move by nature. In truth, they move because they approach their origin or "common mother," by which they are attracted **electrically** <note>original: *electrice*; in the 17th century, this often referred to an attractive force similar to magnetism or static electricity, rather than modern circuitry.</note>. For this reason, they rush even more swiftly when they are nearby. This is also due to the duration and continuation of the motion, just as objects move more quickly near the earth after a fall of a hundred cubits <note>original: *ulnarum*; a unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18–24 inches.</note> than after five or even ten, and they strike the ground more violently. Furthermore, compressed and dense things, such as gold and lead, fall more quickly. 

Therefore, the inclination of bodies toward a common origin—or toward their own globe—is a drive toward **unity**, not an impulse toward some specific place or position in the world. Since nature has distinguished all bodies into globes, the parts of those globes incline toward their own masses and are attracted by them—not only the parts of the earth, but those of other bodies existing in the world. This is a propensity of body for body, of parts for the whole, and of fragments for their own proper globe, rather than for the "places" of those globes. 

Fragments of the moon would tend toward the moon, not toward some specific point in the circle in which it is carried around. And those things in which the condensed matter is narrower, tighter, and united through the smallest parts are carried more strongly and vehemently. Things that are loosened, more rare, or fluid move lightly, slowly, and more modestly—especially in a thicker and material medium. Wherefore lead more in-

...inclines toward the earth, as do the thinner parts of the earth and magnetic things; and a magnet that is much more powerful in its strength is sometimes less heavy than another, weaker magnet. No bodies are carried upward of their own accord, unless they wish to flee from the earth toward the earth <note>The author is likely being ironic here, suggesting that "rising" is just a different interaction with the Earth's mass.</note>, or if certain parts seek the whole while others shrink away. They are, however, moved away from the earth when they are lifted up by thicker bodies, either in water or in air. For instance, a piece of cork at the bottom of a body of water moves immediately to the surface, but not because it is seeking its "natural place"; for if the water is removed, the cork falls back to the bottom. Instead, it is lifted and squeezed out by the denser water, which is a fluid body. 

The same occurs when heat melts matter, which then seems to ascend: (but the vapor driven by internal heat does not rise beyond its first bursts, and it immediately floats in the air; it is not raised any further once the heat no longer melts it). Or it occurs when a thinned body finds a suitable space, just as the motion of ignited **gunpowder** <note>original: *pulveris tormentarii*; literally "powder for engines of war."</note> does not happen because of "lightness," but from the sudden dissolution and melting of the matter, until that expanded matter becomes quiet across larger spaces, beyond which it cannot extend. 

Earth is traditionally ranked as the heaviest of all the elements, as if its nature were such that it is not merely heavy, but the heaviest thing possible; the element of water is also called heavy, though not as heavy as earth. But we see that there are bodies made of earth and water that far exceed in weight any part of the earth ever seen or excavated: such as **gold** and **lead**, which surpass any equal volume of earth in weight. Therefore, they do not derive their gravity from "earth" or "water" as elements; nor is gravity a condition of being an element. Instead, bodies tend more vehemently toward their origin because of the nature of their matter; a denser substance <note>original: *corpulentior substantia*; literally a "more corporeal" or "fleshier" substance, referring to density.</note> exerts more pressure, because in that united and compressed state, there is more matter. **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose physics the author is currently dismantling.</note> maintains that the Earth is carried toward the middle [of the universe] because it rests there. # BOOK I.

...lightness is not the cause of motion, nor is motion the cause of immobility. The parts of the Earth move toward a place: therefore, if the Earth were outside of its place, it would move toward its own place; yet if it possesses this capacity for mobility, it is not entirely immobile. But **place** does not act, nor does it rule in the nature of things, such that it might stop bodies or move them <note>The author is refuting the Scholastic idea that "Place" was an active force or "final cause" that pulled objects toward it.</note>. The Moon does not move in a circle in its monthly course because it is in a certain "place": nor is it the nature of places that causes Mercury to move around the Sun (as some think) or, as others say, to never travel far from the Sun but instead return to it. We must argue the same regarding rest. The fixed stars remain in determined places, but not because of the nature of the place itself: for "place" is neither a being nor an efficient cause; rather, a force often flows from surrounding bodies into what is contained within them.

Let us proceed to better-known things: Clouds are carried high in the air and remain suspended, not because of the place; but either they remain while they are lifted by the air, or at a greater distance they incline less toward the earth, or because, having arisen in the upper air, they remain in it as if it were their natural seat. For bodies claim for themselves the places of their origin, not because of the place itself, but because of the bodies themselves, by a most excellent right. For spaces are immense in the nature of things, in which bodies, while they are arising, claim their seats by a most excellent right (nature so willing it). Therefore, comets also, as long as they remain, occupy places: and even if, driven by the Sun, they imitate a circular motion, they are nevertheless carried through certain boundaries in the **ether or vacuum** <note>original: *æthere seu vacuo*; the author acknowledges the possibility of a vacuum, a controversial idea at the time</note>, not toward the earth or into the globes of the planets. 

The motion of the parts of the earth toward the center is not that "simple motion" <note>In Aristotelian physics, "simple motion" refers to the natural straight-line movement of elements—up for fire/air, down for earth/water.</note> of some element. They say that motion is attributed to every element and simple body: but the whole earth does not move, nor do its principal parts: therefore, no motion is destined for it. For the primary parts around the center, as well as all others, remain at rest on the periphery, unless they have been loosened by some accident. ...created things have never been shaken from their very beginnings. Therefore, it is futile to impose such a "natural motion" upon bodies. Aristotle, in Chapter 4, Book 4 of *On the Heavens* <note>original: *de Caelo*</note>, asserts that all things have weight in their own place, except for fire; he says this can be understood from the fact that inflated bladders weigh more than empty ones. In reality, this happens because of the steamy air generated inside the bladder, not from any air that is truly comparable with the surrounding atmosphere. To suggest that enclosed air is heavier than the surrounding air, and that it sinks when placed within air of an equal and like nature, is so frivolous that nothing 

<margin>See also Galileo, *Dialogue on the Two Chief World Systems*, Dialogue 1.</margin>
more foolish could be imagined or devised. Therefore, straight-line motion <term>rectus motus</term>—for all parts of the earth as well as for the parts of all the celestial spheres existing in the universe—occurs only when they wander from their place (that is, their natural sphere), or are pushed out, or are in any way outside of it. Nothing is so contrary to the order of the whole and the form of the world as for a thing to be outside of its own sphere and mass. The stars themselves have fixed positions and defined paths; they offer mutual aid to one another or oppose each other, and the combination of all their parts is such that they strive toward their respective wholes. Truly, straight-line motion <note>In traditional Aristotelian physics, "rectilinear" or straight-line motion was considered "imperfect" because it had a beginning and an end, unlike the "perfect" circular motion of the heavens.</note> does not occur except to things that are not in their proper state, nor perfected according to nature, such as when they are separated from their "whole" and abandon its unity. Thus, vapors ascend by the heat of the Sun and the stars when thinned moisture turns into spirit. Thus those "meteors" <term>meteora</term> <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" was a broad term for any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note> and lofty things are carried from the earth by the expansive motion of heat to regions further away, until that force of heat grows faint, and the moisture is no longer expanded or carried by the impulse of expansion. And those straight-line motions, which Aristotle called "simple," are always unequal, as well as being lateral and mixed; they do not produce a simple, uniform, and equal motion, for they cannot be moderated by lightness or by the force of their own weight.

...by falling. <note>original: *cadendo*</note> Indeed, we see that the rising smoke of earthly fire and exhaling vapors <term>exhalationes</term><note>The author uses this term to describe gasses or misty substances thought to be released by the earth's heat.</note> are carried up for a certain distance and then immediately weaken as the force <note>original: *violentia*</note> of the earthly matter is released and its momentum <note>original: *impetus*</note> is diminished. They are like arrows or projectiles <term>globuli tormentarii</term><note>Literally "balls of the engines," referring to musket or cannon balls.</note> shot through the air; the more they tend toward the heights, the more they lose strength. The opposite would happen if they were moving toward a specific place ordained for them by nature <note>In Aristotelian physics, an object was supposed to speed up as it approached its "natural home," but the author observes that rising objects actually slow down.</note>. These motions, therefore, are not so much the movements of simple bodies or some fictional "elements," but rather the violent tossing and stretching of parts near the surface of the earth, which eventually sink back down and flow together when they become solid. In this way the earth is united, and so too are the other globes; in this way, parts are carried in a straight line toward the centers of these globes. On the surface of the earth, things are called "heavy" <term>gravia</term> when they are carried toward the earth after being placed outside their natural state. No force is destined for a "place" or "places," but only for physical bodies.

It is ridiculous to think that the globe of the Earth possesses gravity, while all other globes are not heavy at all; or that the gathering and unification of parts into a whole occurs in this one globe, but not in the planets, nor in the fixed <unclear>stars</unclear>, nor in the many thousands of other stars and great globes which are not seen by us because of their incomprehensible distances.

### *On the Separable and Inseparable Vacuum.*

<meta>This page continues the author’s investigation into the physical structure of the universe. Following the previous page's discussion on gravity and the motion of elements, the author now addresses the controversial topic of the "vacuum" (void), transitioning from a critique of Aristotelian "natural places" to the mechanical arguments used by "modern" thinkers to deny the existence of empty space within the atmosphere.</meta>

64 [OF] PHYSIOLOGY

...not to admit, and not to acknowledge in assigning the causes of things. Everyone disputes about a twofold vacuum: the separable and the inseparable void <term>inane</term>, about which we must also speak; especially about the separable one, so that the limits of the earth, which end in a vacuum, may become clearly known, and the various properties <term>affectiones</term> <note>original: *affectiones*; in this context, it refers to the physical states or behaviors of matter.</note> in them may be better understood. 

But a vacuum is absolutely not admitted by any of the moderns, with their universal approval, in whatever way it is taken. For they believe that nature dreads nothing more than the admission of a vacuum. <note>This refers to the famous concept of *horror vacui*, the theory that "nature abhors a vacuum" and will move any available matter to fill an empty space.</note> They show this by a familiar example: in a vessel or water-clock <term>clepsydra</term> <note>A device used to measure time by the flow of water, or more generally, a vessel with small holes used to demonstrate air pressure.</note>, water cannot flow out through a hole or the mouth of the vessel unless a path is opened on the other side through which other matter may flow in, and that vessel be successively refilled. A bellows closed on all sides cannot be stretched at its sides, even if you strive with great force, unless it is broken apart so that air may have entry. Many are the ingenious motions, such as heavier things tending toward higher places—as seen in the drawing of water and other instruments, as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose works were foundational for Renaissance engineering.</note> demonstrates in his *Architecture*—lest, as they believe, a vacuum be admitted into the nature of things. 

Truly this is certain: that bodies do not admit a "separate vacuum" within their inner recesses and spaces surrounded on all sides by bodies. For bodies that are united or contiguous flee from division by means of a vacuum. If there were a vacuum in a bellows, a pipe, a water-clock, or a jar, there would be a space without a body, without quality, which cannot exist within the surrounding environment <term>circumsistentia</term> of bodies or qualities. For bodies are arranged in globes, and these globes are separated by a vacuum. The globes—in the interiors of both the earth and the water, as well as the surrounding air—stubbornly and unconquerably maintain their unity; otherwise, the globes of nature would perish and be scattered.

Although Hero of Alexandria <note>A mathematician and engineer from the 1st century AD who proposed that while large vacuums do not occur naturally, small "interstitial" voids exist between particles of matter.</note> maintains that a vacuum exists in nature, disseminated according to small parts, and that the bodies themselves through com-

# BOOK I.

...filling the scattered voids through pressure. Thus, in a vessel full of air, more air is forced in through a pipe, which we attempt to blow into with our mouths. For this reason, he says <note>Referring to Hero of Alexandria, an ancient Greek mathematician and engineer known for his work on pneumatics.</note>, it is necessary that there be intervals <note>original: *intervalla*; here meaning the tiny empty spaces between particles.</note> which, when compressed, occupy a smaller mass. However, this would not be plausible if no vacuum existed at all. Yet, that air forced in by violence clearly shows that a contraction of the bodies existing in the vessel occurs within the enmeshed voids. This contraction, however, occurs against nature because of the violence of the injection. If, therefore, the person blowing, placing their hand against the mouth, immediately plugs the siphon <term>siphōnem</term> <note>A tube or pipe used for transferring or compressing air and liquids.</note> with a finger, the compressed air will remain in the vessel indefinitely; but if they open it, it will burst out again with a great noise. 

Hero insists on such arguments in favor of a scattered vacuum <term>vacuo disperso</term>. But we know that thicker bodies transform into thinner ones, as water is expanded into air through heat. Indeed, just as air is expanded by heat, it is expanded even more by greater heat; conversely, it is contracted back to its original nature by other causes. Thus, it also undergoes contraction by force, even if it contains no scattered voids. For neither water nor air consist of atoms or a heap of bodies, but they are continuous bodies <term>corpora continuata</term>, united in all their parts. 

But we must speak of the separable void <term>inani separabili</term>, although that was less frequently posited by the ancients. We define a separable vacuum as the space between the worlds' spheres <term>globos mundanos</term>, in which no body exists—such as the space between the highest part of the air and the moon’s globe, or the lunar effluvia <note>original: *effluvia*; in 17th-century science, these were invisible flows or atmospheric vapors emitted by celestial bodies.</note>, rather than that concave surface of the moon. For the moon has its own material effluvia around its globe, just as the earth does, as we will teach at some later point. When Aristotle disputes the separable void, he brings forward certain trifles <note>original: *nugamenta*; the author is dismissive of Aristotle's traditional arguments here.</note> against the "confused and scattered" vacuum. If there were no vacuum in the heavens, we would see the earth's pyramidal shadow <note>This refers to the conical shadow cast by the Earth into space (the *umbra*), which causes lunar eclipses.</note> every night—which never happens. For if the world were entirely full of bodies, they would shine with the light [of the Sun]...

...it contains a smaller quantity of matter. Thus, the more **transparent** <note>original: *diaphanum*</note> a substance is, since it consists of very little matter, the more the free passage of light is opened to it. From this, it follows that the smaller the quantity of matter there is in a given space, the more clearly the light will pass through. It follows, therefore, that where there were no matter at all, the entirety of the light would strike the objects; yet the light would not truly pass "freely" through empty spaces <note>The author is making a subtle philosophical point: light only becomes manifest when it hits an object. If the intervening spaces were not empty, how useless would those vast bodies and idle spheres be, unless they were meant to carry the bodies of the stars? In such a case, the most noble **Sun**, the glory of the world and the director of the world's motion, would be rendered helpless; he who moves other bodies would himself have to be carried by spheres that were extremely thin, transparent, subtle, and offering the least resistance—and yet those spheres would serve no purpose in nature and would be entirely idle.

We, however, perceive no power, no light, no motion, or any action from these intervening spaces, which exceed the bodies themselves and the stars in their total dimensions by many thousands of miles. There is, therefore, a **void** <note>original: *vacuum*</note>. Indeed, we believe that "discrete voids" <note>Small, separated pockets of vacuum within matter.</note> are in no way refuted by any of the experiments or reasons brought forward by him <note>The author is likely refuting Aristotle, who famously argued that "nature abhors a vacuum."</note>. The highest emanations of the air or the **earth** <note>original: *telluris*</note> are bounded by the vacuum, or have their limits ending in their own void; yet they rise more or less, and further into the space of the void, just as watery vapor extends into the air. **Air** is nothing but thinned moisture, or an emanation from the dampness of the earth. Above it, there is no body, unless some force gathered from these emanations should occasionally wander through the void. In this way, the stars move through the void by the innate powers of their own bodies, and they are not rotated by material spheres. <header>OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY</header>

A **vacuum**, and one without any physical body, as the ancients proposed, must necessarily exist in the nature of things; otherwise, the bodies of the **planets** and the **fixed stars** would by no means strike our sight and the earth with their lights. For just as doubled glasses become **opaque** <note>original: *opaca*; dark or non-transparent</note> from being **transparent** <note>original: *diaphana*</note>; and as water in a deeper channel creates opacity at the bottom, and shows that in a longer passage light is dulled, and finally lost: so, over a great and very long distance, even the clearest air or the imagined **ethereal** <note>referring to the "ether," the weightless substance once thought to fill the upper heavens</note> transparent substances take on the character of opacity, or are perceived as opaque.

For first, if the celestial spheres are substances, and the stars themselves are their denser parts, then without a doubt those rare physical substances are also dense in some way, though not in comparison to the stars. But if any density (which must necessarily happen) were inherent in them—no matter how it might be imagined—it is manifest that when extremely translucent things are added to other translucent things, they become very dense through that addition. And just as the **Moon**, being opaque by nature, causes an eclipse of the **Sun**, and even the star **Mercury** casts a spot of opacity upon the Sun; so too would that great depth of the elements and the wondrous heights of the celestial spheres [act as obstructions]. Therefore, such a vast height of heaven—even if made of the thinnest and rarest spheres—would block their lights, so that they would never strike the sharp gaze of our eyes. 

But [this would be] much more so in the **sublunary region** <note>the region of the universe below the Moon, which in ancient science was considered the realm of change, decay, and "thick" elements like air and water</note>, where a certain misty thickness stands in the way over long distances, from the hollow of the moon to the earth, polluted by the common decay of the elements. And although the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>the followers of Aristotle, who famously argued that "nature abhors a vacuum"</note> dream of a wondrous subtleness of air and fire, they would still possess the thickness of the elements derived from opaque matter, thinned out to that quantity and proportion of size. But even if all these things did not prevent the stars from coming into our sight, they would nevertheless yield fainter images. But we [perceive] no apparent [variation] in the stars...

When the **Philosophers** <note>Referring generally to the schoolmen and classical thinkers like Aristotle.</note> fashioned the excellent **mechanism of the elements** in the nature of things, they also desired a proportion between the elements, certain laws, and a most balanced structure. Thus, some believe that the continuous quantity of the elements consists of a **tenfold proportion** <note>original: *proportione decupla*; a traditional scholastic theory that each successive element—earth, water, air, fire—occupies ten times the volume of the one beneath it</note>; this, however, cannot happen unless the far greater part of the interval between the **Moon** and the **Earth** is a **vacuum**.

Some of the ancients, when they discussed motion, posited a certain "dispersed" vacuum between bodies; yet they did not want a separate, distinct space to exist in the world. **Aristotle**, in order to refute them more easily, rose up against the idea of "separate" space—a concept he thought was more incredible. Yet we, despite the opposing opinions of all recent thinkers and the views of some ancients, defend this and admit it as proven; through it, many difficult and uncertain points in philosophy are easily understood. For unless those intermediate spaces between the celestial globes are empty of physical bodies—spaces in which no substance measured in **three dimensions** <note>original: *trine dimenſa*</note> pushes back, resists, or is shoved or driven by another—it would follow that by the total absence of bodies from that space, all action and all presence would be removed.

For that reason, neither light nor any heat is conceived within that space, but there exists a complete **privation** <note>original: *privatio*; a philosophical term meaning the absolute absence or lack of a quality, rather than a thing in itself.</note> of all actions, presences, qualities, and affections. Therefore, since **cold** is merely a privation, in a world that is a vacuum (or in bodies and effluvia closest to a vacuum), cold presses in; and because of a great defect of heat, bodies become cold. Therefore, the air in the **Frigid Zones** <note>The polar regions of the Earth.</note> is colder than any ice. For the privation of activity <note>original: *actus*; in this context, the active physical principle that maintains a substance's form or state</note> does not immediately change a body into another form, unless that privation is absolute and accompanied by the accumulation of matter. For in all northern air, even the most frigid, there is some heat and activity, without which it would not flow. But that thin, cold air, if it becomes thicker as it moves, is immediately transmuted into snow or some other solidified atmospheric phenomenon <note>original: *concretum meteorum*; in early modern science, "meteors" referred to any phenomenon in the air, including rain, snow, or hail</note>. For bodies are not transformed by heat and cold alone; rather, they take on other forms through the motion of matter, from their surroundings and neighbors, and through the accumulation of matter—as will appear more clearly when we discuss the nature of heat.

Therefore, just as a vacuum is a privation of bodies—beings of three dimensions with resistance—so too is it a privation of activities. For this reason, neither light nor heat exists inherently throughout empty spaces. Light leaves the intermediate empty space undisturbed when it passes through. Thus, the most distant lights of the fixed stars are as if present; they are only reflected by the vapors of the earth <note>original: *effluviis*; the term refers to the "exhalations" or particles rising from the Earth's surface into the lower atmosphere</note>, or suffer a kind of delay. Once a vacuum is admitted, the explanations for many things become known. Because of the vacuum, the stars are as if near to us; the Sun, hindered by nothing, refreshes the Earth, the Moon, and various heavenly bodies with its light. Because of the vacuum, the frigid zones remain frozen within the narrow depth of the atmospheric system. Because of the vacuum, the motions of the planets—such as the Earth—are free. For they do not suffer delay from obstructed paths or resisting bodies; instead, they flow and glide as the primary power of each dictates, or as they interact with others. Once a vacuum is admitted between bodies, the inexplicable dispute regarding whether the world is finite or infinite ceases; for that vacuum is neither finite nor infinite. Every vacuum is a containing space, yet it is never itself contained by any body. Therefore, it did not creep into the celestial spheres as if scattered within them, nor is it inseparable from the substance of those spheres. ->**BOOK I.**<-

Bodies in nature were made diverse, which would otherwise, through physical continuity, run together and be confounded. Thus, the **matter** <note>original: *ὕλη* (hyle); the Greek philosophical term for the underlying substance or "prime matter" of the universe</note> of the whole world has receded into many spheres. Because of the vacuum, those things which are positioned as if at an infinite distance are present nearby; and the immense world on all sides breathes together and agrees through all its globes, and even the most disjointed things are united, even to the small eyes of mortals. Because of the vacuum, the planets are not worn down or scattered by their motion. Because of the vacuum, the earth is revolved by its daily motion, and its light is not separated from its **exhalations** <note>original: *effluviis*; the vapors or particles rising from the Earth that make up the lower atmosphere</note>, but the system of air proceeds forward together, unshaken. Because of the vacuum, comets are also carried peacefully in the higher regions, and, though driven by the Sun, they are not scattered by physical resistance or **impenetrability** <note>original: *antitypia*; a Greek-derived term meaning the resistance of matter that prevents two bodies from occupying the same space at once</note>. For if ignited matter were to rush through a vacuum with the swiftest motion, it would not drag a point of flame behind it in any way, but the whole flame would proceed forward uniform and unshaken on all sides. But **"flying stars"** <note>original: *stellae volantes*; a historical term for meteors or shooting stars</note>, which arise burning in the air not far from the earth, leave a flaming tail behind them when they move, due to the resistance of the air.

A vacuum must exist, unless bodies were standing packed together on all sides.

If there were no separation and distinction of the celestial globes by a vacuum, they would run into each other.

If there were no vacuum, the motions of the globes would shake those intermediate natures too much and scatter them.

If there were no vacuum, it would be necessary to posit many frivolous and intricate spheres (with the most absurd contradictions of motions) and confusions of the heavens.

### C H A P T E R  X X I I I.

->*Philosophers, being ignorant of the nature of the Earth, imagined that there were four bodies among us which were elements and the first principles of bodies.*<-

We have previously spoken concerning the firm substance of the terrestrial globe, and of the power and quantity of the waters floating upon its surface. It will now also be necessary to explain the nature of the bodies immediately surrounding it, since there has been various debate among the ancients, as well as some more recent scholars, concerning the number and powers of certain **elements** <note>original: *elementorum*; the basic building blocks of matter in ancient science, typically Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note>. For not all of them believed that the globe of the earth was so predominant or supplied so much of the world's matter. Instead, because air was poured around everywhere outside the uppermost surface to an uncertain height, and because they saw many bodies being generated in that higher place, they thought that this lower world possessed diverse bodies, serving as certain elements from which the **first principles** <note>original: *primordia*; the fundamental origins or "seeds" of natural things</note> of natural things emerged. They held that elements are, as it were, the sources of things and of matter.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
An element is that from which something is made, in which it is inherently contained, and which is indivisible according to its kind.

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
Elements are bodies which can by no means be divided into bodies of different forms, and from the mixing of which the diverse species of generated things are made.

<margin>Zeno</margin>
An element is that from which things that are made proceed, and into which they are finally dissolved.

<margin>Speusippus</margin>
An element is that which composes things and dissolves those that are composed.

<margin>Galen</margin>
An element is the smallest portion of a thing.

Thus, the definition of an "element" has been treated in various ways, with no less contention than that concerning the elements themselves and their number; for false suppositions give birth to infinite chatterings.

<summary>This page critiques the traditional Greek and Medieval understanding of the four elements by providing various historical definitions from figures like Aristotle and Galen, arguing that ignorance of the Earth's true nature led to these complex but flawed theories.</summary>
