## CHAPTER XXIV.

->*Concerning the elements, and those primary qualities, and how they exist within mixtures.*<-

They say that the elements, in the generation of a **mixture** <term>mixtio; the process of combining the four basic elements to create a new, unified substance</term>, temper one another; and that heat, cold, moisture, and dryness are reduced, their intensities and sharp points blunted, so that they are made suitable for the nature of the mixture, and thus the mixture is born. In this view, neither the elements themselves nor their extreme contraries serve as the matter of the thing; instead, it is their "mean" or middle state, tempered to the nature of the mixture, by which the nature and species of the mixture receives its limit and direction. From this, the various species of mixtures arise from the various proportions of their **temperament** <term>temperamentum; the specific balance or "tuning" of the four primary qualities in a body</term>; for example, one might be hot to cold in a twofold proportion, another in a threefold; and the same for the dry and the moist.

Furthermore, they claim that all **concrete bodies** <note>original: *concreta corpora*; solid, physical substances formed from the condensation or "growing together" of simpler parts</note> which are situated around the central place consist of all the simple elements. They believe Earth is mixed into all things because they seem to participate in the nature of the place where they were born; and Water is mixed in because those things which are composed of many natures must be bounded or given form, and Water can easily provide boundaries for all simple things. Moreover, they argue that Earth cannot hold together without moisture, but that Water contains it: for if moisture were entirely taken away from it, it would crumble away. They further claim that all things consist of Air and Fire because these are the contraries of Earth and Water. For since the origins of things come from contraries, if one of the extreme contraries is present, they believe the other must also be present. 

Perhaps they would have spoken more truly if they had said that concrete bodies arise in the generation of mixtures according to the "climate" of the mixture, and are tempered to the norm of their species. For how can things be tempered if they do not exist, or if they are not found among us according to their own dogmas? But it is most absurd of all to suggest that the various species of mixtures arise from a varying proportion of...

Yet crystal is a stone, a concrete body formed from water, in which no heat exists. Ice arises from extreme and stiffening cold, by which all fiery power is more certainly driven away. This same permanent cold, prevailing over all else, through the long passage of time compels ice to become crystal. But from cold itself no fire can arise, nor can fire be admitted into crystal or the coldest ice. 

Now, if a mild fire can change other elements—especially water, its contrary—then how much more so the fervor and glowing furnaces in which, by art, all things are burned beyond any power of nature. For this reason, water is entirely driven out of **lime** <term>calx; calcium oxide, produced by heating limestone. Nevertheless, lime remains a mixture. Therefore, we should be less inclined to believe that all elements exist in all things.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

->On heat.<-

Just as they believe bodies consist of the elements, so they think their qualities—which they call "primary"—are changed and transformed into various natures. Heat, indeed, which is both foremost and most celebrated for the frequency of its many effects, is observed by philosophers with the greatest reason and held in the highest honor. Yet it seems to me they have never understood what that most powerful force truly is, since they importunely thrust upon us one or two wretched shadows of a definition. For what does that definition show, or what distinction is made by an effect found only in certain bodies, namely: *gathering things of the same kind, and separating things of different kinds*? <note>original: "congregans homogenea, & disgregans heterogenea"</note> It is as if you said a human is an animal that pulls up thistles and briars and brings forth fruit; though that is the labor of the farmer, not the definition of the man. In the same way, heat in metals and certain other things gathers what is similar and separates what is different; but in most things, this effect never appears. ### CHAPTER XXVII.

->*That celestial heat so often mentioned by Philosophers; elemental heat; and also the heat in the bodies of animals, are heats of one and the same nature.*<-

There is great weight and authority in the assertions and agreements of all the Philosophers regarding the power of celestial bodies operating upon the earth; and the heat which seems to flow down divinely from the stars, especially the Sun, appears to act upon lower things with a greater and more excellent power, and to move them, than any other heat that is excited among us in any way. This is not only because all things are seen to grow and flourish because of it, but also because without it all things lie rough and desolate.

The Ancients and the Platonists thought this was not merely a quality, but a certain ethereal body, extremely thin, penetrating all things equally; which some of them were even accustomed to call the "great nursery of nature" <note>original: *magnum naturæ seminarium*</note>. Others, indeed, thought it was not a body, though it permeates the elements; they believed that the celestial, ethereal body is separate from the elements, and that its natural motion is circular. From this body, however, light, motion, and ethereal warmth flow into the elements—not as a body itself, but as an ethereal quality that penetrates and permeates all elements. Aristotle says this is not the heat of fire, but "something proportionate to the element of the stars" <note>Aristotle argued in *On the Generation of Animals* that the heat in seeds and living things was different from fire, being more akin to the element of the stars</note>; a sentiment which indeed wanders far from the truth. For heat is not produced by the motion of the stars; for bodies only grow hot through motion when more solid or material things clash and are shaken together with sufficient resistance. But neither do bodies among us, when drawn by circular motion...

### C H A P T E R  X X V I I I.

->On the nature of heat.<-

If anything in the nature of things is especially to be understood and cherished, it must be that by which we live, and by which the globe of the earth exists and is transformed with such incredible variety and perpetual succession. Indeed, this study is most especially to be embraced after so many errors about heat have been repeated over and over; because although countless authors have written countless volumes about heat and commented on it in various ways, no one until now has correctly defined what heat is, nor properly demonstrated its essence, nature, power, or quality. Only a certain definition of Aristotle regarding heat has been accepted, through which its nature is no more clearly seen than when a baker sits by his oven, or a metal smelter sits by his glowing furnaces. Thus he says in Book 2 of *On Generation*: "For heat is that which brings together things of the same kind" <note>original Greek: θερμὸν γάρ ἐστι τὸ συγκρῖνον τὰ ὁμογενῆ</note>; that is, *heat is that which gathers homogeneous things.* <term>Homogeneous: things of the same nature or substance.</term> Here heat is defined by a certain secondary effect found in specific bodies. But even that effect does not follow from every kind of heat. Perhaps a metal smelter, seeing lead flow out through fire purified from its **dross** <note>original: *recremento*, the waste matter or slag left after smelting.</note>, was the first to dream that such an effect was a perpetual and essential characteristic of all heat. Yet a small amount of heat does not gather anything in such a way, and the most intense heat consumes it entirely. If **wax** <note>original: *Cera*</note>, **resin** <note>original: *Resina*</note>, and **cinnabar** <note>original: *Cinnabaris*, a toxic red mineral used as a pigment.</note> are firmly mixed together in **sealing wax** <note>original: *sigillaria cera*</note>, are they gathered back into their individual parts by fire or heat? They grow hot, they melt, they burn, but they are not gathered separately. That interpretation of Aristotle's followers is ridiculous: *heat gathers things of the same kind and scatters things of different kinds* <term>Heterogeneous: things of a different nature or substance.</term>; as when wood is applied to fire, it joins fire to fire, such as smoke,

...and air to air, just as vapor flowing and breathing out from moisture goes to vapor; and water to water, as moisture dripping through the extremities goes to moisture; and earth to earth, as ash goes to ash. But these are more than **old wives' tales** <note>original: *anilia*; the author is dismissing traditional scholastic explanations as superstitious or unlearned.</note>, which have taken such impure roots in philosophy that it has been permitted to gather almost no suitable fruits from the vast heaps of writers and interpreters.

Therefore, what heat is will appear better, and we will understand it more easily, once we have investigated its origin and growth, its failures and effects. Heat arises first from above, from light. For when the light of the Sun is sent down into bodies, it heats them by striking them. Furthermore, harder bodies, which also contain moisture within, grow hot by rubbing and strike out fires; bodies also grow warm from motion, yet not because of the motion itself, but from an external source. Thus animals **boil over** <note>original: *effervescunt*; referring to the internal "heat" of living metabolism.</note>, and thus fires once conceived glow more brightly. But all heat does not remain; rather, without a continued cause, it perishes and is extinguished.

Now indeed, it has been sufficiently confirmed before that heat is not in that "superior element" of fire <note>The author rejects the medieval concept of a "Sphere of Fire" located between the Earth's atmosphere and the moon.</note>, because that does not exist in the nature of things. In the air, if the Sun is absent, heat vanishes. <margin>Chapter 7.</margin> Just as bodies that are generated conceive heat, so after some time that heat vanishes. It seems, therefore, that heat is an **act of the body**. However, all heats have **kindling** <note>original: *fomites*, meaning tinder or the material that sustains a fire.</note>. And fire is only an excess of heat, while its **fodder** <note>original: *pabulum*; the fuel or nourishment for the heat.</note> is like nourishment. Moreover, the kindling and fodder are **humors** <term>Humors: the vital fluids of a body—typically blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperature.</term>; for the most violent heats and fires, these are fatty humors, but for other moderate heats, they are fatty and watery ones. All of these, while they provide the matter for the heat, are **thinned out** <note>original: *attenuantur*; the process of a liquid becoming vapor or a thinner substance through heat.</note>. Almost all philosophers maintain that heat in bodies is of two kinds: either **actual** or **potential** <note>original: *actu, aut potestate*; standard Aristotelian terms for something currently manifesting a quality versus something having the latent power to produce it.</note>. Especially by reason of matter, when it is acted upon by internal heat, it ignites the nearest humors by thinning them. Pure wine, however, performs this powerfully through its own internal action, and is most easily dissolved by the animal's heat, sending a burning spirit into the blood. The same is achieved most of all by **burning wine** and that which is called the **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini*; an early term for distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note>.

Now indeed, since some things are called **actually cold** <note>original: *frigida actu*</note>, such as icy water, or **potentially cold**, such as Plantain or Purslane, it is manifest that all these things are hot by nature, and they arise and grow by means of heat. However, they are called cold because they do not possess a degree of heat that corresponds to human heat. For this reason, water is felt by us as cold, being different and foreign to our own **temperament** <note>original: *temperamento*; the unique balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's health and personality.</note>. ### CHAPTER XXIX.

->*On the heat of the Earth, Air, Water, and Fire.*<-

We must consider whether that firm nature of the earth possesses its own heats, and also whether the entire power of the waters is warm, as well as the air that surrounds us. Now, the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for walking about the Lyceum in Athens while teaching. They categorized the world into four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> define the whole true earth as a cold and dry element; and yet, since it is situated furthest from the sources of heat <note>Likely referring to the sun or the celestial spheres.</note>, it ought to be even colder than water, if only that empty ordering of the elements were true. But then the fable would not fit in all respects, since coldness ought to predominate in water.

Throughout the entire periphery of the earth, vapors flow out as effects of heat; the earth also, as if in a womb and matrix, nourishes all plants and fosters them with an implanted heat. Fires erupt in the bowels of the earth, and hot springs burst forth from the ground. All the waters that spring up across the whole world have an innate and natural heat. In winter, men in deep caves and caverns feel the air to be milder, not harsh and frozen as it is above the ground and in the open air. Likewise, in summer, they live underground without shivering, feeling only that temperate state destined for the earth itself. It has been said quite often that the earth is not a body so foul, as if it were the dregs of the universe, nor is it immobile, rigid, and barren, ex— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the author is likely about to argue that the earth is a living, productive body.</note>

...[the earth's] juice <note>original: *succum*</note> is impure; for it excels, like the other stars, by its own primary powers. It possesses a motion implanted within its mass, and a perennial activity of its innate humor. Indeed, that activity is propagated by the light and alliance of the other stars, not by the motion of the heavens or the stars as the common crowd of philosophers <note>original: *vulgus philosophantium*</note> believes. For this reason, all the fluids around the earth possess heat: the rivers, ponds, seas, and the surrounding air. Indeed, all waters flow as much from heat as they do with an innate warmth.

The ancients, however, maintain that water is the coldest element.

Yet Aristotle sometimes holds that the sea is warm due to the mixture of "burnt matter" <note>Aristotle's theory in *Meteorology* suggested that "dry exhalations" (smoky or salty) mixed with water to create the sea's warmth and saltiness.</note>, even while maintaining that the element of water itself is supremely cold. The commentators and the common mob of philosophers "give their hands" <note>original: *dant manus*; a Latin idiom meaning to yield or agree.</note> to Aristotle on this point. <margin>**Francesco Patrizi** in his *New Philosophy* <note>Francesco Patrizi da Cherso (1529–1597) was a prominent critic of Aristotelianism who argued that heat and light were the primary principles of the universe.</note></margin> Truly, all water is warm—not from some "primeval heat" discovered by **Francesco Patrizi**, but from that heat which concurs with its own form and existence, and which is common to the entire earth. It is from this heat that water possesses its fluid nature.

But if this activity should cease, or if it should slacken greatly in the surrounding air, then the heat of the water and its natural power (derived from that activity) suffers a "failing" <note>original: *deliquium*</note> in its immediate parts and surfaces, and **ice** <note>original: *glacies*</note> comes into being. Water—which is preserved by the air as if by a garment—recedes from its own power when the heat within it is greatly diminished or extinguished. It cannot save itself, but is wretchedly vexed by a miserable "privation" <note>In Aristotelian logic, "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present (like blindness being the privation of sight).</note> and puts on a different form. 

Hence, ice is formed from water when its heat is extinguished. **Crystals** <note>original: *Crystalla*</note> also, as well as shining **specular stones** <note>original: *lapides splendentes speculares*; likely refers to transparent minerals like mica or selenite.</note> and transparent **gems**, are formed from "juices" in the same way. In the air, too, icy hailstones exist; for there are both snowy and icy varieties of **hail** <note>original: *grandines*</note>.

Indeed, unless perpetual auxiliary forces were excited from the earth, the **Air** would both slacken its activity and yield to the incumbent vacuum, leading to the privation of all existing things. For this reason, cold seems to dominate, yet cold is actually nothing, just as it is brought in from nothing <note>The author argues that cold is not a "thing" or a force, but merely the absence of heat.</note>. # BOOK I. 87

In the frigid zones, when the Sun is absent and has moved toward the opposite Tropic, almost all the air in those regions seems to have vanished. The upper parts of the land and the seas—having set aside their warmth and ceased their activity—remain rough, frozen, and inaccessible. Nor can the internal forces of the earth emit their "vital breath" <note>original: *spiritum*; in this context, it refers to the life-giving vapors or heat believed to circulate within the globe</note> and warm disposition, or produce flowering growths on the surface, without the brilliance of the Sun. 

For although the earth is capable of emitting this breath through its own internal activity, the outer parts of the ground are rendered so rigid by the cold of the air that these vapors cannot break through; instead, they are extinguished before they can flow into the open when the Sun has been absent for a long period of time. In the same way, because of the lack of light or the cold of the surrounding air, the waters freeze—not at the bottom, but in the closest and superficial parts, which are exposed to harm and injury. 

However, when the Sun returns, the ice is melted and the waters recover their former natural state; for their natural heat is restored by the light of the Sun. Therefore, all waters are warm, including both the rivers and all the seas. Within them, animals are born and live; indeed, life emerges more abundantly in the waters than it usually does for other animals in the air—from the smallest creatures to the largest, and across a vast number of species. 

Since all life is bound up with heat, it would be foolish to think that so many living things could emerge in a body that was "supremely cold" <note>A direct challenge to the Aristotelian definition of water as the element of cold.</note>. Furthermore, those things which flow, flow because of heat; it is by the loss of heat that they become hardened, just like all metals, glass, pearls, and the fatty juices that become firm. Therefore, all water is warm. 

As for the fact that waters feel cold to our senses, this occurs because our own bodies are warmer; we judge something to be "cold" simply because it is *less* warm than we are. Nevertheless, water possesses its own heat, which is warmed more or less by its surroundings.

# PHYSIOLOGY

### CHAPTER XXX.

->*Heat is not produced by the motion of the Sun and the friction of the air.*<-

<margin>See chapter 7, pages 11, 12, 13.</margin>
Aristotle believed that heat and light were produced by the stars because the air is rubbed <note>original: *fricatur*; friction was a common explanation for celestial heat in ancient physics</note> by their motion; for motion typically ignites wood, stones, and iron. He thought it was therefore more reasonable that this should happen in the air, which is closer to the element of fire. However, the heavens do not rub against the air, because the celestial sphere does not drag or move the air along with its own motion. We have sufficiently debunked the opinion elsewhere that the elements are drawn or rotated by the heavens; furthermore, the "element of fire" does not occupy the upper regions in the way taught by common error. Aristotle’s supporting argument is no less flawed: he says that this occurs with arrows in flight, claiming they are heated so much that the lead within them melts; and since this happens to the arrows, he concludes the surrounding air must necessarily suffer the same effect. This is entirely false; for even a motion a thousand times faster than an arrow has never forced lead to melt. Even musket balls <note>original: *Sclopetorum globuli*; this reference to firearms serves as a "modern" 16th/17th-century rebuttal to Aristotle’s ancient examples</note>, which travel much faster than any arrow, do not melt at all, even though they are propelled by a penetrating fiery force.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

->*Heat is not a quality.*<-

Heat is not truly a "quality," whether primary or secondary <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "qualities" were the basic properties of matter, like hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>; rather, it is an activity <note>original: *actus*; the author argues heat is a process or dynamic state rather than a static property</note>. It can be labeled with the name "quality" only insofar as it is recognized by our senses, and because bodies that are hot are described as having that "quality." Heat is truly an activity, and all things that grow warm do so in conjunction with moisture; for every part of the earth, though it may seem dry, nevertheless possesses its own "juice" or internal moisture. Those things which are extremely dry are nonetheless heated by the surrounding environment,

### CHAPTER XXXII.

#### ->*That the thinning of moisture occurs through friction, and does not follow after heat as if caused by it, so much so that the cause of thinning is joined simultaneously with the heat.*<-

Perhaps some will insist that heat does not come from friction <note>original: *attritione*; the rubbing or wearing down of substances</note>, but rather that the thinning of moisture <note>original: *humorum*; in this context, "humor" refers to a fundamental fluid or subtle substance within all matter</note> is caused by heat. Yet, when flint is struck against iron, in that very blow—as the moisture is thinned—heat is felt, or rather an excess of heat, which is called fire. And in this case, the thinning does not follow the heat; instead, the heat follows from the thinning, or from the moisture that has already been thinned. Therefore, heat is moisture in action, or fire is moisture in a more vehement state of action. 

Light, which flows from the Sun's brightness, is not hot in itself until it strikes a body, thinning the moisture implanted within it or immediately surrounding it; from this comes that sensation of heat. Those who think that the heat of the day exists because of the reflection of light or rays upon the earth are greatly mistaken, as we shall teach more extensively elsewhere. Likewise, light burning through a mirror creates heat by melting <note>original: *fundendo*; literally "pouring out" or "liquefying"</note> the humors, whether it be a concave mirror or transparent glass.

Therefore, the origins of heat are derived from the thinning <term>attenuatio: the process of making a substance less dense or more "subtle," which the author views as the primary cause of thermal energy</term> of moisture; indeed, fire and heat, through continuity and proximity, thin the neighboring humors and excite heat. For action brings about action, and the fiery act creeps through the moisture.

# CHAPTER XXXIII.

## On Cold.

The nature of cold was also debated in various ways by the ancients. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the "peripatos" or covered walkways of the Lyceum in Athens.</note> maintain that cold is a "primary quality" <note>In ancient physics, the four primary qualities were Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry; these were the building blocks of all matter.</note>—active and efficient, not inert and passive like moisture and dryness. They establish that cold is that which compels and gathers *both things of the same kind and those of a different nature.* In this way, cold shares the same defining characteristic as heat in most respects. For, in their opinion, heat gathers homogeneous things <note>original: *homogenea*; things of the same kind or substance</note>; and so too, cold gathers homogeneous things. Thus, things that are positioned as complete opposites and produce opposite effects are granted the same efficiency as their singular and notable distinction. But this praise of cold—as with the praise of heat before—derived from a single effect, is a meager and barren tribute, drawn from a quite sterile and empty storehouse.

But we must first ask whether there is some primary force of cold, and a matter innate to cold, by whose presence and perception all other things become cold; or rather, just as they say darkness is the deprivation of light, and rest the deprivation of motion, so too cold might be the deprivation of heat. This indeed seems to be the case, since cold appears quiet while heat appears mobile; and a warm thing is cooled not by the addition of anything new, but by the departure of heat. If the power of cold were so illustrious in nature, it ought to prevail most in those elements <note>Namely Earth and Water, which were traditionally categorized as "cold" elements in the Aristotelian system.</note> thought to be cold; but anyone can easily see that this is not the case.

For neither any parts of the earth nor the water are so cold that they are not far surpassed by other intensities of chill. Do not snow, hail, ice, and frost contain much colder matter? Water hardens into ice because of cold, yet that cold is not derived from the water itself, but is implanted...

...from the surrounding exterior. For if water were the coldest of substances, why would it not freeze by itself? In that case, freezing would happen to it just as much—indeed even more—in the middle or at the bottom than on the surface. But who has ever seen rivers frozen in their middle and deepest parts, rather than on the outermost surface? Or who has ever dug up earth that was colder than ice, snow, or hail? Or found water solidified into ice in the deepest caverns? Therefore, that which is coldest exists in the surroundings <note>original: *in ambienti*; referring to the atmosphere or the air surrounding the earth</note>, not within the globe of the earth. How it exists in the surroundings, however, must be determined later.

But that reasoning regarding cold might seem suspicious, as it could overthrow many of the illustrious powers of things; it would mean they are no longer qualities or habits <term>habits: from the Latin *habitus*, referring to a stable state or physical disposition of a substance</term>, but should be considered privations <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should normally be present, such as "silence" being the absence of "sound"</term> of habits and qualities. For example, gravity would be the privation of levity, hardness the absence of softness, sweetness the absence of bitterness, blackness the absence of whiteness, and ultimately all those things which are opposites by their very nature. But since the logic for most of these is quite different—because some are merely bare conditions and names we impose, while others are clearly existing entities—no assertion that cold is a distinct "existing thing" can be drawn from comparison, similarity, or analogy.

They also say that every privation is lazy and idle, like blindness, deafness, silence, or death; since privation is both a removal of forms <term>forms: the essential "blueprints" or defining structures of matter in ancient physics</term> from their proper state and an overturning of nature, rather than being a nature in itself. Yet cold is able to affect and change the bodies it inhabits no less than heat can. For by its efficiency, many things are frozen, many things accumulate and grow upon objects, and many are made dense. Nor should its stability and sluggishness be considered "inert"; rather, it is a strong and firm power, possessing the momentum and vigor to restrain and hold things together. Yet, we conclude that cold is brought about by nothing other than the "flight" of heat, as the moisture itself, having been worn down by force, strives to return to its original state: just as blindness occurs when the passages of sight are blocked.

# PHYSIOLOGY

Thus, in the case of heated bodies, cold follows as if it were a **privation** <term>privation: the absence of a quality that is normally present</term>, caused by the flight of heat. That this happens because the body is casting out heat, rather than because some "quality of cold" is pressing upon it, is apparent from this: gold, iron, or any other metal, when they are glowing white-hot from fire and then placed in the shade for several hours, become much colder than the surrounding air with which they ought to be balanced. Nor are they cooled beyond their current effective power; rather, they later return to their original **temperament** <term>temperament: the characteristic balance of qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a substance</term>. 

Indeed, if they want water to be frozen by a "quality of cold," I would ask: in what subject does that quality reside, and from where is it derived? If it comes from the air, how is it that all air—which is otherwise warm—always overcomes that most cold element in winter, constricting it and changing it into an almost new form? In the same way, **opaque bodies** mixed with bright and transparent ones take away their splendor; even more, opaque bodies placed near luminous ones diminish their clarity. 

Nothing, therefore, produces cold that is not also produced by the **flight of heat** <note>original: *caloris fugâ*; the idea that heat physically leaves a body</note>. Since bodies are acted upon by heat in various ways—being made of dissimilar matter and driven by various forms—it is by that same flight of dissimilar heats that the various "faces" of things arise, which are mistakenly thought to be created by the strength of cold as if it were an existing nature. 

Furthermore, bodies that are "less warm" are rendered cold. Water, which by its own nature (as said before) is warm, is frozen in winter by the air, which is less warm. Vapors, when they stretch upward into clouds that are less warm, are constricted into hail by the surrounding area of a colder body; this happens especially in the springtime, because of the unequal temperament of the air. 

Bodies that are less warm, such as marble or metal, when placed against the human body, sometimes affect and injure it severely—not so much by "sending in cold" as if it were a quality, but rather by **extinguishing and destroying the heat** of the person through the mass of the less-warm matter in an unfavorable proximity. Thus, the worn-down moisture thickens, and the heat is diminished;

This happens because of a violent and sudden return to its former state, as the moisture produced by friction <note>original: *attritus humor*</note> is suddenly constricted, a constriction made stronger by the sudden **flight of heat**. In the same way, things thrown with force are carried beyond their own proper destination.

They also claim that no **privation** <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</term> allows for increase or decrease. You could not rightly say, for example, that among those who are blind, one is more blind than another; nor that among those who are silent, one speaks less than another; nor that among those who are dead, one is more dead than another. Yet in cold things, "more" and "less," "greatly" and "slightly," as well as **intensity and relaxation** <term>intensity and relaxation: *intensio* and *remissio*, technical terms in medieval and Renaissance physics for the strengthening or weakening of a physical quality</term> are found far and wide, just as they are in hot things. 

But we also truly understand that if any body in our presence were to contract due to the flight, breathing out, and extinction of all heat, no other body could be found colder than it. Death is indeed the total privation of health and life, just as sickness and madness are the privation of perfect health. Blindness, too, is the absolute privation of sight; yet those who see poorly are deprived of the desired light according to "more" or "less." 

Thus noise, screeching, silence, and deep silence, the dead of night, or subterranean caves contain the deprivation of light and extreme darkness. Nevertheless, darkness is less heavy when clouds are thin, so that the light of stars appears a little, and even less so when dawn approaches. Therefore, just as air is made dark as light departs, so too when heat migrates, cold air remains—and it is nothing other than a mere privation. For this reason, all such reasoning is vain and **sophistical** <note>original: *sophistica*; referring to logical fallacies or deceptive arguments</note>, since they always present privation as if it were the total removal of an existing quality; whereas privation, from the full strength of quality and heat to its ultimate extinction and in— <note>The catchword "teritum" completes the word *interitum*, meaning destruction or ruin, on the following page.</note>

# PHYSIOLOGY

...destruction, it is in reality nothing that exists, but a name applied to cold according to the manner and degree of vanishing heat. They also claim that we perceive cold through our senses just as we do heat. However, a **privation** <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present, like darkness being the absence of light</term> cannot be seen, touched, heard, or known through any other senses. But in truth, cold is not known or perceived by the senses; rather, less-warm bodies affect our warmer bodies and diminish our heat. This is not because "cold" is sent from one body into another as a physical quality, but because a body lacking in heat strikes and **tempers** <note>original: *temperat* — in this context, it means to modify or "cool down" the temperature of a hotter object through contact</note> another body through contact. Thus, in succession, the nearest parts change those adjacent to them, being changed themselves in the process.

Those who consider cold to be an actual quality are also greatly troubled; they create confusion with conflicting opinions regarding which specific body or element it primarily resides in. For the **Stoics** <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that held the universe was composed of active and passive principles</note> attribute primary cold to the air; **Empedocles** and **Strato** <note>Early Greek natural philosophers</note> attribute it to moisture. To others, it seems to reside in the earth, while **Aristotle** <note>The highly influential Greek philosopher whose "four elements" theory dominated science for centuries</note> assigns the primary quality of cold to water. It is easy for anyone to see how stubbornly all of them defend their opinions with the poorest and most futile arguments. And it is no wonder, since—poor souls!—they wish to present that which is nothing in nature as if it were something existing, and they foolishly try to establish it upon the broadest foundations. 

But that cold is nothing, and of no consequence—neither a quality contrary to heat nor an opposing active force—appears clearly from this: water is converted into air by heat, and the water cannot resist this in any way without perishing. However, air does not always turn into water because of cold, nor does it return to water with such certainty. For in the **Northern regions** <note>original: *Borealibus regionibus*</note> during winter, or even in the greatest cold, the air does not liquefy. It is also obvious that rain rarely if ever falls there in winter; the air there far surpasses all water in its degree of coldness. For there is another reason for the generation of moisture from air, other than that which [comes] from cold...

Heat arises from motion and light; if cold were governed by the opposite principle, then cold would grow from rest and darkness. However, warm bodies remain warm even while at rest; likewise, they do not grow cold in the darkness unless the surrounding body is first cold, the proximity of which changes the other body.

Solid bodies, such as metals, harder stones, and especially glass and gems—such as crystal and diamond—seem colder than other bodies because they are not warmed by their surroundings in the same way. Air does not have the same access to their surfaces as it does with wood or clothing; therefore, they receive little warmth from the air.

Cold proceeds neither from water nor from earth, but it is a **privation of action** <note>original: *privatio actus* — the idea that cold is not a thing itself, but simply the lack of the "action" or energy that creates heat</note>; thus, in a vacuum, it is the privation of heat.

->On Natural Attraction.<-

<page-num>96</page-num>
<header>ON NATURAL PHILOSOPHY</header>

...actions, as well as violent motions in mechanics. We must therefore speak of attraction in natural things: how it occurs, in which types of natures it flourishes, and what its true causes are.

True attraction, as **Averroës** <note>original: *Averroës* — also known as Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to Renaissance science</note> teaches in the seventh book of his *Physics*, is that in which the attractor moves along with the thing being attracted; this happens when the attracted object is not at rest in relation to the attractor, as seen in voluntary powers and in most natural powers. An attraction in which the attractor remains at rest while the attracted object moves is not "true" attraction; rather, the attracted object moves by its own impulse toward the attractor in order to reach its own perfection. However, we use the term "attraction" to describe the local motion of one body toward another—specifically of the attracted toward the attractor—in cases where the attractor remains still.

Philosophers establish certain causes for attraction, while Physicians enumerate many others, as well as many different bodies that act as attractors. Indeed, all things that grow <note>original: *vegetantur* — referring to the "vegetative soul" or the life force of plants</note> lure a healthful and beneficial juice to themselves, just as plants do by driving their roots into the earth. Animals likewise draw in what benefits them through their stomachs and the primary veins of the **mesentery** <term>mesentery: the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall; here, it refers to the pathways of nutrient absorption</term>, with heat promoting the entire process along with the specific form of the organism; the bodies of all growing things attract nutrients in this same way.

However, heat and warm things applied from the outside—whether they be physical bodies or medicines—are falsely said to "attract." Thus, that entire vast collection <note>original: *sylva* — literally "forest," a common Renaissance metaphor for a dense collection of information or examples</note> of "attracting medicines" is vain and useless. For no heat, whether from the Sun or from any burning object, lures bodies or humors to itself, despite what the entire schools of Philosophers and Physicians falsely teach. Likewise, natural attractions do not occur because of the properties of a substance, as was the opinion of **Galen** <note>original: *Galeni* — Galen of Pergamon, the Roman-era physician whose theories on the four humors dominated medicine for over a millennium</note>. Those things which are drawn or lifted up by the succession of bodies—due to the **avoidance of a vacuum** <note>original: *vacui fugam* — the classical theory that nature "abhors a vacuum" and moves matter automatically to prevent empty space</note>—are indeed real motions, but they are "violent" motions, not according to the natural order. We must discuss these attractions, which are commonly attributed to nature, so that these perverse and useless follies—which are supported by the judgment of almost everyone—may be utterly erased.

For we have established that the vegetative power, or the **soul**, is a formal organic act; and that the heat of plants (just like that of animals) is the act of **thinning the moisture** <note>original: *attenuationis humoris* — the process of making fluids less dense so they can move through the organism</note>. Life, then, is the combined act of heat and the soul. Whether you prefer to call it the soul or the "working substantial form," life exists through the vigor of both. 

Indeed, the substantial form remains dormant for a long time without suitable heat and produces no effect, as can be seen in **seeds**. Seeds do not germinate or grow until they are moved by being soaked in warm sap. But when the suitable moisture is dissolved through thinning, they pour themselves forth and send out roots as proper instruments for nutrition; they germinate further and rise up. 

In this way, once the matter has been attracted by a vital act, it is carried through the power of life into the roots, the trunk, the branches, and the fruits; and this attraction is truly natural. However, those who believe the **four elements** are the primary origins of things—and who rely on the four primary qualities—preach much about heat. But the **Physicians** <note>original: *Medici*</note> insist that humors are drawn to specific parts by heat, as when **thapsia** <term>thapsia: a genus of plants known as "deadly carrots," used in ancient medicine to cause skin irritation and "draw" fluids to the surface</term>, a **mustard plaster** <note>original: *sinapismus*</note>, or a **pitch plaster** <term>dropax: a topical plaster made of pitch and oil, used to warm the skin or remove hair</term> is applied externally to the skin; the skin becomes flushed with redness, and the part often rises and swells. They argue this could not happen unless those hot medicines possessed a power of attraction.

But this is judged to be the work of heat through poor reasoning. Acrid substances "bite" the skin, and when applied to the human body, they wear down the humor; this worn-down humor grows hot and flows, and **Nature** <note>the internal "vital force" or intelligence that governs the body's health</note>—disturbed in a fluid body—raises the part and sends blood to that location to bring assistance and dilute the evil. In those who are **plethoric** <term>plethoric: having an excess of blood or bodily fluids</term> or **cacochymic** <term>cacochymic: suffering from "bad humors" or an unhealthy balance of bodily fluids</term>, even greater amounts of humors flow together. Thus, humors often gather at the application of a hot medicine, yet not because the heat itself attracts them. In the same way, **pain** <note>original: *dolor*</note> is said by Physicians to "attract," yet pain does not truly allure the humors; rather, so that Nature may succor the aching part, she sends blood. From this, tumors and **inflammations** <note>original: *inflammationes*</note> often arise, as the humors weigh down too heavily from such stimulation.

Full bodies attract little or nothing, as they are less in need of saturation, until the internal humors have been altered by the flow of heat. Growing bodies, however, attract immediately, because their internal spaces become wider and nutrients flow in more abundantly.

## CHAPTER XXXV.

->*On attraction caused by pain.*<-

And truly, these things happen because of pain no differently than when a riot is stirred up in some part of a city; the people flock to that area in crowds to bring help, sometimes even so hastily and confusedly that a greater disturbance follows. No **Philosopher** <note>original: *Philosophus* — in this period, a "natural philosopher" or scientist</note> would say that those first rioting attract the others who run to them; although the common people might say in everyday speech that brawls and much more serious riots "attract" [others]. Therefore, in the same way, pain causes **fluxions of humors** <note>original: *fluxiones humorum* — the movement of bodily fluids like blood or lymph toward an injured or inflamed site</note> by accident. 

External heat, or hot things applied to bodies in any way, do not attract at all—not glowing iron, nor a **cautery** <term>cautery: a hot iron used by surgeons to sear tissue, stop bleeding, or "draw out" impurities</term>, nor eroding or septic substances. But it is thought that there are medicines which can extract splinters, arrows, and spears, even though no such thing can be done by a **plaster** <note>original: *emplastrum* — a medicated paste spread on cloth and applied to the skin</note>, or an ointment, or a **malagma** <term>malagma: a soft, soothing poultice used to soften the skin or reduce inflammation</term>. Rather, by relaxing the skin, irritating nature, and strengthening the parts in which those things are stuck, nature finally (at the proper time) pushes them out, and the splinters and fixed objects exit more easily. 

There are also "drawing" plasters used against the inflicted force of poisons, which do not drain the poisons at all; instead, once the passages are opened, the poisons are excreted together with **pus** <note>original: *sanie* — an old medical term for the discharge from a wound or sore</note> by the work of nature, or else their specific malice is overcome by the form of the medicine. Likewise, crushed garlic or onion applied to a wound inflicted by a rabid dog is an excellent medicine, both by opening the passages and by resisting the malice of the poison.

# PHYSIOLOGY

...medicaments, when applied to the navel and belly, attract [humors], such as the ointment of **Artanita** <term>Artanita: also known as sowbread (Cyclamen), its root was used in ointments to induce purging through the skin</term>. However, those who hold this view are frequently refuted by the great flow from the bowels that results from anointing the body with **mercury** <note>original: *hydrargyri*</note>, even when only the arms and legs are rubbed. Therefore, there is no natural "attraction" belonging to a drug at all. 

Rather, the reasoning behind purging by a medicine should be considered similar to that of a **deciding crisis** <term>deciding crisis: in traditional medicine, a *crisis* is a sudden change in a disease—such as a fever breaking or a heavy sweat—marking the point where nature expels the "morbific" or disease-causing matter</term>. In both cases, an offense and a disturbing annoyance, along with the irritation of a present evil, promote excretion. Nature is led to this—often even against her will—because of intolerable stinging and agitation. This is caused not so much by the heat stirred up by the medicine, but by a certain tumult, gas, and shaking in the intestines provoked by the troublesome **specific form** <term>specific form: a philosophical term meaning the essential character or "inner blueprint" of a substance that dictates its effects</term> of the medicine. 

Nature is so stirred up that she expels not only the medicine itself, but also a quantity of corrupt or swelling humors. Sometimes, when these corrupt humors are lacking—as in healthy bodies—even healthy humors, or quite often even blood itself, flow together so that the harmful medicine may be cast out. This happens especially when sharper substances stick more firmly to the **villi** <term>villi: the small, hair-like fibers or "shaggy" lining of the intestines</term> of the bowels, such as **Scammony** <note>A harsh resinous juice used as a powerful purgative.</note> and **Colocynth** <note>Bitter apple; a desert vine used as a violent laxative.</note>.

For just as nature is inclined to attract those things which are suitable and necessary for nourishment, so she is inclined to expel and send far away from the inner parts those things which are harmful, if she has been irritated by them. In this way, those corrupt humors—sometimes acting on their own—being swollen and stinging, bring about a purging. The same logic applies to certain poisons, such as **mercury sublimate**, **Arsenic**, and **Spanish Fly** <note>original: *Cantharidum*; toxic beetles used in medicine to cause blistering or irritation</note>. When these pass through the body—especially a "slippery" or well-lubricated one—they move through the intestines with a massive evacuation of humors. This is how many who have drunk from poisoned cups escape death (though not without extreme and very serious damage to the intestines). 

But why this or that medicine is better suited to a particular disease is not because it possesses a "familiar" humor of its own which it draws out,

There is also another type of "attraction" which common philosophers attribute to "place." These people think that a place itself attracts, because bodies are moved toward it. Pitiful are those who admire shadows and empty things, and do not investigate the true natures of bodies! In truth, the attraction of a **cupping glass** <term>cucurbita: literally "gourd," these were glass or ceramic vessels used in bloodletting or suction therapy</term> is violent, not natural. For the air, which is thinned by the flame, is forced into a narrow space when it returns to its natural state once the flame is extinguished; it cannot fill the entire space of the cupping glass. Thus, the skin is drawn in by a **flight from a vacuum** <term>vacui fuga: the Aristotelian concept of *horror vacui*, or "nature abhors a vacuum," suggesting that matter is pulled into empty spaces to prevent a void from forming</term>, not by the heat of the cup itself. This is not a consumption of the air, but a thinning; thus the vessel is filled with very thin air.

The rising of vapors from the earth, or from wet linens, is not an "extraction," but rather the breaking down and dissipation of that moisture.

The drawing of oil or fat into the wick of a lamp is likewise not attraction; so that this may be better understood, we provide a description of the lamp.

### ON PHYSIOLOGY
<note>original: *Physiologiae*; in this context, the term refers to the general study of natural philosophy and the properties of matter, rather than just the functions of the human body.</note>

...is rubbed, **B** is not ignited. In a closer approach, it would be extinguished by excessive proximity. For that which nourishes also extinguishes. Fatty substances, however, when rubbed, tend toward a flame of their own accord as they rise from the heat.

Dry things, such as ashes, when they soak up moisture, are incorrectly called "attraction." For since ashes have been placed outside of their natural state once their moisture is consumed, nature tends toward its original consistency, and they now cling together; for all things possess their firmness through moisture. But ashes also soak up moisture when they do not cling well or coalesce tightly into one, because air is pushed out by the water: this is evident in such an experiment by the bubbles rising from the inflow of water.

We must first see, therefore, what attraction is, and in what way—
->it is twofold.<-
<margin>twofold</margin>
Here we deal only with natural attraction, where a body, by a natural instinct, moves another body toward itself. **Attraction** is the motion of a body toward a body that has drawn it. Bodies are drawn by other bodies either while they are moving or while they are still. Thus, a body that has moved returns again to its own seat, having brought another along; even when it does not depart from its place, it sends out a force to move a body, by which it attracts it to itself. Thus, attraction is truly and properly so-called, as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a highly influential Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle shaped medieval European science.</note> teaches.

True attraction, therefore, which is recognized even by common people, is like when a chariot is pulled by a horse, or a plow by an ox. Another type of attraction, more obscure and less apparent, occurring through some faculty, is also called attraction; but improperly.

Attraction from:
- **Plants.**
- **Life.**
- **The spontaneous inclination of nourishment.**
<note>The original uses a large bracket to group these three items under the heading "Attraction from."</note>

The union of a **magnet** <note>original: *magnetis coitio*; the author uses "union" or "coming together" to imply a mutual movement rather than a one-way pull.</note> is not merely attraction by a faculty, but a motion from a faculty in both—in the magnet itself, where it is constant, and in the iron, where it is newly excited.

<term>Magnetis coitio</term> (Magnetic union): The mutual meeting of a magnet and iron.

**B O O K I. 105**

The **attraction of iron by a magnet** is spoken of improperly and in a common way; for the magnet runs to the iron no less than the iron runs toward the magnet. Therefore, the power and efficiency of the meeting of *both* is shown, not just of one. In this way, a strong, **unarmed** magnet <note>original: *inermis*; in the context of historical magnetism, an "unarmed" lodestone is one without a "nasus ferreus" or iron cap/armature used to concentrate its strength</note> (for so we call it when it is without its iron "nose") draws a weight of iron equal to itself. That stone is also lifted high by that same iron, though it is not seized by a smaller quantity of iron. Thus, iron strengthened by the power of the magnet is not able to lift the magnet unless it is also proportional in its own mass; namely, when the magnet seizes an equal weight of iron, and no more.

For if the magnet were so lively and powerful that it did more, the iron—even in a smaller quantity—being more strongly acted upon, would also allure the magnet, just as iron of a smaller quantity becomes powerful enough when acted on by a strong magnet. Thus, the magnet allures more iron than its own weight, and the iron allures more weight than it weighs itself.

The movement of straw toward **amber** <note>original: *electrum*; while this can mean a gold-silver alloy, here it refers to amber, which exhibits static electricity when rubbed</note> is not called "attraction," but rather an **incitement of bodies** through the mediation of moist effluvia <note>The author is describing static electricity, which early modern thinkers often attributed to "effluvia"—invisible, vapor-like emissions that reached out to pull light objects.</note>.

**Attractions are either:**
*   **Absolutely violent.**

**Absolutely violent attractions include:**
*   All mechanical motions.

# BOOK TWO.

## CHAPTER ONE.

### *Concerning the Perceptible Substance of the Earth.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' containing a large letter surrounded by ornate floral and scrollwork designs within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>See chapter 17 of Book 1, *On the Magnet*, and many other places in those same books.</margin>
**D**egarding the magnetic form of the entire earth and its primary force, we have treated it in the preceding sections by looking at its more conspicuous and powerful parts, and we have confirmed by clear and most certain experiments that the whole earth is magnetic. Now, its body and entire substance—which until now has remained hidden from everyone—must be investigated and understood. Setting aside the <term>dogmas of the elements</term> <note>The traditional Aristotelian theory that the world is composed of four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>, we must debate its nature: whether it is one and simple, or composed and joined from various and dissimilar parts. Some of the <term>Ancients</term> <note>Gilbert refers to early Greek philosophers like Thales, who believed water was the primary substance (arche) of the universe.</note> thought that moisture and water were the sole principle of all things; or indeed that dry earth, without moisture, is useless, fruitless, and sterile, and that the entire mass of the earth took its origins from waters and fluids. Thus it must be asked: whether the power of the waters comes from the firm earth, or whether that which is firm in the earth comes from the waters; whether they are distinct and diverse bodies, or born from one beginning; whether they are mutually transformed into one another, or whether all moisture is drawn from the earth; or rather if they are mixed together within the globe, as in other natural things.

The terrestrial globe, which appears diverse to our eyes on its surface, is seen as solid and firm in roughly half of its convexity; but in the other part—dispersed variously among the lands—it is seen as moist, fluid, and more inconsistent in its mobility. Yet the seas, pools, [and lakes] <note>original: *lacus*; the catchword indicating the first word of the next page.</note> have bottoms that are not exceedingly deep...

...lakes and rivers, in which the whole power of the waters is contained; besides the bubbling springs which originate from them and from vapors, and which flow and merge back into those same bodies of water. However, since the depth of the waters is so shallow compared to the entire mass of the globe, water is merely an appendage; it is not a magnitude that is equal to, comparable with, or greater than the Earth itself.

Nor should we judge these two bodies <note>Earth and Water.</note> to be fighting one another with contrary qualities, as the <term>common crowd of philosophers</term> <note>Gilbert refers here to the Aristotelian or Scholastic thinkers who believed that elements were defined by opposing pairs like "Hot/Cold" and "Dry/Wet," and were thus in constant conflict.</note> believes, regarding them as opposing elements and simple bodies. For the body of the Earth is one and uniform, yet it is not "simple" in its qualities in the way many people imagine. Even though it flourishes with a great variety of things on its surface—stirred by its own innate powers and the light of the stars—it suffers a certain decay and imperfection to the depth of a few miles, even as its upper parts bloom with an admirable array of new forms.

The primary substance of the Earth, however, is firm, unified, and stable; it is entirely **magnetic**, filling the interior. It is not dry and parched like lime or inert ash heaped together; rather, it possesses its own "juice" and innate moisture, just like all those things that grow or are generated upon its surface. 

However, the power of fluid matter is more apparent on the surface heights than in the deep interior. This is because the active moisture within the internal parts is thinned into a <term>spirit</term> <note>In the science of Gilbert's time, a "spirit" was a refined, volatile vapor or essence, often thought to be the bridge between matter and life.</note> and rises toward the surface heights, where it turns into water—as if the waters were the very sweat and outpourings of the Earth's massive body. Yet by the light of the stars, and most especially the Sun, this moisture is constantly refined and driven throughout the Earth’s circuit. Although it may sometimes seem to us to vanish due to the Sun's heat, it is merely thinned out; it eventually returns to its original state and falls back upon some region of the surface. For this reason, the Earth feels drier in many places than it is by its true nature, while in other places it is bathed by moisture that has traveled across vast distances. These thinkers judge the dignity of the celestial globes incorrectly and meanly. It is also a vain idea that the earth was once scattered dregs which—lest it be scattered again (as they imagine)—required a "glue" to hold it together and keep it firm; for such a great mass requires its own inherent firmness.

Therefore, Francesco Maurolico <note>A famous 16th-century mathematician and astronomer.</note> considers the entire body of the earth to be rigid rock; for if it were sand, or a fragile clod of earth, it would absorb moisture to such an extent that it would be, as it were, dissolved by it. Furthermore, because minerals and rocks—which are the heaviest parts—are mostly found on the very surface, they ought to be much more present at the center. For it seems more consistent with reason that heavier things are closer to the center, and that everything located there is more tightly bound together.

## CHAPTER II.
### *Of the Earth’s Location.*

<margin>This is to be explained from what was said elsewhere; see also Chapter 8 of this book.</margin>
Throughout the whole nature of things, bodies appear to be distinct in certain fixed and destined places. In the world further removed from us, those called the fixed stars <note>Stars that appear to maintain the same position relative to one another, unlike the "wandering stars" or planets.</note> claim a unique stability and position, and they are never disturbed from their seats, as far as human sense can perceive or reason, supported by any instruments <note>original: "machinis." This refers to astronomical tools like the astrolabe, quadrant, or early telescopes used to measure stellar positions.</note>, can judge. For this reason, all the constellations <term>asterismi</term> endure with the same forms and the same arrangement of stars as they were once understood by the Chaldeans and Egyptians <note>Ancient civilizations famous for their early and precise astronomical observations.</note>; and that whole visible world is seen intact, with no lights confused or changed. But if those stars themselves each moved with their own motion, either that change of place is minute, or they seem to frustrate all observation due to their incomprehensible distance from our senses. Yet they are not positioned in this way because of their locations or the power of a place (for "place" is nothing in itself), nor are they fixed into some firmer heaven like nails in a vaulted ceiling <note>A critique of the traditional Aristotelian and Ptolemaic models, which imagined stars as being physically embedded in solid, crystalline spheres.</note>, but by...

However, it is not certainly persuaded from this, or from any other reasons drawn from elsewhere, that the Earth remains in the center, or about the center, of the whole nature of things. For concerning the circuit and form of the universe—whether it be circular or of some other figure—no demonstration is urgent, and no reason persuades us; we philosophize anxiously with certain conjectures. 

For although the Earth and the whole moving world are surrounded by the visible ornament of the stars, and the stars appear to ascend and descend variously according to the change of the horizon, and the constellations seem to rise, culminate, and set as if they embraced the universe in a belt or an even system; nevertheless, it is not inferred from this that there is a vaulting or an evenness of a convex surface of the Fixed sphere <term>Aplanis</term> <note>original: "Aplanis," referring to the *Aplanes*, the sphere of the fixed stars which was traditionally thought to be the outermost, non-wandering layer of the cosmos.</note>. Therefore, the position of the Earth relative to the fixed stars and their sphere is grasped by no certain evidence. ...they might designate. Those arguments are imperfect which are drawn from straight-line motions from the center and toward the center, based on heaviness <term>gravitas</term> and lightness <term>levitas</term> <note>In traditional physics, "gravitas" was the tendency to fall and "levitas" the tendency to rise.</note>. By these qualities, the so-called "lower world" and the globe of the Earth are said to consist, with the heavier parts gathering at the bottom and toward the center. 

For heavy things do not strive toward that spot as if it were a specific "place," nor is there a force implanted by nature in the parts of a body to drive them to a place, nor does a place itself attract any bodies. Rather, the primary bodies themselves arrange themselves through spaces by their mutual actions. Truly, the parts of primary bodies (such as the celestial globes) have an inclination toward those bodies and are attracted by those primary ones. All parts of the Earth are attracted by the Earth—both those that are loose and fluid, like water, and those that are firm and solid. 

Therefore, water is also carried perpendicularly toward the body of the Earth as if toward its own origin <term>principium</term>; it joins itself to it and penetrates its inner parts, unless other things placed there act as barriers and stand in the way. Therefore, the Creator of things—so that all things would not be in all places and become confused—did not ordain specific locations for individual primary parts around which they should gather and cling. Instead, He ordained bodies endowed with primary powers <term>virtutibus</term> <note>The author uses "virtues" here to mean inherent physical powers or properties.</note>, by which they arrange themselves toward one another and are combined throughout the world in a wonderful order across great distances. 

For the Earth does not remain in place because of a center, or a specific location, or heaviness; nor does *the Earth hang in the surrounding air, balanced by its own weight* <note>original: "circumfuso pendet in aëre tellus, ponderibus librata suis." This is a famous line from the Roman poet Ovid’s Metamorphoses, which the author is here disputing.</note>, as the poet sang and some philosophers believe. For if balancing around a center achieved anything, it would rather assist circular motion; but heaviness exerts no such pressure. Truly, the parts of the primary globes are bound to the whole; they lean into them by a natural desire. 

For whatever is of the nature of earth flows together into the globe of the Earth: likewise, whatever is of the same nature as the Sun flows into the body of the Sun, all things of the Moon into the Moon, and so it is with the other bodies of the universe. Furthermore, their individual parts adhere to their respective wholes and do not move from there of their own accord; but if they should be moved from there, they not only strive to return, but [are drawn] by the powers <term>virtutibus</term> of the globes...

...by these virtues they are enticed and called back. For if this did not happen, and if the parts were separated of their own accord and did not return to their origins <term>principia</term>, the entire world would in a short time be dissipated and thrown into confusion. However, there is no appetite or inclination toward a specific "place," or a space, or a limit; rather, the inclination is toward the body, toward the source, toward the mother, and toward the origin, where they are united and preserved. There, all wandering parts, recalled from danger, find rest. 

In this way, the Earth allures all magnetic things, as well as all other things in which the primary magnetic force has ceased due to the nature of their matter; this inclination in earthly things is called gravity <term>gravitas</term>. Truly, the position of the Earth in the order of nature is determined by the Sun and Moon; likewise, the Moon’s position is determined by the Earth, and the wandering stars <note>Latin: *errones*, a term for the planets</note> by the Sun. From these, they receive their motion and their various paths of movement. Thus they hang and cohere among themselves by an admirable chain, governed by the power of flowing forms. These are the eight instruments of the moving world: the seven so-called planets and our Earth which we inhabit, which does not fall below the dignity of the stars. 

Hence, they possess their own specific spaces and are separated by empty spaces; by their own specific forms, they drive others away or are themselves driven away, and are brought back into order and persist within it. For it must not be thought, following the Aristotelian teaching <term>Aristotelica disciplina</term>, that the Earth is the lowest of the four elements and occupies its seat in the center of the world because of "heaviness"—a place to which all heavy things are carried like ash, dust, mud, or some imaginary, simple, crude body, as if it were a lifeless chaos. 

Nor should we believe what the modern philosopher Francesco Patrizi <note>Francesco Patrizi da Cherso (1529–1597) was a prominent Neoplatonist who criticized Aristotle.</note> established—drawing from Zoroaster, Plato, and the unrefined opinions of the ancients—namely, that God set aside these "dregs" of the material world <term>hylæi</term> <note>From the Greek *hyle*, meaning matter; Patrizi viewed the physical Earth as the lowest, most material part of creation.</note> as the thickest and darkest of all things. He claimed God placed the Earth furthest from all heavenly beings as something most unworthy to be mixed with others, which should not even touch the purer essences, nor be touched by them. According to that view, the Earth was set aside furthest from everything, as far down as could possibly be imagined.

# BOOK II. 117 #

A rash man fails to notice that God, the ruler of the world and nature, has placed the Earth—which is endowed with a more than astounding integrity of primary magnetic virtues <term>vires magneticæ</term>—as the seat of His marvelous work. In organizing the Earth, as Holy Scripture testifies, God spent more time than on the other globes. He cherishes the Earth even more because it nourishes the human race, a miracle of nature, whom the other globes serve and, in a way, attend as servants. 

Therefore, the Earth remains in its place through its own magnetic powers and through a fellowship <term>confœderatio</term> with the nearby globes. It is guided by a connection of flowing forces and harmonic neighborhoods; its boundaries, or poles, constantly face specific regions of the universe due to these same magnetic powers. Because past philosophers were ignorant of these powers, they could offer no true explanation of the Earth’s location or position. Instead, they wretchedly sought Wisdom <term>Sophia</term> in filth, in mud, and in "elements" as they conceived them—viewing the Earth as a simple, useless, inert, and weak element. 

However, there is no reason to be persuaded that the Earth is placed in the center of the universe any more than the Moon or the Sun; nor is it necessary for any one of these to be at the center in a moving world. For these bodies are not placed because of "locations," but are arranged according to the internal forces inherent in those bodies by which they either move or remain at rest. They claim their own spaces, established from eternity or granted from the very beginning, and from these they are never dislodged. 

In the universe, the globes remain in their ancient seats and do not drift; there is no truly "erroneous" or wandering motion among them. Even the wandering stars <note>Latin: *errones stellæ*, the traditional term for the planets</note> have true and definite periods of motion <term>motuum periodos</term> within defined spaces. If the Earth, the Moon, the Sun, or any other star were in the center of the universe <term>centrum universi</term>—meaning it would have a specific proportion, analogy, and conformity to the circle of the higher world and the ultimate outer sphere—then there would need to be an active cause that placed and maintained it there in relation to that outer circle (since a "center" is only defined in relation to a "circle"). But what causes could possibly place and hold the Earth still from the vantage point of the first heaven...

...in the center, not the Moon, nor the Sun? Or what can that power be called, and from where is it born? The common crowd of philosophers, when they dispute the Earth’s location, bring in common and worn-out arguments about the center of the world, about being in the center and around the center; they argue about the Earth's center, the center of gravity and of magnitude, the center of the waters, and whether the Earth and water form a single spherical body. They occupy themselves with these matters; just as Francesco Patrizi <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597) was a Venetian philosopher who challenged Aristotelian orthodoxy; here, the author critiques his rejection of the Earth's perfect roundness.</note> recently rose up against the spherical nature of the Earth and the rounded, convex surface of the sea. He argued that the Earth is uneven and misshapen because of the higher mountains and the plains, seeking arguments from the length of Mount Taurus and the story <note>original: "fabula"</note> of Mount Pico's height rising to 72 miles <note>Mount Pico in the Azores was often cited in early modern texts as the highest mountain in the world, with its height vastly exaggerated.</note>. But these ideas are laughed at even by beginners <term>tyrones</term> and should be wiped away with sponges, not refuted with writings. For it must not be thought that the Earth is perfectly circular and equal and uniform in its exact dimensions; rather it is jagged, with larger continents lifting themselves up, and mountains that are as long as they are high. For every beginner in mathematics admits such a deformity is far from the perfection of a circle; yet the Earth still represents a complete globe and sphere, and because of its enormous diameter, these great inequalities become obscure and of no consequence.

## BOOK II.

...in A. And since G-D-A is viewed directly through a dioptra <note>A dioptra was a classical surveying and astronomical instrument used for measuring positions and angles of celestial bodies.</note>, G-D-A will be a straight line measuring the diameter of the Zodiac and the sphere of the fixed stars. Furthermore, when the constellation Leo is seen rising at B through the same dioptra, and Aquarius is seen setting directly opposite at E, the line B-E will be the straight diameter of that same Zodiac, since it also divides it exactly in half. Since the center of the Zodiac and the sphere of the fixed stars must lie on both diameters, the center must necessarily exist at their intersection. That intersection is the point around which the dioptra is moved; therefore, that point would be the center of the Zodiac or the sphere. 

But these conclusions do not follow. For if the Earth were located outside the center, the starting points of Cancer and Capricorn in the star-bearing sphere (assuming that sphere were circular) are not truly opposite points in the orb of the heavens, but they hold that opposition only according to terrestrial appearances <note>original: "Φαινομένοις" (phainomenois) - refers to how things seem to an observer regardless of their physical reality.</note>. The same occurs in other oppositions of the Zodiac as we look out from the Earth. Nor can any necessary demonstrations conclude anything certain regarding the spherical hollow of the star-bearing sphere. As for the fact that celestial arcs correspond to terrestrial intervals, and that stars seem to rise and set to our sight, these points prove nothing, as has been sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding pages.

# PHYSIOLOGY

...it can be argued that the universe is spherical only through probable conjecture, rather than it being some continuous substance; it is instead dispersed into globes. Except for those closest to us, all these globes seem to us to be fixed and at rest—just like the Earth—unless they are also moved by some revolution that we cannot perceive at such an incomprehensible distance. Furthermore, the claim that the Earth sits at the center of the structure of the universe cannot be confirmed by any arguments from the Ancients <note>Referring to classical authorities like Aristotle or Ptolemy.</note> or the Moderns. The Earth's location is not in the middle, because the planets in their circular motion do not respect the Earth as the center of their movements, but rather follow the Sun. Nor is it the center simply because the heaviest things are drawn toward the Earth; for gravity <term>gravitas (heaviness): at this time, "gravity" was often understood as a natural "inclination" or tendency of objects to return to their "natural place" or parent body, rather than a universal force of attraction.</term> is an inclination not just toward the Earth, but toward each object's own source and star. Nor is it the center because the densest part of nature is stored there; for while those things that rise further from the Earth and stand higher seem thinner <note>original: "rariora" — meaning less dense or more rarefied.</note>, many stars are themselves dense, opaque, and non-transparent, such as the Moon, the planets, and the fixed stars. As for the reasons brought forward regarding the "fabric of the elements" and those they call the "primary qualities" <note>In Aristotelian physics, the four elements (Earth, Air, Fire, Water) were defined by primary qualities: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note>, these all vanish along with the fable of the elements—a theory which, combined with those poorly understood qualities, can in no way hold up, and has been more than sufficiently rejected and exploded by us.

To think that air has a blue color is not philosophical at all, since there is no color in the air itself. Rather, the blue
