## BOOK II.

Q

That color appears only as a representation of color; it is not, however, an actual entity or a true color. It occurs in a clear sky because light received in a thin, transparent medium <term>diaphano (diaphanous): a substance through which light can pass, such as air, water, or glass.</term> is reflected back. From this comes a slight brightness; furthermore, because no specific object is illuminated by the light—as if from a lack of objects to strike the senses—a kind of blackness is represented, as if in darkness. Thus, from both circumstances combined, the color appears blue <note>original: "cæruleus" — sky blue or azure.</note>. This is also why even in the clearest air, mountains that are far away—twenty or thirty miles distant from us—are seen in that heavenly color because they strike the senses unclearly due to the distance. Painters, too, when they depict distant things, illuminate them with a certain shadowy blue so that they appear to be further away. 

Yellow color <note>original: "Flavus"</note> is the color of burning and inflamed thick matter, not of the element of fire itself. Some say that Earth lacks color; others classify it as black; Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath who wrote extensively on natural philosophy and the qualities of matter.</note> wants it to be dusky <note>original: "pullam" — a dark, grayish-brown color often associated with fertile soil.</note>, specifically because dusky soil often appears fertile and best for generation. But such qualities are more for peasants and farmers to seek out; it is not the inherent quality of the whole earth found deep within its interior. Rather, that genuine color seems to approach whiteness <note>original: "candorem"</note>, as evidenced by ash, once the moisture has been consumed by heat. 

Yet, we do not mean that the Earth is naturally dry and scorched like ash, nor arid and powdery. Therefore, the consumption of all moisture by fire will not give us that renowned "Earth," but rather a kind of corruption and the corpse of the true Earth, turned away from its own nature. Just as when a portion of the true Earth is dissolved in moisture, it passes into foreign colors. Therefore, many people search ignorantly for a "white earth," which they claim appears in ash once the moisture (which created the tint) has been burnt away. For they establish the Earth as being like ash—completely juice-less and dry—yet such a substance never comes into our hands when digging. However, those things that are very white and born of the earth, such as

<header>

### ON NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

</header>

Chalk, gypsum, white marl, and often clay, as well as limestone and very many other rocks—all of these contain moisture. When they are burned into ash and lime, they do not take on the character of the "simple earth" described by the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, who defined "Earth" as one of the four basic elements: cold, dry, and inherently heavy.</note>. While these are suitable materials for constructing buildings, they are not the principles and first beginnings of physical bodies. 

Indeed, because many things become white or ash-colored when thoroughly burned, some people claim that the simple element of Earth, as conceived in the imagination, must be white. They argue this because whatever is separated from moisture appears white; however, these people "philosophize from the furnace" <note>A critique of those who base their universal laws of nature only on what they see in a fireplace or laboratory furnace.</note>. They see that wood, when burned, turns to ash, the proper color of which is ash-grey, appearing as if fused with white. Therefore, they conclude that this simple color belongs to a simple element, and that ashes are either the element itself or very close to it. 

Yet, the renowned "earth" of the Peripatetics does not actually arise from wood in a furnace in such a specific way. If you burn clay, or darker earths, or certain veins of metals—such as **iron dross** <term>stercus ferri: literally "iron dung," referring to the slag or waste scales produced during smelting or forging</term>—no amount of heat will ever produce a white color. 

In the case of wood, it becomes white when burned because it contains salts; as the wandering and unstable moisture flees from these inherent salts, they turn white, for all simpler salts turn white upon heating. However, those bodies and parts of the earth that contain no salts, or only very coarse ones, cannot be made white by any power of fire, unless the material serving as fuel for that fire happens to burn its own salts and ashes into them. 

We see that when the surface of the earth is furrowed by the plow, or when deeper ditches are dug, clods of various colors are brought to light. In our **England**, across vast fields, the earth sometimes appears yellowish; in other places it is ash-grey, and often it is reddish, black, white, or **dusky** <note>original: "pulla" — a dark, somber color often associated with rich, fertile soil.</note>. In all of these varieties, both grasses and grain crops grow successfully. This is true in all other regions as well—in **France**, **Italy**, and **Germany**. 

But the interior and truly magnetic earth is not something that farmers need to seek out. For on the surface are born clayey earths, gypsous earths, and others which are more magnetic, [and others] less...

# BOOK II.

<header>

### BOOK II.

</header>

...[some earths] are less fruitful, and others are useless. How much marl <term>marga: a lime-rich clay or mudstone traditionally used as a fertilizer</term> is sometimes dug out from deeper places to bring fertility to the lands! This occurs because a richer, oily moisture grows within certain elevations of the earth; for marl pits do not descend very deep. Therefore, we cannot firmly assert that the earth is yellowish, or ash-colored, reddish, black, white, or dark brown. Indeed, even the lodestone <term>magnes: a naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite</term> is marked by as many colors as there are materials of earths and minerals, as many as there are varieties of mixtures, and as many as there are differences in the appearance and color of things. <margin>Chapter 2, Book 1, *On the Magnet*</margin> Truly, the best magnets are of a brownish-iron color <term>fusco-ferrei: a dark, metallic grey-brown characteristic of high-quality ore</term>. 

I, however, think thus: the thick and opaque internal body of the earth has no certain color. Nevertheless, the entire exterior nature is not naturally endowed with a red or yellow color, because colors arise from the interior parts; nor is it white, which does not suit a perennial opacity; nor is it black, which belongs to scorched things—which often turn black either from heat born in the pits, from vapors arising from metals, or from bitumen. Even though the earth consists of similar and homogeneous parts, it would by no means reflect the same colors in all its internal magnetic parts if they were brought into the light. For those parts closest to the center would be colored differently than those closer to the surface. Indeed, nature "plays" everywhere with variety in those qualities. But if some specific color seems to prevail in the internal parts, it will be that which is seen most often in the best lodestone (the earth’s most perfect offspring): namely, a brownish-iron color. This color seems especially to suit its opaque nature and eternal darkness.

### CHAPTER IV.

#### *On the colors and innate powers of the earth.*

Since very few parts of the true earth ever come into the light, nature was not much concerned with the colors of the earth, which are nothing unless they are illuminated by the brightness of light. The Elementary Philosophers <term>Elementarii Philosophi: scholars who followed the ancient theory that the world is made of four simple elements—Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</term>, who imagine elements to be simple and pure, search for a dry, simple earth marked by one specific color, yet they have never found it. In truth, the earth has no certain color, as all colors can be seen within it if it were brought into the light, or if it were dug out from its very foundation and magnetic globe.

It is false to claim that the greatest part of this globe is fluid or consists of separate water. For the Earth prevails in the nature of things—firm, solid, and constant: the loose fluids <note>original: "humores"</note> of the seas, springs, and rivers can hardly be compared with the earth in any proportion. The earth itself possesses an innate moisture, not one separate from it; for that which is dry, extremely parched, and powdery is a part of the earth placed outside its genuine nature, weakened by a heavier and immoderate heat.

The earth possesses an internal activity by which waters flow, and spirits <note>In early modern science, "spirits" (spiritus) referred to subtle, active gases or vapors thought to drive natural processes</note> break out from the earth through the waters; this heat is its "form" and serves its soul <term>anima: the animating principle or life-force; the author suggests the Earth behaves like a living organism</term>, no less than in plants. Therefore, it is ridiculous to think that the earth and waters are cold and lacking in activity and heat, since the earth is the source of moisture and heat for us. While the surface is refreshed by the Sun and stars through their light, in the internal and deep parts, the heat is the earth's own genuine property.

The Earth is a primary globe in the universe, solid, round, and endowed with internal juice <note>original: "succus," referring to a vital internal fluid</note>, whose outflows <note>original: "effluvia"</note> are the sources of springs and seas.

Even the moss of trees, sponges, and the most wretched little grasses—which are but the refuse and, as it were, the decays of the lands—possess a soul. What? ## CHAPTER V.

### *That the Earth did not originate from moisture, flow, or water.*

It would seem to be not far from the truth that the Earth was firm and solid from its very origin, and that this entire globe did not solidify out of a "flow" <note>original: "fluore" — referring to a primordial liquid state</note> and water, as some of the Ancients believed. Homer and Orpheus attribute much to the ocean—the source of all waters—treating it as the parent of gods and men; they poetically and freely imagine that the soul comes from water and indeed *is* water. Thales <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624 – 548 BCE), often cited as the first Greek philosopher, famously proposed that water was the primary substance of all matter.</note> established water as the primary element because he saw that in this entire circuit of the lands, all things produced took their beginning from a certain flow and moist matter. Yet, whenever something is born, that which appears as the seed or offspring is not merely "flow" or water, but a certain fluid in which it is manifest that a firmer and more constant nature exists. For the Greatest Architect <note>A common philosophical term for God as the creator of the universe's geometric order.</note> established globes that are stable in their firmness, distinguished by the primary dignity of their parts—qualities that cannot exist in flowing things, nor be born within fluids. Thus, and confusion...

Therefore, either the celestial globes were formed from more solid matter from all eternity, or the world was so arranged in the beginning by the Supreme Ruler that its principal parts—the material globes—were constructed and stabilized on more certain foundations. For that divine power which created them did not create something wandering, but rather something already constant, and it infused primary powers into suitable matter to govern the position within the globes. 

If He had produced only a primordial liquid flow <note>original: "fluorem" — referring to a state of matter that is fluid or flowing</note>, He would have acted no differently than someone who committed small, crudely built boats to the high sea without yardarms, masts, anchors, or even the sailors themselves. For there are innate powers within the Earth <term>tellure: the Latin term for the physical and personified Earth</term> that regulate its motions and positions. 

Thus, the position held by Francesco Patrizi <note>Francesco Patrizi da Cherso (1529–1597) was a Venetian philosopher who argued that all physical things originated from a "primordial flow" or space.</note>—that all bodies are either a flow or congealed from flow—is poorly founded. For the firm land is as old as the dissolved moisture; it existed from the beginning and did not congeal from moisture later. Although water often passes into a stable hardness in certain parts, and the earth or earthy things are sometimes dissolved into moisture. 

Much less should dissolved moisture be ranked before the Earth, since its quantity is quite small compared to the Earth’s mass. Moreover, the Earth everywhere emits parts of its own internal "sap" <note>original: "succo" — referring to the life-giving fluids or mineral essences thought to circulate within the Earth.</note> that have been melted by heat toward its surface <note>original: "peripheriam"</note>, thereby increasing the moisture gushing on its exterior. Indeed, moisture and "ash" <note>original: "cinis" — here used in the alchemical or natural philosophical sense to represent the solid, dry, and stable residue of matter.</note> are not different elements, but different bodies which are one in the whole and are born together, even if they are separated in their parts. Thus, every true and uniform <note>original: "homogenica"</note> part of the Earth is separated into dissimilar matter. Francesco Patrizi <note>Francesco Patrizi da Cherso (1529–1597), a philosopher who proposed that "flow" (fluor) was a fundamental state of matter.</note> maintains that the earth is a "flow" <note>original: "fluorem"</note> and contends that it congealed from flow, because earth and even mud are poured out and are liquefied by fires. By the command of the Creator, he says, the earth was gathered into one place and ceased to flow, and it remains thickened within itself; yet it has not completely erased the memory of its primeval origin. For even when it flows—as when bricks are formed from earth and water—these are baked in kilns so that they may harden. Of those bricks that are nearest to the fire, the heat not only drives the water within them into a juice <note>meaning the moisture is rendered into a liquid state</note> as it does to all the rest, but they are even dissolved, liquefied, and they flow.

Ash, as Aristotle teaches, is earth. That ash, when cast into glass-making furnaces, first becomes a flow, and then glass. These things, he says, are evidence that all earth can be turned into a flow by a violent fire. Therefore, all earth, if it is not itself a flow, is nevertheless fluid, because it was formed from a primordial flow and is melted back into a flow. 

But Patrizi, wandering far from the truth, by no means prevails with this little line of reasoning. For neither earth, nor ash, nor sand, nor any of the drier dross <term>recrementa: the waste or dross left over from metal processing</term> of metals flow by their own strength and innate power; this is something that ought to have been confirmed by reasons and experiments. Rather, earth, dust, and sand flow only when fires are applied; thus they possess a glassy fusion when fire—which is itself a flow—is mixed through their smallest parts, and the body, thinned by the fire, [is turned] into moisture...

After having spoken of the truer parts of the earth and of magnetic forces, it remains for us to give an account of the earth as a whole. This is not so that we may run through all those things which have been handed down by the learned concerning the earth, its parts, and the bodies added to it (the subjects in which <term>Natural Philosophy</term> <note>The precursor to modern science, focusing on the study of nature and the physical universe.</note> is engaged), but rather that we may speak only of those things which especially and chiefly pertain to the knowledge of the whole great earth, and which were either unknown to or wrongly established by our ancestors. The spherical Earth, like other celestial globes, was ordered by nature to be firm and constant; it is merely bathed in a wandering moisture on its uppermost parts and in its superficial cavities. It is not overcome by a much larger quantity of that moisture, as those who commonly philosophize dream; so much so that the moisture does not even equal the earth in the proportion of its body, but all the power of the waters is surpassed far and wide by the massive depth of the earthly substance. Therefore, the opinion of those who think the water exceeds the earth by ten times <note>A reference to ancient and medieval theories, often attributed to a misunderstanding of Aristotle, which claimed the sphere of water was ten times larger than the sphere of earth.</note> must be utterly exploded. Indeed, in the more prominent parts <note>i.e., the Earth's surface or crust</note>, it is mostly imperfect, defiled by wandering and foreign humors, changed into various forms, exposed to the injuries of many causes, or reduced by vehement heats into sterile sands, dust, and ash.

But all the interior substance is firm earth, and is firmly congealed, endowed with all the powers which are seen here in the loadstone <note>original: "magnete lapide"; magnetite, a naturally magnetized mineral</note>; these are recognized also in many other magnetic bodies. The entire mass of the Earth is spherical, with the chief quantity of waters gathering and flowing into the cavities and deeper places; these waters, in the vastest seas, form an arc of a circle on the periphery, as they conform themselves into a spherical shape along with the Earth.

The great lands and higher mountains, although they create a certain inequality on the periphery, this is nevertheless small in respect to the whole, nor do they deform the world-orb. For although there is no single opinion on the highest altitude of mountains, yet no sounder opinion is contrary to the nature of a spherical figure, which is suitable for motion and conservation. Eratosthenes <note>A Greek polymath (c. 276–194 BC) who first calculated the Earth's circumference</note> held that the highest mountain rose 10 stadia <note>A Greek unit of length; 10 stadia is roughly 1.1 miles</note>, Cleomedes 15, Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), a pioneering physicist and mathematician</note> 8 miles, and Dicaearchus 1256 paces <note>A Roman pace or "passus" was about five feet</note>; this last is contradicted by many because the ascent of the Alps is a long journey of 10 miles. But the length ascending in a journey is one thing, while the perpendicular altitude is another. Aristotle writes that on Mount Caucasus the sun shines at night, both in the morning and evening, for a third <note>Aristotle claimed the mountain was so high the sun was visible for a third of the night</note>...

On the Canary island of Tenerife, some write that the peak of the mountain <note>Mount Teide</note> exceeds 72 miles; but the more experienced sailors who pass that way report this to be false. For Nature never exceeds appropriate limits with such monstrous shapes of its parts; and yet, that mountain is indeed quite lofty, and in its sheer upright height, it seems to surpass all other mountains. 

It is easy to understand why there are cavities and seas in certain places rather than others, or why mountains and steep cliffs exist elsewhere due to long-term changes in nature. The structure of the entire circuit of the earth is subject to various transformations: the violence of winds, the waves of the waters, and regional movements of the earth <note>i.e., earthquakes or tectonic shifts</note>. Thus we have learned from our ancestors, and we have seen everywhere in almost every maritime region, that the lands have been broken through and convulsed by waves, the sea has been blocked in certain places and converted into firm land, the mouths of rivers have been corrupted, and the courses of waters have changed—such as the Don <note>original: "Tanais"</note>, the Nile, and the Rhine.

The Greeks, Aristotle, and others write that through the vast length of time it has come to pass that many places which were once overwhelmed by waters are now free from them and inhabited, while many regions once flourishing now lie hidden beneath the waves. ## CHAPTER VII.

### *That the Earth moves circularly.*

<margin>See Book 2 of *On the Magnet*, chapters 8, 9, 10 etc.</margin>
It seems probable that the Earth revolves with a daily motion; however, whether it is moved by some annual circular motion is not the subject of inquiry in this place. <note>The author, William Gilbert, is focusing here on the Earth’s 24-hour rotation on its axis rather than its yearly orbit around the sun.</note> The revolution of the Earth is the completion of day and night; or more accurately, it is a certain revolution of a specific meridian of the earth toward a fixed star near the Equator. It is clear that the cause of this effect lies in the earth: because all **magnetic philosophy** <note>original: "philosophia magnetica," referring to Gilbert's revolutionary study of the Earth as a giant magnet</note> shows through many experiments that nature has established permanent, natural poles in the earth, which are natural and not merely mathematical points. A **verticity** <note>original: "verticitatem," a technical term for the directional power of a magnet or the Earth's orientation toward the poles</note> rises up on both sides with powerful forces through the cooperation of the whole; and the daily revolution agrees with these poles.

On the other hand, no turning of the celestial bodies, no motions of the planets, nor any sensible moving nature distinct in its poles is recognized in the **firmament** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars</note> or in some **first mover** <note>original: "primo aliquo mobili," referring to the *Primum Mobile*, the hypothetical outermost sphere of the universe in ancient astronomy</note> that agrees with the daily revolution—at least not one that is visible or confirmed by any reason, as it is in the **body of the earth**. Rather, such a motion in the heavens is only supposed and inferred to be true. Therefore, following nature, we judge that the earth moves on its own poles (which are made apparent to us through the magnetic art). For the earth is not imbued by nature with a verticity solely for the sake of constancy or a fixed, permanent position; since it could just as easily be bound to the whole world by powers spread out toward the East, the West, or any other regions of the firmament. But if it remained at rest only by reason of its weight, as the philosophers <note>Referring to the traditional Aristotelian view that the Earth remains stationary at the center of the universe because of its heavy, "earthy" nature</note> argue, for what purpose in nature is that observed verticity, which neither [helps] motion...

These forces have conspired in a perpetual pact with the powers of the moving globes for many centuries, and from the very beginnings of the **cosmic system** <note>original: "systematis mundani"</note>, about which we shall speak in another place. Just as the earth turns itself and is restored to its position, so is it rolled by these same forces.

I understand the poles of the Moon's body as always aiming, according to the system of the lunar course, toward certain parts of the heavens. Similarly, there must also be a polarity <term>verticity</term> (original: "verticitatem" — the innate power of a magnetic body to align its poles in a specific direction) in the Earth because of its motion. The whole Earth—with forces flowing from its Equator toward both poles, following the common inclination of the rest of the planets—is carried from west to east. For there is one and the same progression toward the east, following the sequence of the zodiacal signs, for all the celestial spheres, whether Venus and Mercury are positioned below the Sun according to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy was a 2nd-century astronomer whose Earth-centered model of the universe was the standard for over a millennium</note>, or whether they revolve around the Sun itself.

Furthermore, it is not likely that the Earth’s polarity was born, derived, or propagated from some impression or influence of the *primum mobile* <note>original: "primi mobilis" — the "First Mover," which in ancient astronomy was the outermost sphere believed to drive the rotation of all other celestial spheres</note>. For the Earth alone (according to the opinions of those scholars) is free and immune from the forces of the *primum mobile*; instead, it seems to have conceived its forces of polarity and primary form from other spheres of the Sun and planets that are closer and more influential.

But just as magnetic science reveals the natural poles, so it also shows the Equator, both in the whole and in any part broken off from it. The Equator, which is a great circle equidistant from both poles, would seem to be imposed by nature upon a stationary Earth in vain. Rather, it is a destined, natural, and active boundary between the two hemispheres. From the Equator's plane down to the center and toward the poles, the entire force of the Earth is extended meridionally. This exists for no other reason than this: while the shifting middle parts are rolled along, they are held in a fixed steadiness at the poles. In this way, axes are fixed and bodies rotate exactly like wheels, or globes, or spherical instruments. When the axis is fixed in a permanent meridian, the whole body is carried around freely.

...circular motion, by which nature settles into its own seat? Therefore, the Northern parts of the Earth look toward the **North Star** <note>original: "cynosuram" — the constellation of the Lesser Bear or the Pole Star</note> with a constant nature; thus, every genuine part of it, if not deformed, seeks its seat in the world at the same time and moves circularly toward that position. The natural motions of the whole and its parts are the same; therefore, since the parts move in a circle, the whole also possesses the power of moving circularly.

An **orbicular loadstone** <note>a spherical magnet</note> moves circularly upon its center in conformity with the Earth: just as it appears on the plane of the horizon in a vessel upon the water, so it does in any other great circle, if it were allowed to be free. In a <term>declination instrument</term> <note>a device used to measure the vertical "dip" of a magnetic needle toward the Earth's center</note>, the circular motion occurs in the meridian, if there is no variation; or in a great circle drawn from the Zenith through the point of variation on the horizon, if variation exists. Everywhere, the **terrella** <term>little earth</term> <note>original: "terrella" — a small, spherical model of the Earth made of loadstone, used by William Gilbert to demonstrate magnetic principles</note> is moved circularly by nature through its own strength, so that it may align itself conveniently with the Earth.

And that circular motion toward its correct position shows that the Earth itself is fit and suitable, and sufficiently equipped with its own powers for a **daily circular motion**.

The **Platonists** <note>followers of the philosopher Plato</note> believe that the heavens are moved not by an elementary nature, but by life—not an external life, but an internal one through which the heavens live. This life, so celebrated by them, is that primary virtue of the globes—in the Earth, indeed, it consists of the **magnetic faculties** which flow from the primary form, or that "Platonic life."

In other globes, each has its own peculiar action and instinct. The **Sun's** is the most excellent, for he is the leader and driver of this world, within the circuit of the path of **Saturn**, which consists of eight bodies <note>Gilbert likely refers to the Sun and the seven "planets" known to antiquity: Mercury, Venus, Earth/Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>; for all the other **wanderers** <note>original: "errones" — a traditional term for the planets, which appear to wander against the fixed stars</note> follow the motion of the Sun.

Since the parts of the Earth do not have weight within the Earth, and especially not at the center of the Earth, they only have it when they have been separated from the Earth. ## CHAPTER IX.

### *On the reason and necessity of the ordering of things placed in nature, and the imitation of parts toward that conformity.*

The Lord of nature ordered the entire world with admirable providence and distinguished the principal bodies as globes with innate powers; just as these have their specific paths and fixed ways, so too do they have firm and constant positions. For a permanent force within these globes has brought about perpetual directions of the poles—not wandering or errant, nor subject to uncertain turnings toward every region of the sky, but rather respective <note>meaning: oriented in relation to one another</note> and linked to specific boundaries of the world (to its certain fixed points). 

And for that reason the Moon, although it is moved around the Earth in a certain path and circular course in 27 days—and sometimes is carried further from the Earth, sometimes approaches closer, and seems to speed up or slow down its course—nevertheless it always observes the circle of motion or the middle of its orbicular journey. It does this without a carrying Epicycle <note>a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used in Ptolemaic astronomy to explain planetary variations</note>; for we wish the motion of the heavens to be simple. The Moon tends toward the center of that circle with a specific part, which we rightly call the pole of the Moon. 

In the same way, the Earth—whether it rests in some center (as the common crowd of philosophers thinks) or is moved by a daily revolution—directs its northern terrestrial pole toward the North <note>original: "Boream"</note>, toward those Seven Oxen <note>original: "Septemtriones" — the seven stars of the Big Dipper/Great Bear used to find the North Star</note>: and it aims this...

## CHAPTER X.

### That the motion of the globes is from the globes themselves, not from spheres.

Lest the opinion of some "first mover" <note>The *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere in traditional geocentric cosmology thought to drive all other spheres</note> of corporeal construction, or a material sphere, further grip the minds of the learned, it will be necessary to show how—not only because of its motion—such a "primary orb" is unfit, but also that the wanderers <note>original: "errones" — a term for the planets, which appear to "wander" against the background of fixed stars</note> themselves do not stick in spheres and corporeal heavens, nor are they carried around by them. Although among the Ancients, the first opinion of planetary orbs took its origin from the imagined rolling of the firmament and the Fixed Stars <term>original: "Aplanis" — the sphere of fixed stars, from the Greek for "not wandering"</term>; because if the Earth were fixed in the center of the world without circular motion, it was necessary for all apparent stars to be whirled around, as if held together by some certain framework.

But that this is a fictitious disturbance of the entire system can be persuaded even more truly and certainly, because the motion of the globes is rather from the globes themselves, driving their own courses, than from those structures of spheres and celestial machines. Mathematicians, so that they might measure the motions of the planets with certain numbers and dimensions, have imagined circles, spaces, and spheres. By these, they have been forced to divide individual spheres into many—eccentric and concentric <note>In geocentric astronomy, an "eccentric" is a circular orbit whose center is not the Earth, while a "concentric" shares the same center</note>—both because of the apparent inequalities of motions and because of retrogradations <note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky</note>. In the outermost parts they place other eccentrics; in the hollows, eccentrics; then eccentrics in the outermost and concentrics in the hollows. Upon the eccentric circles they place epicycles <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; a mathematical tool used to explain planetary paths</note>; yet they do not all use the same spheres, since some [use] epicycles...

However, those circles are not physical bodies, but only imaginary spaces through which the celestial bodies are carried; or if they were carried by them, they would agree with the times of the revolutions; and the various circles were conceived for the purpose of occupying the spaces and times of each revolution. As soon as the writers of natural philosophy understood this—though they were unmathematical <note>The author is criticizing "natural philosophers" (Aristotelians) who lacked mathematical rigor</note>, as most and the chief among them were—they immediately assigned corporeal spheres to each planet. [mathe]maticians assume certain circuits and imagine them as if they were real and material bodies; these artfully crafted fictions the Philosophers have seized upon and argue are fixed or necessary in the world. The Ancient Philosophers, because of that visible blue vault <note>original: "concamerationem" — a vaulted ceiling or dome</note> and the motion of the stars, saw that the heavens moved in a circle. However, since they did not perceive through their senses the diversity of the heavens and the multiple orbs, they believed in only one heaven above, a divine body, and a simple system for the entire world.

But the following age judged the celestial heights differently. The Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Greeks—especially Plato and Aristotle—when they noticed eight distinct motions which could not be set in motion by a single subject, asserted that there were also eight heavens: the firmament, in which all the fixed stars were secured, and the "wanderers" <note>original: "errones" — the planets</note>. They considered the firmament to be the same as the "First Mover" <note>original: "primum mobile" — the outermost sphere in the geocentric model that gives motion to all others</note>, possessing the same power of inciting and revolving.

Afterwards, others who were more diligent and industrious in Astronomy and observations—such as Timocharis <note>A 3rd-century BC Greek astronomer</note>, and after him Hipparchus, and then Menelaus the geometer; who, as knowledge grew daily, contributed their own records and found through various observations over different centuries that the fixed stars move with a double motion. Therefore, since they believed that only a single motion should be attributed to a single simple body, they were forced to assign this newly discovered motion to the fixed stars and transfer the daily revolution to another higher heaven; thus, nine celestial spheres were created.

One thousand one hundred and forty years after Ptolemy, King Alfonso <note>Alfonso X of Castile, r. 1252–1284, who sponsored the "Alfonsine Tables"</note> in the year of our Lord 1300, and later Georg von Peuerbach and Johannes Regiomontanus, discovered a third motion in addition to those mentioned, which they called "access and recess" <note>original: "accessus & recessus" — also known as trepidation, a historical theory that the equinoxes oscillate or "shiver" rather than moving at a constant rate</note>. For this reason, another new heaven was fabricated in that system so that this new motion could be completed; thus ten heavens were designated by these craftsmen for the purpose of defining the motions. But many more recent philosophers, [treating] all the oracles of Ari[stotle]... <note>The text cuts off here at the name of Aristotle</note>

-># PHYSIOLOGY<-

[Aris]totelian scholars, therefore, admit only eight heavens and do not accept newly discovered ones; they argue that those which carry no star and are not discerned by any visible body should not be regarded with the dignity or reality of "heavens." Others, however, do admit them, and they rush into the mathematicians' harvest and "put in their sickle" <note>An idiom meaning to interfere in someone else's specialized work or business</note>; just as the older Philosophers accepted the eight heavens provided by the Mathematicians, so these thinkers embrace all of them, following the common crowd of philosophizers, and describe ten orbs above the basic elements. The ancient mathematicians discovered paths and imagined circles; the even older Philosophers, who were still unrefined in philosophy (although the knowledge of modern thinkers does not seem to differ much from their simplicity and ignorance), posited physical bodies, such as eccentric orbs, concentric orbs, and epicycles <term>epicycles: small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger ones, used to explain planetary variations</term>.

**Eudoxus** assigned several concentric orbs to each planet and arranged 25 in total. **Calippus** created 33 concentric orbs; others created 55. **Ptolemy** introduced a ninth sphere; **Thabit** <note>original: "Tebith" — Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century astronomer</note> added a tenth to these. **Averroës** removed all except eight orbs. **Al-Bitruji** <note>original: "Alpetragius" — a 12th-century Spanish-Arab astronomer</note> removed the eccentrics and epicycles. **Nicolaus Copernicus** revived older opinions and inverted the order of the planets, and like a new Atlas of Astronomy, he corrected the celestial motions with new hypotheses. **Giambattista della Torre** and **Girolamo Fracastoro** brought the number of homocentric <term>homocentric: spheres having the same center, usually the Earth</term> orbs up to 77.

Regarding the motion of celestial bodies, both of the firmament and the spheres, they imagine real circles or spheres, involving "movers" led around, "opposing carriers," and "counter-movers." In the **Aplanes** <term>original: "Aplane" — the sphere of the fixed stars which does not "wander"</term> they imagine 6 or more; for the revolution of **Saturn** ten, for **Jupiter** eleven, for **Mars** nine, for the **Sun** 4, for **Venus** 11, for **Mercury** the same number, and for the **Moon** 7; so that there are 69 in total. Thus, those who think that the celestial globes are mechanically led around, carried, or dragged within material spheres fall into many absurdities. **Tycho Brahe**, inferior to no one in this century and a great observer of *phenomena* <note>original: "Φαινομένων" — appearances or observed events in the sky</note>, found another way...

-># BOOK II.<-

...[brought/found] a different view from Copernicus, from whom we have received excellent things in Mathematics, and so we eagerly expect even greater things at some time. A certain Raimarus Ursus <note>Nicolaus Reimers Baer (1551–1600), an Imperial mathematician and rival of Tycho Brahe</note> in his *Astronomical Foundation* also proposed a new arrangement of the entire system of the world. These theories, although diverse and contrary, are not however the ravings of Astronomers; rather, every learned man seeks how he might find hypotheses <note>original: "ὑποθέσεις"</note> more convenient for calculation to match the courses of the phenomena <note>original: "Φαινομένων" — the observable movements of stars and planets</note>. This necessarily ought to be done, even if a true Philosophy of bodies and a science of the heavens were known and fully understood. 

But the Philosophers who seek the physical nature of the orbs and spheres err more, insofar as they admit mathematical positions as if they were real, physical things. For the sake of saving the appearances <term>saving the appearances: the practice of creating mathematical models that match observed data without necessarily claiming they represent physical reality</term>, Mathematicians necessarily imagine many circles. Nor are these "delusions," according to the judgment of Patritius <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), a Venetian philosopher and critic of Aristotle</note>, a modern Philosopher, who also thinks that the stars are carried by their own spirit, moved by soul, and governed by intellect and order. 

But what will the idle Philosopher look at then in vain—satisfied with his own opinion—in a heaven without use and without the prediction of motions? In that case, such science would be of no use. Therefore, those most learned and hardworking men are worthy of the greatest honor, who busy themselves observing appearances, measuring motions, indicating courses, and showing syzygies <term>syzygies: the alignment of three celestial bodies in a straight line, such as during an eclipse or a new moon</term>, and who strive to ascend into heaven on geometric wings—even if they use various principles, foundations, and hypotheses. 

We, however, are going to speak about the nature of the heaven and the superior bodies, yet not in such a way that just honor does not remain for the Mathematicians. And first, we shall take our beginning from the Moon, the lowest star. ...with violent and rapid rotation, and perpetual, placed in no certain seats, they would collide and cause ruin, since that containing matter would be dispersed. Those who wish for the expanse of the heavens to be a solid and firm body can imagine whatever they like. For how, through solid and firm things—even if transparent—could the true and precise light of the stars reach us through such immense spaces, when even the thinnest transparent things here, and the air itself, which is very thin in the greatest clarity, dulls and obscures those lights somewhat?

In the upper regions, therefore, there is no solidity, no hardness, no permanence, no tenacity, and no grasping or detention of bodies. They are contained in the most liquid, or thinnest, or even in a vacuum, no more—indeed much less—than this earthly globe is contained in the thin and fluid [atmosphere] surrounding it on all sides. What insane friction <note>original: "attritiones"</note> would occur at such high speeds? One would fear that the entire sky on all sides—all the spheres, all the vaults <note>original: "concamerationes" — referring to the arched, chamber-like structure of celestial orbs</note>, and all the frameworks—would perpetually catch fire and, being ignited, would perish and lose their integrity.

**Aristotle** says: "The reason may be asked why other planets move in individual spheres, and not two [together]..."

...three, or more in one sphere? But Aristotle brings forward no reason for this. For if two **wandering stars** <term>errones: "wanderers," the classical term for planets as opposed to fixed stars</term> were spurred by one and the same motion, it would have been probable for them to be carried by a single framework. And yet, in the stars rather—distinguished, luminous bodies, pouring out their **virtues** <note>virtues: inherent powers or spiritual/physical influences believed to emanate from celestial bodies</note> in every direction—a greater force and greater power is seen; and since spontaneous motion is the most notable of the world’s virtues, a greater motivating power must be sought [within the stars themselves]. 

But these "wheel-spinners" <note>original: "rotatores" — a dismissive term for those who envision the heavens as a mechanical system of wheels</note>, more than mere mechanics, make **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Deum Opt. # BOOK II.

[The stars] are carried along and combined among themselves in fluid forms; they are stirred, raised up, and summoned by both mutual and inherent forces, and they show us various **phenomena** <note>original Greek: Φαινόμενα — "appearances" or observable events</note> and different appearances. Those "paths" used by mathematicians are mental concepts which must be accepted for the sake of computations and stellar calculations; however, physical spheres that actually carry these globes ought to be considered entirely foreign to the principles of the Philosophers.

Nor should it be believed any longer that the planets are merely the "denser parts" of their spheres—as the common crowd of the "Wise" <note>original: Sophorum — often used sarcastically here to refer to traditional Scholastic thinkers</note> thinks—or that the **concavity of the Moon** <note>In the Aristotelian model, the sphere of the moon was the boundary line: everything below it was "corruptible" (subject to change and decay), while everything above was "incorruptible" (eternal and unchanging)</note> serves as the dividing line between the corruptible and incorruptible world. For bodies congeal above the Moon and then vanish; they experience birth and destruction, as well as constancy and motion. **Albumazar** <term>Albumazar: Latinized name of Abu Ma'shar (787–886), a leading Persian astronomer/astrologer</term> left a record that he saw a comet above the body of **Venus**. **Albategnius** <term>Albategnius: Latinized name of Al-Battani (c. 858–929), a famous Arab astronomer</term> reported that a comet was detected in his time within the orbit of Venus. Certain **tailed stars** <note>original: caudati — a literal translation of the Latin term for comets</note> of our own century were carried high above the Moon and moved in circular paths; and yet no one is so foolish as to think new spheres were suddenly created in that heaven to carry them in a manner different from any other planet.

The admirable and prodigious star of **Cassiopeia** <note>This refers to the "New Star" or Supernova of 1572, which appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia and stunned the European scientific world</note> was carried into the **Aristotelian heaven** <note>The supposedly unchanging realm of the fixed stars</note> at a vast distance, as witnessed by the most noble **Tycho Brahe** (a most skilled and tireless Mathematician), the most learned **Michael Maestlin**, the Englishmen **Thomas Digges** and **John Dee**, the German **Hagesius**, the Spaniard **Jerónimo Muñoz**, **Cornelius Gemma**, and many other most learned and skilled men who applied themselves to this study. For it was easily seen that this star maintained the exact same distance from the nearest fixed stars whether it was at the highest point of the sky or near the horizon. This could not have happened if it had been so close to us that the Earth’s diameter caused a noticeable **parallax** <term>parallax: the apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from two different locations; if an object has no parallax, it must be extremely far away</term>, which is what must happen if an object is located in the **elementary region** <note>The sublunary world made of the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire), where change occurs</note>. Thus, that star showed no difference in aspect whatever, and seemed to revolve in relation to the Earth just like the fixed stars.

# ON NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
<page-num>156</page-num>

Just as that **tailed star** <note>original Latin: *caudata illa* — referring to the Great Comet of 1577</note> which was visible from the tenth of November in the year 1577 until the 26th of the following January, was—according to the testimony of those same experts using the refined discipline of **parallaxes** <term>parallax: the apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations; astronomers used this to prove comets were further away than the Moon</term>—revolving above the Moon in the ether more remote from us. This is also confirmed by the observations of the most illustrious and worthy prince, **William, Count of Hesse** <note>William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel (1532–1592), a pioneering astronomer who built one of the first modern observatories</note>. But more shall be said regarding these matters in our *Meteorologics*.

The ancients, such as **Aristotle** and others, more easily formed the opinion that the motion of the **diurnal revolution** <note>the apparent 24-hour rotation of the heavens around the Earth</note> resided in the heavens, because they were unaware of any other sphere there besides the **firmament** <note>the "fixed" sphere of the stars</note> or the orb of the fixed stars. For the slow motion of the fixed stars was not perceived by the ancient mathematicians and those few investigators of nature; only the diurnal motion from east to west was admitted. This held until the time of **Hipparchus** <term>Hipparchus: a Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who discovered the precession of the equinoxes, a very slow wobble in the Earth's/stars' orientation</term> and down to our own times, when through the observations of many people over many centuries, another motion was detected in the **eighth sphere**.

For this reason, the diurnal motion was later attributed to a "fantastic" **ninth sphere**. Yet, because of still other motions, they are forced to establish a **tenth sphere**, or the **prime mover** <term>original Latin: *primum mobile* — the outermost sphere in the Ptolemaic system, supposed to provide the motion for all inner spheres</term>. If those ancient writers, both Greek and others, had understood these requirements of the celestial orbs, they never would have dreamed of a diurnal revolution occurring in some supreme heaven. Instead, they would have shed more light on the Earth itself, so they might understand that this motion serves the Earth alone and not the rest of the world. In this way, they might have found the cause for the Earth's magnificent adornment and for the generation and propagation of natural things across its entire circumference.

It is ridiculous to think that the diurnal motion benefits the fixed stars in any way, or that it confers anything to the **three superior planets** <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, or provides any convenience to the Sun. Nor does it make Mercury, Venus, or the Moon "more blessed" in any fashion. It remains, then, that this is a natural arrangement for the Earth: so that there might exist within the Earth an illustrious power to receive, in turn, the longed-for joys of the solar rays, the lights, and the forms poured out from every direction.

## BOOK II.

The Moon, as well as the benefits of the other stars. Thus, the **monthly revolution** in the Moon successively brings the most welcome rays of the Sun to the Moon from every side, and rescues all parts of the Moon from solitude <note>original: *solitudine* — here meaning a state of being cut off or unlit</note>. For this reason, it both turns itself in a monthly circuit and is revolved by the powers of the Sun. For any globe, wherever it may be, leaps forward by a **natural instinct**; it is moved not by some conscious plan, but by a certain natural necessity by which it is carried through the **ether** <term>ether: the rarefied element once believed to fill the upper regions of space</term>, and that motion is measured by **innate forces** <note>original: *insitis viribus* — the author is arguing for internal physical laws rather than external mechanical pushing</note>. In the same way, the distances of moving bodies are certain—though at some times they vary—arising from the action and **confederation** <note>original: *confoederatione* — an early way of describing the interconnected physical relationship between celestial bodies</note> of different bodies, with the **Sun as the principal driver**.

Therefore, the stars are not moved by **carrying spheres** <term>carrying spheres: in the old Ptolemaic system, planets were thought to be physically embedded in solid, transparent "orbs" like layers of an onion</term>; instead, they are carried through the ether and combined by their own innate forces and mutual impelling powers. If **Aristotle** had foreseen these more carefully when he spoke of the spheres, and if he had not introduced that **absurd crowd of eccentrics and epicycles** <term>eccentrics and epicycles: complex mathematical circles used to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backward or change speed</term> into nature, he would have admitted no material spheres at all. But it is likely that he was less skilled in motions and theories; it would have been better for him to have introduced the reasons and science of motions and **phenomena** <note>original Greek: *Φαινομένων* (Phainomenon) — appearances or observable events</note> into his books *On the Heavens*, rather than certain **sophistical and useless contentions** about the infinite. 

We see also that **comets** have motion in the ether—not indeed as certain as the stars, but circular and (while their bodies remain) continuous. But it would be ridiculous to assign **material spheres** to these newly-born things, even when they linger above the Moon in the orbits of the planets; or, when the sky is already full and burdened, to admit new bodies or new motions. Furthermore, they have motions peculiar to themselves, so that they do not seem to be rotated by a sphere borrowed from any star. Therefore, they are either carried by innate forces or rotated by the impulse of other bodies. But since innate forces are constant in a body so...

# PHYSIOLOGY
<note>original: *Physiologiae* — in this period, "physiology" referred to the study of natural science and the laws of the physical world, rather than just biology.</note>

since they cannot exist in a fresh and fluid medium, it remains that they are agitated only by the impulse of others, or at least for the most part; especially by the **Sun**, who alone has the greatest power of acting and impelling. He is also the center of the world’s motion, exercising his empire everywhere, as can best be proven from the differences and periods of the **phenomena** <note>original: *Φαινομένων*</note> and their motions. Globes are not "heavy" or "light" by their very nature; **gravity** and **levity** are merely the inclinations of parts toward their own origins. Indeed, the globes are distinct principles, distinct provinces, which are carried and remain in the empty space of the universe—the **ether** <term>ether: the "aether" of the ancient philosophers, thought to be a subtle fluid filling space</term> of the ancients. They are not balanced by their own weights; for nothing in the entire universe possesses weight or boundaries directed toward a fixed limit, except for the motions of parts toward their own origins; nor is anything moved toward a specific place, body, or space simply because it is the "center of the universe." <note>The author is refuting the Aristotelian idea that objects fall because they seek the center of the universe; he argues instead for a form of local gravity where parts are attracted to their own parent planet.</note>

There are two kinds of globes: the **shining** and the **non-shining**. The shining are the Sun and the more brilliant fixed stars. The non-shining are the Earth, the Moon, and the "nebulous" stars. These globes, by their own **innate virtue** and **soul** (just as the Earth is magnetic), possess their own motions. They do this without the need for real eccentric orbs, little spheres, or circular tracks—as if it were necessary for motion to be kept going by such intricate machines, in the same way that craftsmen equip **clocks** with little mechanical parts. Therefore, it is better to say that they are carried by their own soul within their body through open, non-resisting spaces, than to be carried and hauled by a soul residing in spheres or on little wheels, as if they were lazy, idle bodies.

# CHAPTER XI.
## *Concerning the earth and its poles.*

The poles are in the Earth, both of which are below the **horizon** <term>finitor: the "finisher" or boundary of sight; the horizon</term>; except in that location where one is trodden under our feet, in the center of the other cold Zone. as Virgil poorly sang. For what do the poles have to do with the spirits of the underworld? Neither does a pole project among the **antipodes** <term>antipodes: people or places on the opposite side of the Earth</term>; rather, it is simply situated at the southern pole of the earth. The star which is called "Polar" by sailors and **Cosmographers** <term>cosmographers: early scientists who mapped the general features of the universe and Earth</term> cannot be so named because of its proximity to a celestial pole, but because it is most perpendicular to the Earth's own pole. In a **right sphere** <term>right sphere: an astronomical perspective where the celestial equator passes directly overhead, occurring at the Earth's equator</term>, the poles are indeed on the horizon, separated by the distance of the Earth's semi-diameter. No horizon divides the equinoctial into any parts, except in a right sphere.

A magnetic stone, of whatever weight or size it may be, moves in a circular fashion toward the unity of the Earth so that its entire form may be preserved. Although this movement is singular within our horizon, it nevertheless appears as a double motion in different instruments and positions: namely, **direction** and **declination** <term>declination: here referring to magnetic "dip" or inclination, where a needle points downward toward the Earth's center</term>. For just as it is granted by nature to every living creature to protect itself and its body, and to turn away from those things which seem harmful: so the **Magnet** possesses its own impulses and is moved toward its own well-being. For this reason—since the Earth is affected by the lights and influences of the stars, and in its prominent parts has departed somewhat from its own nature due to the powers of the Sun and the stars—the entire Earth has composed itself into certain motions so that it might remain in a good and blessed state, flourish with incredible and pleasing variety, and bear fruit. ### PHYSIOLOGY

...[and] if the earth were not rolled about in its daily revolution, the Sun, with its constant lights directed toward one single side, would aim at a certain destined part and burn it, reduce it to dust, and scatter it. The earth would receive the deepest wounds, and no good would come of it: it would not be made fertile, it would not grant life to animals, and the human race would perish. In the other parts, however, everything would be bristling and stiff with extreme cold; and from there all the highest points would be hardest, barren, and inaccessible in perpetual shadows and eternal night. 

Since the earth itself would not suffer such a wretched and horrific appearance on either side, it revolves in a circle, so that by a perpetual changing of light, there might be a perpetual succession of things: heat and cold, birth and decay, day and night, morning and evening, noon and deep night. Thus the earth seeks the Sun and seeks it again, turns away and pursues it, by its own admirable **magnetic virtue** <note>The author refers to the 17th-century theory, famously advanced by William Gilbert, that the Earth's rotation is driven by its nature as a giant magnet.</note>, by its own motion upon its poles, which we have previously shown and demonstrated in various ways to be inherent in the earth. 

Furthermore, not only would evil threaten from the Sun if the earth were at rest and deprived of the solar benefit, but heavy dangers would also threaten from the Moon. For we see how the Ocean swells and surges at certain positions of the Moon; if the Moon did not pass by in its swift course during the daily rotation, the fluid sea would be driven more than is right into opposing parts, and with immense waves it would, in turn, utterly overwhelm all the shores. 

Therefore, lest it perish and be thrown into confusion in various ways, the earth itself turns by its own magnetic and primary virtue—just as in the other **wanderers** <term>wanderers: from the Greek *planētes*, referring to the planets</term>—urged especially by the vigor and light of other bodies. For even the Moon turns itself in its monthly motion, so that it may successively receive the lights of the Sun, in which it rejoices and is refreshed no differently than the earth; for to endure this light perpetually on only one side would not be without great evil and certain

## BOOK II.

...[escape] from destruction. Thus, each of the celestial globes is carried in a circle for its own preservation, either in some larger orbit, or by the rotation of its body alone, or by both. Indeed, for a philosopher to think that all the **fixed stars** <note>Stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to one another, as opposed to planets.</note>, the **wanderers** <note>original: *errones*; a common term for the planets, derived from the Greek *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer."</note>, and the even higher heavens are turned for no purpose other than the benefit of the earth is ridiculous; unless one considers that the Sun, the Planets, all the fixed stars (which are incomprehensible in number and magnitude), and even the physical spheres—much larger still—serve only the earth among all other bodies.

But the earth, while it receives the light of the Sun and all the stars successively from all sides through its daily revolution, also receives another change of light from its annual motion, as well as from the motion of the planets through the **oblique ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky; "oblique" refers to the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit.</note>. This occurs lest the lights of the Sun, pressing upon only one parallel circle, should make too violent an impact in that region, while in other places they would be utterly weak and fruitless; in such a case, no variety of days and nights or seasons of the year would exist. 

Furthermore, the fixed stars also have their own powers, by which the earth is affected; which, although they are smaller and meager, would nevertheless—through the length of time and because of a longer stay in parallel circles—send a more serious and troublesome change to every perpendicular point. For that reason, provident nature has another slow motion (because the applied force is not sudden) by the tilting of the earth's axis. Through this, the lights of all the fixed stars are gradually transferred to new positions on the earth and migrate peacefully. This happens not by the motion of the entire heaven and the universal nature of things, nor by the most absurd **motion of trepidation** <note>A discarded medieval theory used to explain the precession of the equinoxes, suggesting the spheres "shook" or oscillated.</note> of **Thabit ibn Qurra** <note>original: *Thebit Becorae*; a 9th-century mathematician and astronomer who proposed the theory of trepidation.</note>, nor by the new, fictitious, monstrous heavens of the ninth and tenth spheres.

[Critics argue that if the Earth moved,] all buildings and even the highest places would fall; and arrows shot upwards would not fall back to the same spot. Yet there are some who think that even the Ocean is carried by the rush of the First Mover, even while the air above the Ocean—either within its range or where the clouds are gathered—is not carried in a circle, nor driven by that first motion; they are so absurdly intoxicated by this concept of motion that they dare to invent anything to support this fable.

<margin>See Chapter 21 and elsewhere in Book 1.</margin>
They say the circular motion of the earth must be either natural, or violent, or "contrary to nature," because for one simple body there can be only one motion. But this idea of "simple bodies" is a most vain daydream; the earth is not a simple body, and for a single body there can be several motions. Indeed, straight-line motion is not a "natural" motion, as has been said elsewhere, but rather the return of a body that has been pulled away from its seat back toward rest and unity. Therefore, circular motion can also be natural; we do not want this motion to be called "violent" <note>In Aristotelian physics, "violent motion" is motion caused by an external force against an object's natural inclination.</note>. They say it is not "contrary to nature" because it would suit the Earth by reason of some other body.

Thus, the solid parts of the Moon are carried toward the Moon, and those of the Sun toward the Sun. ...serve as physical instruments. Thus, one may see how they construct even ridiculous problems from the most false suppositions.

**Clavius** <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician who was a leading defender of the Ptolemaic (Earth-centered) system.</note> also believes there is no other reason for the Earth to rest in the middle of the world than **gravity**. For this reason, he argues that the Earth always seeks to be in the lowest place, which is the farthest from heaven—namely, the center of the entire universe. Once it has occupied this center, it cannot naturally be torn away from it, because it would have to "ascend" against its own nature and inclination. In truth, this is no reason at all; for **gravity** grants motion, not rest. Whatever is heavy in any given place is only held still by the <term>resistance<note>original: *antitypiâ*. A philosophical term for the quality of a solid body that prevents another body from occupying its space.</note></term> of another object; otherwise, it moves. Indeed, all parts of the Earth, unless they were in the center itself, would be "outside their proper place" because they tend toward that center.

The arguments that follow, which are commonly believed by the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, are even further from the truth. They claim that heavy things are carried toward the center of the world with the greatest force unless something stands in their way. They argue that if the entire Earth were perforated from one side to the other, and a heavy object were dropped into that hole, it would reach only as far as the center with the greatest force. It would not pass to the other side, because then it would be "ascending." They allow that in the beginning, due to the force of its motion, it might fluctuate back and forth for a little while, until the momentum gradually slackens and it comes to rest in the middle. 

Such is the philosophy of those **"place-mongers"** <note>original: *locastri*. A derogatory term the author uses for those who believe objects move simply to reach a specific "place" rather than being acted upon by physical forces.</note> who claim that parts flow toward the whole because of "location," and move faster as they approach the center—as if there were some great power in a single point of space, or as if that lowest place were endowed with such a virtue. We, however, following a truer discipline of bodies and globes, say that if a heavy, non-magnetic body descended toward the center through such a hole (if one existed), it would not descend with such an accelerated course that it would overshoot the center and swing back and forth like a pendulum swinging in the air. Rather, just as it falls downward, it would begin to decrease in speed and momentum...

The reasoning of **Aristotle** <note>Referring to Book 2, Chapter 14 of *On the Heavens* (*De Caelo*), where Aristotle argues that if the Earth moved, it would need to have two different motions like the other planets.</note> limps badly when he says that everything carried in a circle seems to be left behind by the primary motion and carried by multiple motions besides the first sphere; thus, it would also be necessary for the Earth—whether located around the center or in the central seat—to be carried by two motions. But we do not think the Earth is necessarily moved by a double motion, even if the rest are driven by various motions; this does not follow at all. The argument is much less valid because the Moon is not carried by diverse motions, even though it shows us various appearances of motions in its simple course. Furthermore, if the Earth were carried by a double motion, then we would see progressions, regressions, and reversals of the fixed stars. This follows no more than the fact that our visible horizon is seen as different from the true horizon through the center, given the immense distance of the fixed stars. The mover of the Earth is not in its center any more than in its own or another’s circumference (as a certain **Nolan** <note>Giordano Bruno (1548–1600), born in Nola, Italy. He was a radical philosopher who proposed that the universe was infinite and that the Earth and stars moved.</note> thought), nor in any other part; but all the homogeneous and primary parts, which are also magnetic, contribute to the motion. The motivating force and constitutive direction (if I may call it that) come from the "soul" or primary form, which is present in every part just as it is in the whole.

The spaces and nature are similar both beyond the moon and within its orbit and the Earth.

See more on these matters in Book 6 of *On the Magnet*. This "third motion" introduced by **Copernicus** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543) proposed three motions for the Earth: daily rotation, annual revolution around the Sun, and a third motion to account for the stability of the Earth's axis (precession).</note> is not a motion at all, but rather a stable orientation of the Earth while it is carried in its great orbit, as it constantly faces one part of the heavens.

## CHAPTER XII.

### Concerning the motion of the first mover. <term>first mover</term> <note>original: *primum mobile*. In traditional geocentric astronomy, this was the outermost sphere that rotated once every 24 hours, driving the motion of all the inner spheres (the planets, Sun, and Moon).</note>

Many believe that the cause of the slowness or speed of the spheres comes from the first mover. They claim that the sphere of the fixed stars, being closest to the first mover, completes its course most slowly; that Saturn is next, being slower than the rest of the planets; while the Moon, because it has receded furthest from the first mover, completes its course most quickly. It is as if a most frantic motion <note>original: *insanissimus motus*</note> had been established for the purpose of holding back their courses; it is a wonder that over such a long time it does not throw them entirely into chaos. In truth, the stars that move are faster or slower because of the greater space of their circle and path, and also because of the powers inherent in the moving body itself. It does not come from such a foolish, eternal slowing-down of the spheres—as if the spheres would go mad and rage like drunkards <note>original: *debaccharentur*</note> if the "frantic" first mover did not throw a bridle upon them.

If the first heaven were moved, rather than the Earth, and it exerted its force upon the lower spheres, it is likely that some of the heavens would imitate such a remarkable motion and would follow its rotations and poles above all else. But no motion is consistent with the motion or the axis of the daily <note>original: *diurnae*</note> revolution. Therefore, such a thing is neither the primary nor the commanding motion.

The spheres derive their dignity, power, strength, and influence from the stars embedded within them. The Moon moves terrestrial and watery things, not by its sphere, but by its body. The Sun, by the power of its body, gives life to the world. But if the sphere of the fixed stars were

# NATURAL PHILOSOPHY <note>original: *Physiologiae*. In this era, the term referred to the study of the physical world and natural laws, what we would now call physics or cosmology.</note>

...[be slowed down]. This most strong and powerful sphere is adorned and strengthened by countless stars; it is the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>original: *ἀπλανής* (*aplanes*). A Greek term meaning "not wandering," used to distinguish the fixed stars from the planets, which appear to move independently.</note>, not a wandering one. It is, as it were, the firmament and the strength of the world, containing many stars that rival the Sun, and its depth is incomprehensible. Would anyone then dream that the entire nature of things—except for the Earth—could be rotated so rapidly by a heaven lacking strength, lacking stars, and lacking powerful light? Would the universe be spun like straws and scraps in an unyielding whirlwind?

<margin>See Chapter 11, Book 1.</margin>

If the whole heaven moved and not the Earth, it would be necessary for the lower spheres to rotate with that same motion. This would include the element of fire and all of the upper air, which we have established as the location of comets, since they appear to move across the sky with the daily revolution. Why, then, do we not see all the air that exists above the circuit of the Earth—the region where the higher clouds remain—being swept away? It would seem that the heavenly force leaves that air behind. But how? For when force is applied and bodies are continuously rolled, they tend to be drawn into the motion more tightly. For example: why, when the outer sphere revolves along with the massive adjacent spheres, would a tiny little orb of lower air remain still? This air is a mere point in relation to the whole, and it is surrounded on all sides by the continuous movement of the surrounding body, sharing its nature and properties. Why, I ask? What philosopher would be so ridiculous as to think that this air would remain, persist, and stay immobile? It would have to be swept along by that vast, continuous, and touching body; it would not be at rest. Yet, we see that it is at rest. Therefore, that heavenly revolution is not an eternal reality; it is merely a concept of the imagination and does not exist.

### CHAPTER XIII.

->About the Moon, or the Earth's companion.<-

After we have discussed the truer magnetic parts of the earth, as well as the whole earth itself and its <term>effluvia</term> <note>original: *effluviis*. These are the "emanations" or vapors believed to flow out from the Earth, which Gilbert linked to magnetic and atmospheric effects.</note>, there follows the Moon—a companion, friend, and foster-child, and as if **another earth**. She must be examined, described, and observed by us because she looms closest and manifestly affects, shakes, and stirs the earth, the seas, and the effluvia daily; she possesses great significance and value among mortals. We shall judge her better after we have recounted what the ancients thought about the Moon. It will also be necessary in so difficult a matter to bring the fabrications of the **Ancients** openly into the light and to seek the truth from among them all. **Orpheus** <note>A legendary Greek figure; here, the author refers to the Orphic hymns or traditions.</note> considers it to be another earth, which has many mountains, many cities, and many houses. **Thales** affirmed the Moon to be an earth; some **Pythagoreans** felt the same, and even believed it to be inhabited by animals. **Anaxagoras** also held the Moon to be another earth...

<insert>An</insert>axagoras and Democritus posited <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of the Moon's nature.</note>, along with the exceptional beauty of mountains and valleys. For in this way we can pass judgment on it more certainly, and reject uncertain opinions, if we contemplate it through certain steps (by a surer path) through proper and frequent observations. Therefore, that body which is seen on high and called the Moon is solid and opaque, not at all transparent or permeable to light; because the light that flows from the Sun, most brilliant and powerful, is stopped, intercepted, and reflected by the Moon no less than it is by the earth. For we see in <term>solar eclipses</term> <note>original: *deliquiis solaribus*</note>, as if by a most opaque mass, the Sun’s light is stopped and turned away; even if the Moon itself emits certain obscure and almost imperceptible lights and colors even when it overshadows the Sun from us; the reasons for which we will give in their proper place. For it must not be thought that this happens either from the passage of light through a semi-transparent mass, nor from any proper light, or power, or action, as many philosophizing people thought. In the same way, it always turns away the lights of both the <term>planets</term> <note>original: *erronum*, literally "wanderers," a term used for planets because they move against the background of fixed stars.</note> and the fixed stars from the earth whenever it sits directly in front of them, whether it is full of Sun or deprived of it. It is, therefore, an opaque body, and without light, without innate splendor, without fires.
