### ON PHYSIOLOGY

It also appears round; and even when it appears to us as a shadow <note>The author refers to the Moon during an eclipse or when its dark side faces us</note> amidst the greatest splendors of the Sun—at that time when it reflects borrowed light while opposite those same rays—it displays a perfect circle. At such a great distance, the circle appears so smooth that the smallest protrusions or heights do not fall within our sense of sight. However, it is not to be compared to a flat, round table, for it is entirely spherical. This is demonstrated by the precise increases of light at specific distances from the Sun during new moons, and likewise the decreases during old moons <note>That is, the waning phases of the Moon.</note>, regardless of where the Sun or Moon travel through the Zodiac, how much the Moon deviates in latitude from the center of the signs, or its varying distances from the Earth in its eccentric orbits. Therefore, based on the shape of the light reaching our sight according to these causes—by reasons easily demonstrated to anyone—the body of the Moon is spherical and globular.

Next, we must observe the various and uneven differences across the sphere’s edge, which the ancients called the "Face of the Moon," as if the Moon had a face with two eyelashes, a nose, and a mouth. This was born of a vanity no less great than that of our own common folk, who are accustomed to jokingly claim that those spots are a man in the Moon burdened with a bundle of briars <note>A common European folk motif depicting a "Man in the Moon" carrying sticks or thorns as a punishment.</note>. Regarding these spots and blemishes on this star, there was much controversy among the Ancients. 

However, so that we may judge them more certainly, we provide a <term>Selenography</term> <note>From the Greek *Selene* (Moon) and *graphia* (writing/drawing); the art of mapping the Moon’s surface.</note>, or a description of the Moon. All of Antiquity unfortunately neglected this; had they done it, we might understand after the course of so many years whether the visible spots therein had changed. Furthermore, such a description is necessarily required in the observation of the lunar body to determine whether it does not rotate at all (as was argued and accepted by Aristotle) or if it turns in some part. It also allows us to see how, in its monthly motion, it inclines its poles—the poles of its own body—toward certain parts of the world, and in what manner it is joined to the Earth and corresponds with the Earth's position. ## CHAPTER XIV.

->Concerning the Moon.<-

The Moon, being of a different nature than the Sun, is a solid substance without its own light, varying in its elevations. It never originates from the thickening of an imagined "fifth essence" <note>The "fifth essence" or *quintessence* was the celestial material in Aristotelian physics, thought to be perfect and unchanging.</note>, as if it were merely a denser part of some trivial sphere; instead, it is a celestial body <note>original: "astrum"; here referring to a planet or moon rather than a distant sun.</note>, just like the earth, having its own motion through its own spaces. Indeed, the earth is also like another Moon, which, having received light from the Sun, shines back toward the Moon, just as the Moon sends the light conceived from the Sun back to the earth; for every solid object reflects light. 

During a new moon, the earth—full of its own borrowed light—illuminates the Moon; during a full moon, the Moon illuminates the earth. The Moon shows "spots," as it were, through differences in its substance and surface. Likewise, the earth presents spots toward the Moon, consisting of the continental lands which reflect less light; the waters and the Ocean, however, appear more brilliant because of their smoother nature, which is more capable of catching the light. For just as we see our own images in the waves as if in mirrors, so the seas receive light and reflect it more abundantly than the lands do. For the spots on the Moon do not exist because of more transparent parts of the Moon—as Giovanni Battista Benedetti <note>original: "Iohannes Benedictus"; a 16th-century mathematician who influenced Galileo.</note> contends—in which the light is not reflected but hidden from us by penetrating through. For even if light penetrates into waters, the waters still shine and reflect back [the light they have] received...

# ON NATURAL PHILOSOPHY
<note>original: *Physiologiae*; in the 17th century, this term referred to the study of nature and the physical world rather than just biology.</note>

...ich have received light, not only reflected as is usual in solid mirrors. Thus **Crystals**, which do not reflect a distinct image, give back light when illuminated by the Sun, and they radiate it more abundantly than wood or bricks of any color, or similar materials. Likewise, one who is on a very high mountain near the sea while the Sun is shining will perceive a much greater splendor from the deep sea than from the adjacent regions, whether they be sands, forests, or meadows. 

There are mutual services between the earth and the Moon; the Moon offers light to the earth throughout the night, as much as it can from its opaque surface using light borrowed from the Sun. The Earth strikes the Moon with light borrowed from the Sun, though in a small amount; yet it is comparable and equivalent to the Moon's light. Just as the Moon causes an eclipse of the Sun when it lies between us and the Sun, so the earth causes an eclipse of the Sun <note>The author is describing what we now call a lunar eclipse: from the perspective of the Moon, the Earth is eclipsing the Sun.</note>, and deprives the Moon of the Sun’s light. 

Therefore, an eclipse of the Moon for us is an eclipse of the Sun on the Moon, and an eclipse of the Sun for us is an eclipse of the earth for those on the Moon <note>original: *Lunares*; the author adopts the common early modern thought experiment of hypothetical inhabitants of the Moon.</note>; for the earth is seen to suffer from the interception of light just as the Moon does. 

Every celestial body <note>original: *astrum*</note> is imbued with its own specific and primary nature. For if in a meadow or a grassy field there are various herbs endowed with various virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to inherent medicinal or physical properties.</note>, it is consistent that the great orbs are also informed by their own peculiar virtues; their lights are not idle, nor do they pour all their vigor into the earth alone. It is reasonable to think, along with the ancient Philosophers, that the Moon—which agrees with the earth in most respects and which suffers from the Sun with similar affections—is also another earth, and not merely a "denser part of a trivial sphere" <note>This is a rejection of the Aristotelian view that the Moon was a perfectly smooth, ethereal ball with just a few "dense" spots. The author argues it is a physical world like our own.</note>.

Just as the Moon, by its interposition, hinders the light of the Sun from striking the earth; so the earth, falling upon the Moon, intercepts the light of the Sun during an ecliptic full moon. The Moon is affected by the light of the Sun just like the earth: for on it there is dawn and evening, noon and deep night, morning and evening twilight, heat from the presence of light, and cold from its absence. Even among the fixed stars, the **Greater Dog** <note>The constellation Canis Major, containing the star Sirius.</note> seems much changed from that reddish color which it was once thought to possess (because it was marked by astrologers as having the nature of **Mars** and **Jupiter**); yet now it is a very clear star, much more serene and bright than **Spica** in the constellation of the **Virgin**, or the star in the **Lyre**.

# CHAPTER XVII.
->Concerning the Lunar Path.<-

**The Sun** has its own peculiar course in the Zodiac, which is called the ecliptic path <note>original: *via ecliptica*. The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere.</note>, in which its path is always fixed and perpetual—or rather, it stays exactly under the ecliptic itself. The **Moon**, however, which moves around the Earth, does not travel along the ecliptic, but according to its own motion—observed throughout all ages—is driven in a circle oblique <note>tilted or slanted</note> to the ecliptic, in accordance with the observations of everyone. For whether calculated by a homocentric sphere and included epicycles <note>A system of circles within circles used to explain planetary motion.</note>, according to the opinion and calculation of **Copernicus**, or by the eccentric and epicycle of the ancients <note>Referring to the Ptolemaic system, which placed Earth at the center with offset (eccentric) orbits.</note>, the flat surface of the Moon's orbits always intersects the surface of the ecliptic along a diameter passing through the center of the Earth. The mutual angle of this intersection is set at five degrees <note>original: *partium quinque*</note>, always constant and certain, which is the extent of the greatest latitude of the Moon. From this it follows that the axis of the Copernican homocentric sphere, or the axis of those spheres carrying the apogee <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit where a body is furthest from the Earth.</note>, also intersects the axis of the Zodiac in the center of the world; and the poles of this oblique plane of the Moon's orbits decline from the poles of the Zodiac by those same five degrees. The mutual intersections of the ecliptic line and this Lunar path are two points, which are called the **Head and Tail of the Dragon** <term>Lunar Nodes</term> <note>original: *caput & cauda Draconis*. These are the points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path. In medieval and Renaissance astronomy, these points were essential for predicting eclipses.</note>. Indeed, not only does the whole Moon observe the poles of this journey, but even its designated parts—the poles of the Lunar body itself—align precisely with those limits; not otherwise than the Earth, whose poles are directed toward the **Cynosure** <note>original: *cynosuram*. Refers to the constellation Ursa Minor or the North Star.</note> and the opposite part of the sky.

# CHAPTER XVIII.

->**Concerning the motion of the Moon.**<-

Regarding the obvious difficulty <note>original: *scandalo*. Literally a stumbling block or logical problem in the model.</note> of the motion of the **Epicycle** <term>epicycle: A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent); used in pre-modern astronomy to explain complex planetary orbits.</term>, **Fernelius** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a French physician and astronomer.</note> responds: that the Moon has its own motion in the epicycle around its own center, conforming to the motion of the Epicycle but in the opposite direction. From this motion, it follows that the Moon always turns its spotted face toward us. **Clavius** <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a prominent Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who led the Gregorian calendar reform.</note> also agrees with Fernelius’s solution to this objection; nor should this seem strange and absurd, even though **Aristotle** denied that stars have their own individual motions. For since the *Phenomena* <note>original: *Φαινόμενα*, meaning the observable appearances or celestial facts.</note> show that the Moon is carried in an epicycle and always turns the same face toward us, it is necessary for it to be revolved by its own motion around its own center, so that it always remains in a certain stable balance <note>original: *libramento*. A state of equilibrium or counter-balancing.</note>. Thus, first, that most worn-out opinion of **Aristotle**, the astronomers, and common philosophers must be renounced: the idea that the stars are carried by spheres. Furthermore, if the Moon proceeded in its little sphere or epicycle by its own course and the impulse of its own body, would it not be necessary—I say—that when a man or any body whatsoever descended in a circle, one part would be turned toward us, but the other part (which was then turned away) would be brought into our sight once he ascended the little circle again from the other side? But **Clavius** imagines that it remains in a certain stable balance. Perhaps he intends for it to face the Earth by that balance. Therefore, perhaps the Moon is weighted toward the Earth alone: much more foolishly than **Ovid** thinks the Earth is balanced in the air by its own weights <note>Refers to Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, where he describes the Earth suspended in the atmosphere, held up by its own equilibrium.</note>. But it is not permitted to imagine whatever one wishes in philosophy, unless one brings some better reason for that opinion; otherwise, philosophers will exceed even the license given to poets.

PHYSIOLOGY

The **synodic month** <term>synodic month: The time it takes for the Moon to reach the same position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth, approximately 29.5 days.</term> consists of 29 days, 12 hours, and 44 minutes <note>original: *scrup.*, for *scrupulus*, meaning a small part or 'scruple,' used here for minutes.</note>.

**Copernicus** established the distance of the **New and Full Moon** as:
{ Maximum: 65 Earth semidiameters <note>The distance from the center of the Earth to its surface.</note>, 30 minutes.
{ Minimum: 55 Earth semidiameters, 8 minutes.

For the **Half-Moon** <note>original: *Dividuæ*, referring to the Moon when it is half-illuminated at the quarters.</note>:
{ Maximum: 68 Earth semidiameters, 20 minutes.
{ Minimum: 52 Earth semidiameters, 17 minutes.

The average between the New and Full Moon, and the maximum and minimum, is 60 semidiameters and 19 minutes.

The average for the half-moon is 60 semidiameters and 18 ½ minutes.

The average of both is 60 parts <note>semidiameters</note> and 18 ¼ minutes.

Since there are four limits to the Moon’s distance from the Earth—whether determined by **epicycles** <term>epicycle: A small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger circle; used to explain variations in speed and distance.</term> or **eccentrics** <term>eccentric: A circular orbit where the Earth is not exactly at the center.</term>—there is no doubt that, in nature and in truth, there is one single motion of one body, one star. However, they are moved in various ways because of the coinciding strengths of the moving bodies, namely of the planets and the Earth. The Moon, by an innate desire for the Sun’s light, moves around the center of its own course, not the center of the Earth; yet it is also in some way restrained by the Earth and acts in harmony with it. The Sun also organizes and drives this; the path between these limits is 60 parts or semidiameters of the Earth. The Moon moves toward the Sun in 29 ½ days. Since the ratio of circles to their diameter is the same, it is manifest that the equalized or average distance of the Moon from the center of the Earth is 30 diameters <note>Note that 60 semidiameters equals 30 full diameters.</note>. Thus, that circle, or that path, consists of thirty of the Earth's rotations, or returns to the Sun.

Therefore, the entire lunar path from one **conjunction** <note>original: *synodo*, the meeting of the Sun and Moon.</note> to the next consists of 30 revolutions of the Earth toward the Sun. Thus, the Earth turns itself toward the Sun with the same relative speed as the Moon itself. There is, therefore, a true **symmetry** between the monthly course and the daily course. It is the Earth, then, that revolves: it is not some insane rapidity of the **Primum Mobile** <term>Primum Mobile: In older astronomy, the outermost sphere of the heavens that was thought to spin the entire universe around the Earth once a day.</term>, an enormous symmetry without any proportion. The **Eccentric** follows the order of the signs <note>The signs of the Zodiac.</note> above the center of the world, and...

## BOOK II.

...the much-touted "harmony of celestial motions" is not actually as they describe it: namely, that the closer a sphere is to the **prime mover** <term>prime mover: In Latin, the *primum mobile*; in ancient and medieval astronomy, this was the outermost sphere of the universe that was believed to rotate at incredible speed, dragging the inner spheres along with it.</term> and its fictitious, lightning-fast primary motion, the less it resists it, and the slower it is carried by its own motion from west to east; whereas the further away a sphere is, the more it resists and the faster it completes its own motion. By this logic, they claim the Moon completes its cycle fastest because it is furthest removed from the prime mover. These are vanities <note>original: *vanitates*. The author dismisses these traditional explanations as empty or lacking physical reality.</note> accepted only so that the existence of that prime mover might be maintained, making it seem as if it has the effect of slowing down celestial movements. It is as if the movement of the stars resulted from a slowing force, rather than being an innate and natural power—as if the rest of heaven acted with a force of furious impulses! If that were the case, the stars certainly would not proceed among themselves with such harmonious and symmetrical strength.

The Moon possesses its own motion around the center of its own circle within its own space, outside the center of the earth; because of this specific course, it only *appears* to be carried in an **epicycle** <term>epicycle: A small geometric circle used by early astronomers to explain why planets sometimes appear to speed up, slow down, or move backward. The center of the epicycle moves along a larger circle called a deferent.</term>.

That motion which astronomers attribute to an **eccentric circle** <term>eccentric circle: An orbital path where the center of the circle is not the same as the center of the Earth, used to account for the varying distances of celestial bodies.</term> is non-existent. However, in its actual course, there is a shifting away from the earth’s center when the forces of both celestial bodies are "lifted" by the Sun, specifically when those three bodies are in a straighter line. For this reason, the Moon is said to be at its **apogee** <term>apogee: The point in an orbit where a body is at its furthest distance from the Earth.</term> during both the full moon and the new moon; for among astronomers, the motion of the Moon is demonstrated through various and shifting spheres.

**Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model dominated for over a millennium.</note>, based on the nature of conforming spheres, demonstrates that another eccentric sphere can be used in place of an epicycle. **Copernicus** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), who proposed the heliocentric system where the Earth revolves around the Sun.</note> posits a concentric circle to which he adds two epicycles. The motion of the **precession of the equinoxes** <term>precession of the equinoxes: A slow, continuous change in the orientation of Earth's rotational axis, which makes the stars appear to shift position over thousands of years.</term> in the earth is similar to the motion of the **nodes** <term>nodes: The two points where the Moon's orbit intersects the path of the Sun (the ecliptic).</term> in the Moon.

The Moon’s motion in its path—due to the eccentricity of its way, which corresponds to an epicycle—can be conceived of exactly as **Maginus** <note>Giovanni Paolo Magini (1555–1617), an Italian astronomer and mathematician known for his complex planetary tables and his efforts to refine the Ptolemaic system.</note> imagines it. The Moon, and the path of the Moon—as well as those of the other **wanderers** <note>original: *erronum*. This is a traditional term for the planets, derived from the Greek word *planētai*, meaning "wanderers."</note>—are improperly and commonly called "the heavens."

The Moon is magnetically bound to the Earth, which is why its face is always turned toward the Earth.

The Moon fills only a fortieth part of the Earth's volume, according to both Ptolemy and Copernicus, who do not differ much from one another on this point.

## BOOK II.

...is not sent down to the lands, and yet it illuminates the Earth with full light. When the Moon’s course is swift, no manifest difference appears greater than when it proceeds slow and sluggish. When it is below the Horizon, the Moon stirs the seas no less than when it hangs over them with its rays and light above the Horizon. For just as it moves around the Earth—or rather follows the Earth like a captive in a great orbit—so too the Moon clings to the Earth and serves it with poured-out forces. 

The Earth, in truth, acts in concert with the Moon; for this reason, the motions of the seas <note>original: *motus marium*. This refers to the tides, which the author correctly identifies as being influenced by both the Moon and the Earth.</note> are not only from the Moon, but also from the Earth; for the celestial bodies act upon one another. The poured-out Lunar forces reach the Earth and act upon fluid bodies; likewise, the **magnetic powers** <term>magnetic powers: In the early 17th century, before the theory of universal gravitation, many thinkers like William Gilbert and Johannes Kepler believed that "magnetism" was the physical force that kept planets in their orbits and caused the tides.</term> of the Earth surround the Moon. Both come together by their mutual action, and they agree in the proportion and conformity of their motions; yet the Earth commands more, as its mass prevails. The Earth repels the Moon and attracts it; the Moon persists in its own places and paths, yet it repels and attracts within certain limits—not so that the bodies would collide, as magnetic objects usually do, but so that they might repeat their course. 

Hence all the variations that appear in the Moon's motion occur as the celestial body progresses, with the Earth and the Sun moderating its course without **epicycles** or **eccentrics** <term>epicycles or eccentrics: Complex geometric circles used by older astronomers (like Ptolemy) to explain why planets seem to speed up, slow down, or move backward. The author here argues these are unnecessary mathematical fictions.</term>, by a certain and defined motion, yet not in any perfectly uniform circle.

Observation of the full moon in **Capricorn** <note>The sign of the Zodiac associated with the winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere.</note> shows that the distance of the "southern spot" of the Moon from the edge of the circle of light is greater than in **Cancer** <note>The sign of the Zodiac associated with the summer solstice.</note>. This would be the opposite if there were no inclination of the Moon's poles toward the pole of its carrier, or the pole of the **Zodiac** <term>Zodiac: The belt of the heavens within which the sun, moon, and planets move, divided into twelve signs.</term>, because we see more in the lower part of the Moon; otherwise, it would happen the opposite way due to the **parallax** <term>parallax: The apparent change in the position of an object when viewed from different locations. Here, it refers to the shift in the Moon's appearance based on the observer's position on Earth.</term> in the body.

One must observe the Moon at the beginnings of Cancer and Capricorn, and at the middle intervals, to see whether the Moon's poles always look toward the pole of the Zodiac, or toward the pole of the world and the Earth.

### BOOK II.

The inclination of the Moon at the meridian <note>The meridian is the imaginary great circle in the sky passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a specific location.</note> is different when it is in the constellation of Aries than when it is in Libra; this depends on whether the Moon's poles regard the poles of the Zodiac, or the poles of the world and the earth.

**A B C D** represents the visible face of the Moon, and **G E F** is the "deferent" of the Moon <note>original: *deferens*. In pre-Keplerian astronomy, a 'deferent' was the circular path along which the center of another smaller circle (an epicycle) or the body itself was carried.</note>, or the lunar path. The pole of the Moon is at **P**. Since this pole is turned toward the Sun during the full moon, and the other pole is turned toward it during the new moon, the Moon does not perform a "conversion" <note>A rotation on its own axis relative to the Sun.</note> by a revolution of its body toward the Sun. Nor does it require such a conversion as the earth does, for the sake of which it was necessary for the earth to be moved in a circle. Therefore, for the Moon, there is neither a day nor a year, except for the Lunar year, which is completed in 27 earthly days. On the Moon, one summer is like winter, and spring is just like autumn. The "Torrid Zone" <note>The region of a celestial body receiving the most intense, direct sunlight.</note> in the middle, passing through the poles, exists only in the summer; it is cooled in the winter, just like the other parts. **O** and **R** are temperate regions because of the oblique <note>Slanted or indirect.</note> rays of light. **A** and **D** are temperate because of their "perpetual stay" <note>This likely refers to areas near the lunar limbs that experience prolonged exposure or specific lighting conditions due to the Moon's orientation.</note>; and even more so because the Sun, being much larger, illuminates more than half of the Moon's surface.

It was necessary to observe the face of the Moon and a true **Selenography** <term>original: *Lunægraphiam*. The art of mapping the Moon's physical features, similar to how geography maps the Earth.</term> during a full moon when it is near the Tropic of Cancer, and another during a full moon when it is near the Tropic of Capricorn. However, a greater difference is apparent when the Moon is in Cancer, having observed its rising and its highest culmination <note>The point at which a celestial body reaches its highest point in the sky.</note>, when the Moon reaches its Northern latitude in Cancer.

## BOOK II

Observation of the Moon in the tropics and at the equinoxes. For in the Tropics, the Moon reaches its highest point <note>original: *culminat*, meaning to reach the meridian or the highest point in the sky for the day.</note> in the same way, with its upper part looking toward the poles of the Zodiac <note>The poles of the ecliptic, the path the sun appears to follow.</note>. If the [Earth's] pole were to face the pole of the Zodiac at the equinoxes, the inclination of the upper face would be greater, with the star reaching its highest point in Aries toward the West, and in Libra more toward the East. For this reason, the poles are to be established in the visible circle of the Moon on both sides for North and South.

In the year 1592, on December 3, when the Moon was in Aries, its face inclined its pole very much toward the West, so that the top of its face was almost perpendicular at midday. In the year 1593, on December 25, with the Moon being in Gemini, not far from the <term>head of the dragon</term> <note>original: *capite draconis*. This is an old astronomical term for the ascending lunar node—the point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic moving North.</note>, the Moon at the meridian was very upright toward the north. The greatest tides are caused by the Moon in the great Ocean within the Tropics, and are larger than in other places; but nevertheless, due to the position of the seas and lands, the masses of water often rise higher, such as in the Strait of Calais or Dover, where the waters from the British Ocean <note>The English Channel.</note> and the German Ocean <note>The North Sea.</note> meet. This happens because the Lunar rays are more direct, and the body of the Moon is more directly and perpendicularly overhead, from which the earthly breaths <note>original: *spiramenta*. In 16th and 17th-century natural philosophy, tides were sometimes explained as the Earth "breathing" or as vapors being drawn out by the heat or influence of the stars.</note> are more strongly summoned.

The Moon’s nodes move through the entire circuit of the Zodiac in almost 19 years, moving against the succession of the signs <note>This is "retrograde" motion, moving backward through the zodiac from Aries toward Pisces.</note>, uniformly around the center and poles of the ecliptic.

The return of the Moon <note>The sidereal month, or the time it takes the Moon to return to the same position relative to the stars.</note> occurs in 27 days, 5 hours, 5 minutes, and 36 seconds.

However much there may be various controversies regarding the annual course and the revolutions of the other planets, it is certain and admitted by all that the Moon revolves around the Earth. But how its motion is unequal, and how it changes its periods in various ways, and by what paths and circles it can be measured or "saved" <note>original: *salvari*. In classical astronomy, "saving the appearances" meant finding a mathematical model that could accurately predict and explain observed phenomena.</note>, has been discovered by the genius of many most wise men. ### CHAPTER XX.

->*A Hypothesis of the System of the World’s Motion; the visible appearance and arrangement of the further world and the stars commonly called fixed, the distance of most of which is entirely unknown and inaccessible by any devices of machines or mathematical scales.*<-

Since the fable of the <term>prime mover</term> <note>original: *primi mobilis*. In ancient astronomy, this was the outermost celestial sphere that was thought to rotate and drive the motion of all the inner spheres.</note> has now been exploded and stripped away from the machinery of the world, and since we have also demonstrated how and why the Earth is driven in a daily revolution, and how the other globes are carried through the ether by their own powers; it remains for us to describe the structure of the world’s motion, the path of the wandering bodies <note>The planets</note>, and the consistency and stability of the stars that remain fixed forever. 

Certain Pythagoreans, who established the foundations of philosophy with the help of the older Greek mathematics, believed that the Earth did not rest at some center, but revolved in an oblique circle; such was the view of Philolaus, as recorded in Plutarch. The rest of antiquity rejected this opinion. Copernicus, in order to avoid an absurd number of circles and complicated paths, also assumed the motion of the Earth in an oblique circle. The most illustrious Tycho Brahe held that the Sun is the center of the secondary movers, or planets, but established the Earth as the center of the universe; he believed Mercury and Venus were moved around the Sun according to Copernicus’s reasoning. Raimarus <note>Nicolaus Reimers Ursus (1551–1600), an Imperial mathematician and rival of Tycho Brahe who proposed a model where the Earth rotates at the center of the universe while the planets orbit the Sun.</note> places the Earth itself at the center of the universe, around which the Moon moves; but he places the Sun not only outside the center of the world, but outside the center of the moving planets. In the well-worn Ptolemaic hypothesis, with all things [ordered] from the Earth to the Moon, through the spheres, to the fixed stars themselves... <note>The text ends here as the catchword *ipsas* indicates the next page begins with "themselves."</note>

# BOOK II.

...the stars themselves, along paths destined by their own circles. Regarding the fixed stars, almost everyone holds the same view. However, the Ptolemaic distribution of celestial spheres, conceived by the Ancients and accepted for many centuries thereafter, can seem rather absurd. This is due to the overly intricate arrangement of spheres and <term>epicycles</term> <note>original: "epicyclorum". Small circles whose centers move along the circumference of larger circles; used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary motion.</note>, through which they account for <term>retrogradations</term> <note>When a planet appears to move backward in the sky from our perspective on Earth.</note> and <term>stations</term> <note>When a planet appears to stand still in the sky before changing direction.</note>, along with the apparent inequality of their motions. Furthermore, the uniformity of motion is sought not around its own center (as it ought to be), but around the "foreign" center of another <term>eccentric</term> <note>original: "eccentrici". A circular path where the Earth is not exactly at the center, a mathematical device used to explain why planets seem to change speed.</note>.

Copernicus’s system, however, is even more incredible, although it is less absurd in how it harmonizes these motions. It required the Earth to be driven by a triple motion, and most significantly, it requires an excessively vast space between the orbit of Saturn and the <term>eighth sphere</term> <note>The outermost sphere in traditional cosmology, which held the fixed stars.</note>, which is left entirely empty of stars.

To assert that the Earth occupies the center of the world is uncertain. There are no arguments—other than those drawn from a likely vanity and uncertainty—to prove that the entire nature of things rests upon any specific, fixed center. Nor can it be perceived or inferred by any scientific arts that the outermost reaches of nature are enclosed in a circle, especially now that the insane spinning of the entire machinery of the world <note>The ancient belief that the whole universe rotates around the Earth every 24 hours.</note> has been exploded. Nor does it follow that if the world is a cohesive structure and a system of things, the Earth must necessarily be placed at the center. 

It is not likely that a body that is less noble, but rather opaque, sluggish, and less lively—deprived of light (which holds the highest excellence in nature)—should be placed in the center as if in the heart and the inner vitals, as the foundation of all things. The center is a place most commanding, excellent, and worthy, from which power <note>original: "virtus". A life-force, influence, or physical virtue.</note> would be distributed equally in all directions. This is especially true since the moving world is carried most of all around the Sun. For five <term>wanderers</term> <note>original: "errones". The planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> revolve around the Sun itself, as if around their own leader and king,

->### ON NATURAL PHILOSOPHY<-
<note>original: "PHYSIOLOGIÆ". In the 17th century, this term referred to the study of the laws of nature and the physical world, rather than just the human body.</note>

...it is credible that it is carried around and always observes it; as some of the more learned of this century attest. However, according to our physical principles, the inequalities of the **phenomena** <note>original: "Φαινομένων" (phainomenon). Observations or appearances of celestial bodies in the sky.</note> cannot be explained by its circuit or any uniform circular motion: just as the theory of the Lunar course is not inferred to be simple and uniform. The Sun is more than one hundred and sixty times larger than the earth.

The distance of the Sun from the earth is 1,040 Earth <term>semidiameters</term> <note>Radii, or half the diameter of the Earth.</note>. The Sun in the middle fortifies its orbit on all sides; those bodies which are closer are moved more quickly; therefore, Saturn moves the slowest, Jupiter is next, while the Moon and the earth are carried by the same rotations. The motion of the earth, since it is circular, inclines in an **equinoctial** manner toward the North with its poles, so that the change of the Sun toward the **solstice** might occur. 

Mathematicians make the orbit carrying the body of the Sun <term>eccentric</term> <note>original: "eccentricum". A circular path where the center is not the Earth; used to explain why the Sun appears to speed up or slow down.</note>:
1. because of the unequal motion of the Sun beneath the **ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky.</note>; 
2. because of the unequal distance of the body from the earth, which is revealed by its unequal apparent size through exquisite observations (provided the air is not differently affected); 
3. because of the unequal size and duration of Lunar eclipses. 

For when the Sun is in various different parts of the **Zodiac**, the Moon sometimes stays longer in the shadow of the earth—even if its distance from both the earth and the ecliptic remains the same—sometimes appearing thicker, sometimes thinner or narrower; these variations must be resolved through the use of an eccentric orbit. To these, they add two other spheres to make the whole system concentric. **Copernicus**, not content with these spheres because he had observed that the Sun's <term>apogee</term> <note>original: "apogæum". The point in an orbit where a body is furthest from the center.</note> moved unequally and the eccentricity changed, adds an **eccentric of an eccentric**, similar to what is found in the sphere of Mercury. The eccentric orbit of the Sun moves regularly around its own center according to the order of the signs in an annual space; its period is the Solar year.

### BOOK II.

Because the <term>Apogee</term> <note>original: "Apogæum". The point in an orbit where a celestial body is farthest from the Earth.</note> is near the summer solstice, the Sun remains in the North for about nine days longer than in the South. Moreover, this long duration of light causes greater changes over many centuries and makes the generation of things more stable. In the rising of the Sun, when it seems to flicker because of the refraction of light, one must observe whether that wavering light is drawn more toward the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitorem". Literally "the finisher" or "the limiter," an early term for the horizon line.</note> or toward the <term>mid-heaven</term> <note>original: "medium cœli". The highest point the Sun reaches in the sky on a given day.</note>. If it moves toward the horizon, the Sun and the sky seem to move; but if it flickers and inclines more toward the mid-heaven, then the Earth moves while the sky stands still. 

The Sun, which is a most powerful fire, would dissolve the Earth and the Moon if they were not at a suitable distance, even if they protected themselves by their motion and rotation. The upper parts of the Moon are heated more by the Sun than the face always exposed to us, because during <term>conjunction</term> <note>The "New Moon" phase, when the Moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun.</note> they are always closer to the Sun.

## CHAPTER XXI.

->*Whether the light of the Sun removes the sight of the stars by day, or*<-
->*rather the Earth, illuminated by the Sun, disturbs the*<-
->*sense of the eyes with that light.*<-

The stars shine brightly with their own lights and are perceived by our eyes when their light strikes the eye. The Sun moves the eyes and the senses in such a way that hardly anyone can look at it steadily; but if one’s gaze is turned away from the Sun, the Sun does not disturb the sense. However, when the light is reflected above the Earth and the surrounding air is illuminated, the eye is bathed from all sides during the day—wherever it is turned—with a light more immediate than that from the stars. For this reason, the stars are not seen during the day, nor even after the Sun has set below the Horizon during the first <term>twilight</term> <note>original: "crepusculo".</note> while part of the air is still reflecting light. It is not, therefore, because of the Sun's primary light,

# CHAPTER XXII.

->*On the motion of the Sun and the Earth.*<-

The motion of the Earth according to <term>Copernicus</term> <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), the astronomer who proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun.</note>, described here more clearly than he himself describes it, is as follows. The "circle of animals," the path the Sun appears to follow through the stars over the course of a year.</note> of the world A B C D, in which the center of the Earth moves in its annual course <term>in consequence</term> <note>original: "in consequentia". This refers to moving in the natural order of the zodiac signs (eastward).</note> around the Sun; so that the Zodiac of the Earth and the Zodiac of the world are always in the same plane, as in the figure below <note>The diagram mentioned is not present on this specific page of the manuscript.</note>; and the parts of the Earth’s Zodiac and the parts of the world’s Zodiac always maintain a similar position. This cannot happen unless another motion is attributed to the Earth’s Zodiac upon its poles <term>in precedence</term> <note>original: "in antecedentia". Moving against the order of the signs (westward). Copernicus proposed this "third motion" to explain why the Earth's axis always points in the same direction (toward the North Star) even as it orbits the Sun.</note>. For let us suppose, for example, the center of the Earth is at A, which is the beginning of <term>Cancer</term>, and the Earth's Zodiac is positioned similarly so that on the same diameter C A, the beginnings of Cancer and <term>Capricorn</term> fall, both of the world and of the Earth, corresponding to each other. Therefore, the beginning of Cancer in the Earth’s Zodiac will look outward toward the <term>sphere of the fixed stars</term>; however, the beginning of Capricorn will look inward toward the center or the Sun at E. ### PHYSICAL SCIENCE

Therefore, so that their orientation remains the same, as much as center A moves forward <note>original: "in consequentia". Referring to the Earth's forward motion in its orbital path.</note>, by that same amount the circumference moves backward <note>original: "in antecedentia". This refers to the Earth's axial "wobble" or third motion which counteracts the orbital turn to keep the axis parallel.</note>. Thus, when center A has completed a quarter-turn of the circle to point B, D will be in the place of C, and B in the place of D. For this reason, the beginning of **Aries** <note>The constellation of the Ram, marking the spring equinox.</note> will fall upon the line E B, which is perpendicular to the Sun. The Sun will then be seen at the beginning of **Aries** in the world’s <term>Zodiac</term> <note>original: "Zodiaci mundi". The fixed belt of stars in the heavens.</note>. As the Earth turns around its center and the poles of the **Equator** <note>original: "Æquatoris". The celestial equator.</note> to produce the <term>diurnal motion</term> <note>original: "motu diurno". The Earth's daily 24-hour rotation.</note>, the Sun’s perpendicular ray will trace the **Equinoctial line** around the Earth.

In this way, as the center proceeds to C, A (the beginning of **Cancer**) will be at position D—that is, facing the Sun. Consequently, the Sun will be seen at the beginning of **Cancer** <note>The constellation of the Crab, marking the summer solstice.</note>. In this position, as the Earth is moved by its daily motion around its own center and upon the poles of the Equator, the **Tropic of Cancer** will be traced. Likewise, by both motions, it will proceed to D (the beginning of **Aries**), where the Sun will be seen at the beginning of **Libra** <note>The constellation of the Scales, marking the autumnal equinox.</note>. 

From this, it is also clear what ***Copernicus*** says: that the angle of the Zodiac’s inclination to the Equator is mobile. For when the Earth's center is placed at A, that angle will face the Sun; that half of the Equator facing the Sun will be above the Zodiac, and the straight line CB will be the common intersection of the Zodiac and the Equator, perpendicular to AE. 

But after A reaches B, B will be in the place of D; therefore, CB will not form an angle with AE, but will be continued into the same straight line with it. The straight line AD, upon which the angle of declination sits, will be perpendicular to BE. This is what he means when he says the entire <term>declination</term> <note>original: "declinationem". The angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator.</note> will then be from the sides. For AD is the common intersection of the <term>Solstitial Colure</term> <note>original: "Coluri solstitiorum". One of the two principal great circles of the celestial sphere, passing through the celestial poles and the solstices.</note> with the plane of the Zodiac, while CB is the common intersection of the <term>Equinoctial Colure</term> <note>original: "Coluri æquinoctiorum". The great circle passing through the celestial poles and the equinoxes.</note> and the Zodiac. 

Now indeed, when the center of the Earth is placed at C, the angle of declination will face the Sun as before, but the Equator’s semicircle will be below the Zodiacal half CAB. As for what someone might suspect—that the pole of the world must change because of this motion—it does not happen

### *On the change of the pole.*

Since it is assumed, and experience also confirms, that those two motions occurring above the poles of the Zodiac according to **Copernicus** <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), the astronomer who proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun.</note> are not exactly equal to one another; from this arises that **precession of the equinoxes** <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>The slow, westward shift of the equinoxes along the plane of the Earth's orbit, caused by the gravitational pull of the Sun and Moon on the Earth's equatorial bulge.</note>, so that as time proceeds, the vernal equinox will eventually be in Cancer in the star-bearing heaven <note>The "firmament" or the sphere containing the fixed stars.</note>, and at other times in Libra, and at others in Capricorn, and in all the intermediate points. 

And since it must follow from this hypothesis that the **pole of the world** <note>The North or South Celestial Pole, around which the stars appear to rotate.</note> does not maintain the same position in the star-bearing heaven, but changes constantly; if anyone now asks how the pole changes, I respond that it moves in that circle which they call the **Arctic** <note>In historical astronomy, this refers to the circular path traced by the celestial pole around the pole of the ecliptic due to axial precession.</note>. That is, while the pole of the Zodiac remains fixed, if the pole of the world is imagined to move around it, it will describe that same circle in which it moves while the equinoxes anticipate their positions. Let it be noted, moreover, which larger fixed stars fall into this circle: for all of those, in the course of time, will be called **polar stars** <term>polar stars</term> <note>Stars that align with the Earth's axis; our current North Star, Polaris, is only one of many stars that take this role over a 26,000-year cycle.</note>, because the pole will approach them—unless perhaps they themselves disappear over time or change their location.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### *On the twinkling of the stars.*

Aristotle says that the twinkling <note>original: "scintillationem"</note> of stars occurs by reason of our own perception <note>original: "affectus nostri"</note> due to their extreme distance. He also thinks that vision occurs through extramission <note>The "extramission theory" is the ancient belief that the eyes send out rays to "touch" objects, rather than receiving light from them.</note>, which he denies in another place. By his reasoning, Saturn ought to twinkle more than Venus; yet anyone can perceive by sight that this is false. Nor does the twinkling of stars arise—as Giovanni Battista Benedetti <note>original: "Baptista Benedictus," a 16th-century mathematician and physicist.</note> claims—from the unequal movement of the transparent media between us, as if some rising smoke had come between ourselves and an object, making that object appear to tremble. We respond to this in the same way: Saturn ought to tremble more than Venus, especially at its greatest distance, because the light of Saturn would have to penetrate to our eyes through many diverse transparent layers <note>original: "diaphaneitates"</note>, namely through the many celestial spheres of the planets. 

Rather, it should be thought that the light of the fixed stars twinkles because of its own brilliance <note>original: "excellentiam"</note>; thus the Greater Dog Star <note>original: "Canis major," referring to Sirius.</note>, Lyra, and Arcturus tremble the most. The Sun itself trembles <note>The author likely refers to the shimmering effect of intense light or solar "glare."</note> the most, but the Moon not at all, since it enjoys only borrowed light, and its light is merely secondary. Likewise, the remaining planets do not shine as primarily as the fixed stars do; they use borrowed light because of their proximity to the Sun, and if they possess any primary light of their own, it is obscured by the secondary light. Furthermore, distance makes light appear more splendid: for if the Moon were further away, it would not show its spots to us, but would shine in the manner of Mercury; for this reason, it does not twinkle in that way. Even the light of the star Venus, though excellent, is not as clear as that of the Greater Dog Star. There are also some fixed stars of lesser light which do not twinkle. Those which twinkle the most possess constant and inherent <note>original: "propria"</note> lights, yet

BOOK II.

...smaller stars at a greater distance from the Sun. And this **twinkling** <note>original: "scintillatio"</note>, which is so improperly named by authors, is actually a **wavering** <note>original: "vacillatio"</note> and a trembling of light; it does not arise from an extraordinary light [inherent to the star], but is produced in the surrounding air. It is evident that they waver much more near the Horizon than at the summit of the heavens <note>The zenith, or the point directly overhead.</note>, or in any other part. For the light travels a longer path through that more vaporous air; for this reason, it is also refracted more, so that the lights even appear larger in such a position. In truth, that air, moved by the daily rotation <note>original: "volutatione," literally a rolling or tumbling motion.</note> of the earth, also moves the refracted light captured by the gliding air, from which movement the wavering or trembling appears. But someone might say that this would happen more because of the winds. But winds do not ascend so high, nor do they spread so widely as to cause great wavering. Nevertheless, it is evident that when winds blow more violently under a clear sky, the waverings of the starlight are then a little greater.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

->On the Stars.<-

Stars are carried not in fixed orbits <note>The author is rejecting the ancient idea that stars are set into solid, crystalline spheres.</note>, but through the **ether** <note>The subtle fluid once thought to fill the upper regions of space.</note> or the **vacuum** by their own **innate forces**; neither do the theories of the mathematicians regarding the planets—though necessary for calculation—describe the true nature of the stars, nor does the whole chorus of philosophers conclude anything [useful] from those borrowed spheres and their doctrines. Those who observe the impulse and progress of some ball or small sphere on a level surface see the motion produced by the ball being moved and set in flight, and they measure its path and course on that surface. It is reasonable to suppose the same happens in the [celestial] spheres; they measure the paths and the arcs of circles while a star moves, proceeds, and turns within such an interval. They are driven around spontaneously—not like animals on earth, but as primary bodies suited for motion—not by wings or legs, but by an **innate vigor** <note>original: "insito vigore"</note> directed toward the good, and by the power of the Sun on account of the diffused sphere of its vigor and light...

# BOOK II.

Light at point **a** has the minimum **refraction** <term>Refraction: The bending of light as it passes from one medium (like space) into another (like the atmosphere).</term> relative to the distance from the eye at **C** to the top of the air at **B**; at **g B** it is greater, owing to the distance from **g** to **C**; at **M** it is greatest, because of the distance from **c** to **E**. This occurs even though the air is uniform, and the **transparency** <term>original: "diaphaneitates"; the quality of allowing light to pass through clearly.</term> is the same at **C B**, **C g**, and **C E**. Therefore, a ray of light traveling a longer path through a thinner transparent medium produces a greater refraction. Yet, at the longest distance through transparent mediums, even if they were the thinnest possible, there would be refraction—or rather, at those immense intervals, a loss of light—to such an extent that the stars would be perceived [differently] from the fixed stars to the earth, if the sky were a physical substance.

**Alhazen** <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), an influential Arab scholar often called the "father of modern optics."</note> wishes to infer from the refraction of the stars on the Horizon that the heavens are thinner than fire and air. In truth, those spaces are translucent, not transparent bodies; nothing else can be inferred from the study of Optics than that the celestial lights pass through the spaces dedicated to the celestial spheres without refraction. This is because, despite those immense distances, the stars neither appear larger nor vary in their position. Therefore, **Vitello** <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1300), a Polish friar and philosopher whose treatise on optics was a standard university text.</note> did not speak correctly when he said that the transparency of the celestial body is thinner than the transparency of air or fire. Instead, he should have attributed no transparency to the celestial body at all, because there is no observable proportion between the density of the air and any supposed transparency of the spheres (which are merely concepts based on opinion). Rather, light passes through those spaces, not through transparent bodies; nor are they **light-bearing** <note>original Greek: "Φώσφορα" (phosphora); used here to mean bodies that carry or produce their own light.</note>, as they do not carry or retain light. Furthermore, a difference in transparency between the elements—air and fire—and the celestial bodies would disturb our ability to perceive the stars accurately.

**Wandering stars** <term>original: "Stellæ erroneæ"; the planets.</term> do not twinkle, because they either borrow their light from the Sun, or the Sun makes their light dimmer. It is manifest that the brightest **fixed stars** twinkle the most. The powers of the stars would not reach us intact through their rays unless they passed through a **vacuum** <term>A void or empty space, containing no matter.</term>; instead, they would be altered by various bodies over such a long passage, and would arrive weak, dull, and drained of energy.

In the nature of things, position exists before motion. Thus God placed the earth and the stars at certain fixed distances before they were moved. And this motion occurs by the impulse of other bodies, by reason of the forces flowing out from them; or from the bodies themselves, when they seem to incline toward the better and toward perfection <note>This reflects the Aristotelian idea that celestial bodies move toward a state of "perfection" or follow a natural teleological purpose.</note>.

# CHAPTER XXV.

## *Concerning Light and Radiance.*

**Light** <term>original: "Lux"; in medieval philosophy, "lux" usually refers to the internal source or essence of light.</term> is the actualization arising from thinning moisture. **Radiance** <term>original: "Lumen"; "lumen" refers to light as it travels through a medium or is perceived by the eye.</term> is the actualization proceeding from a bright object.

The radiance that proceeds from light penetrates a transparent medium <note>original: "diaphanum"; the term used by Aristotle and medieval scholars for any substance (like air or glass) that allows light to pass through.</note> if it is not too deep; it is also received into every transparent medium and displays its action there. Therefore, not without reason, between the morning dawn and the evening twilight, the night—even if it is clear—appears so dark to us; for in a vacuum no relation occurs, and there is no conception of light <note>The author is arguing that light needs a physical medium, like air, to be visible; without matter to "catch" it, space remains dark.</note>. But as radiance comes through the material world, it affects and illuminates it: for that element of air has a resistance, as does whatever reaches all the way to heaven—a physical substance in which it is necessary for radiance to reside. For we see in mountainous regions that twilights occur under a most serene sky, where there is no opacity and no thickness greater than in the upper air; even in the coldest regions, in the clearest and most frozen winter air, twilights exist, and the air is bathed in a faint light when the Sun is far below the Horizon.

BOOK II. CHAPTER XXVI.

### Concerning twilights and light.

Regarding twilights, it is false what Alhazen, Vitello, and Cardano <note>Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham, d. 1040) and Vitello (Witelo, 13th century) were the primary authorities on optics in the Middle Ages. Gerolamo Cardano (d. 1576) was a prominent Renaissance physician and mathematician.</note> definitely determine—that <term>twilight<gloss>original: "crepusculum"; the period of partial darkness between day and night.</gloss></term> begins at 19 degrees before the rising of the Sun—because the height of the atmospheric system varies due to different circumstances. Morning light (which is also twilight) arrives later in winter in cold regions, and vanishes sooner in the evening; this is on account of the atmospheric system being less high.

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

->On illumination and light.<-

<margin>Miscellaneous notes.</margin>
Illumination <term>lumen: the radiated light or "glow" felt by the eye, as opposed to the source itself</term> enters every body, even the most opaque, to some small degree, by which entry it is tainted <note>original: "fœdatur"; suggesting the light loses its purity when mixed with dense matter</note>.

Light <term>lux: the essential source or "form" of light, often associated with the sun or a flame</term> is the same thing as flame. See the section on fire.

Illumination is the pouring forth of light—the extension or diffusion of a thinning nature or of a thinning moisture—which, when gathered back again from a thick substance, thins that substance out, burns it, and sometimes drives it into a flame. Bodies do not shine without flame.

Those small creatures <note>original: "animalcula"; likely referring to bioluminescent insects like fireflies</note> or bodies that shine in flames do not possess illumination in the deepest darkness, but only glow in the twilight when they collect the fading illumination from the air. Illumination is a being. Light is an action rising up from a thinning moisture. Illumination is an action proceeding from a bright source. Illumination is an immaterial being, poured forth from light and received by a body. Illumination passes through the ether <note>original: "ætherem"; the subtle substance then believed to fill the upper regions of space beyond the atmosphere</note> and does not remain or exist within it, but is stopped by what is dense and opaque. Darkness is the deprivation of illumination. Light is form. Illumination is an action proceeding from light.

## CHAPTER XXXI.

->*On color and its opposites.*<-

Color is the presentation or arrival to the sight of light that has been changed by an opaque object. According to the varying opacity of opaque bodies, various colors are reported. Whiteness is not a color—or rather, perfectly white bodies are not colored. This is evident in primary lights, in secondary lights, and in their relations. From this come the various colors in all things. It is necessary for the opacity of a body to be changed in order for the colors to change.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

->*On the generation of things.*<-

Seeds, while they remain dry, do not grow; but once they are drenched with moisture, they release their contents and germinate. For when they have soaked up moisture, that moisture is further spurred on by its own innate action <term>actus: in the philosophy of the time, "action" refers to the internal driving force or the "doing" of a substance's nature</term> and by the surrounding environment. This movement brings life; it grows through the addition of matter or moisture and germinates. The **form** <term>forma: the organizing principle that gives a thing its specific structure and identity</term> imposes limits, determines the outlines of the shape, and sets fixed boundaries.

The action of the moisture extends the body by dilating it; once extended, or emptied by the flow, it absorbs neighboring moisture. The form operates for its own preservation, having provided suitable instruments: roots spread out in all directions and equipped with many fibers. By action and thinning—namely, by heat—the moistures taken in by the roots ascend into the trunk, branches, and leaves. They follow the same paths, are assimilated, and are adapted to the nature of the whole. This movement, composed by the form and incited by the thinning of the moisture, is the life of every growing thing.

Likewise, in many animals, the male seed from the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>

This back-and-forth movement is called the **pulse**.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.

### On the Ether.

We use the word **Ether** to describe the intermediate entity of the world. The **Void** <note>original: *vacuum*</note>, which the Ancient philosophers also proposed, is the same as the ether; it is space without a body, yet filled with a single and common existence. 

Ether is a permanent being without any specific quality: and because it is a being, or entity, or existence, it is improperly called "substance" or <term>hypostasis: the underlying reality or fundamental nature of a thing</term> <note>original: *ὑπόστασις*</note>. 

In the ether, bodies move without resistance. In the ether, there is neither light nor shadow.

### MISCELLANEOUS NOTES

->*Observations which ought to be sorted under their own respective headings elsewhere.*<-

If a lead vessel floats and carries a load at the same time, does it not become heavier than an equal amount of water? Are those objects submerged in water heavier than the water itself in that same proportion?

Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who was a leading critic of the Copernican system</note> does not understand Copernicus, as he is unable to perceive how the motion of the Earth's poles, within the colure of the solstices <term>colure: one of the two great circles that intersect at the celestial poles and pass through the equinoxes or solstices</term>, causes the declination of the Ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note> to differ from the equator. For when it is moved by another motion as if outside the colure, that motion is not truly outside the colure, since the motion of the equatorial circle also moves the colure itself.

Prepared bricks rubbed with a magnet also acquire a stronger polarity <note>original: *politatem*</note> and attract magnetic iron more firmly. However, wood, bones, other stones, and metals besides iron, do not acquire such forces at all when rubbed, nor do they attract anything as a result.

Fluid bodies or empty spaces do not possess polarity.

Put it to the test: whether a larger object drives a smaller one away from itself in the presence of the Sun in a wave.

Ice floats on water, even though it is heavier and denser than water <note>The author holds the common pre-modern misconception that ice is more dense than liquid water, attributing its buoyancy to trapped air rather than its molecular structure</note>; this is because of the greater quantity of air mixed into it than is found in water.

Observe whether a globe of lead floats in molten lead, just as gold floats in gold, or tin <term>original: *plumbum album* (white lead), a common term for tin in this period</term> in tin.

It then provides observations on the properties of spices and the geological formation of metals, using biological analogies to explain chemical separation.</meta>

<page-num>220</page-num>

<header>PHYSIOLOGY BOOK II.</header>

...generation consists <note>Continuing from the previous page's catchword</note>, much differing from the secondary and specific form of generated things.

That form is singular and peculiar; it is not "specific," nor what the Peripatetics <note>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, who famously walked about while teaching</note> call a "formal cause" or "second form." It is not the propagator of generated bodies, but the proper entity and existence of the first and principal spheres <note>or "globes"—referring to planets and stars</note> and their homogeneous, incorrupt parts. We call this the **primary form**—not to be confused with Aristotle's "first form"—but rather that which protects and arranges its own sphere.

Spices excite heat because of their specific natures and the sharpness of their substance, which is born from long-lasting heat. Therefore, they sting, erode, and irritate through their very substance: heat subsequently follows in our bodies, and the action rises within the humors <note>humors: the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) once believed to govern health</note>. However, if applied to dry objects like iron or stones, they do not excite heat.

Thus, many spices and some herbs seem to contain heat enclosed within themselves, held behind the barrier of their own specific matter.

Metals are generated in a confused state within veins, mixed with dross <note>original: *recrementis*—the waste or impurities found in ore</note> and various other substances. It often happens that several metals which are different in kind actually constitute a single body before they are separated.

From their origin, metals arise together in one and the same vein as a single solid body: gold, silver, copper, and dross. This is much like how butter, cheese, and whey are all contained in milk; or how honey, propolis <term>propolis: a resinous "bee glue" used by bees to seal their hives</term>, and wax are found in honeycombs. Once these substances have been separated, they exist endowed with their own distinct forms. No one can change cheese—even if it is lean—into butter, nor butter into whey; likewise, honey cannot be turned into wax.

# NEW METEOROLOGY AGAINST ARISTOTLE.

## BOOK THREE.

*First, it is clear that the philosophy concerning the air and the elements, which we described in our book on the principles of things, is being accepted and preserved in written monuments; this philosophy is commonly thought easier to grasp and understand, though it is most vain and useless. For besides the fact that trifles delight weak minds (just as monsters do in paintings), ignorance itself desires to philosophize; and the common error of all drags many along, even against their will.*

### CHAPTER ONE.

->*What Meteorology is.*<-

Meteorology is the explanation of all those things which are suspended, or moved, or appear in the heights, in the air; it is a principal and renowned part of natural philosophy. We can call it the doctrine of impressions <note>original: *impressionum doctrinam*—referring to the belief that atmospheric phenomena were "impressed" upon the air by external forces</note>, because they occur for the most part in a higher place and appear as if impressed by the heat and vigor or spirit of the terrestrial globe, or by the influence of celestial bodies. They can also, for the most part, be called omens <note>original: *ostenta*—portents or signs</note>, which keep the minds of men in suspense and doubt. But we, having followed and then challenged Aristotle <note>original: *Aristotelem secuti & persecuti*—the author suggests he has studied Aristotle's work only to "prosecute" or refute his errors</note>, have entered upon a wider field of discourse, since he treated not only the things above, but the lower things, and those spread beneath our feet: the seas, the mountains,

...rivers, springs, and the innermost depths of the earth, having scrutinized them under this single title. Therefore, we must investigate not only "Meteors"—which are commonly called "imperfectly mixed bodies" by the common run of philosophers because of their sudden generation and easy dissolution—but also other things, even more firm and coherent, more perfectly crafted by nature. Therefore, speaking from the elements of the Ancients, we must discuss the subject of these things—their soul and matter—and of the sea, rivers, mountains, and lands. We must speak of those fires which are kindlings <note>original Greek: *ὑπεκκαύματα* (hypekkaumata)—Aristotle’s term for the combustible material in the upper atmosphere</note>; of the vapors born from breath; and of those appearances which exist as specters <note>original Greek: *φάσματα* (phasmata)</note> and by reflection <note>original Greek: *κατ’ ἔμφασιν* (kat' emphasin)</note>. Although these things, when looked at, appear to exist by themselves without a physical substance <note>original Greek: *ὑποστάσει* (hypostasei)—a fundamental essence or foundation</note>, nevertheless they all occur within a subject.

## CHAPTER II.

->*On the matter of more sublime impressions.*<-

Regarding the matter of these "impressions" <note>Atmospheric phenomena like rain, wind, or lightning, believed to be "impressed" on the air</note>, our opinion is far different from the doctrine of the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, who "walked about" while teaching</note>. It is indeed true that the earth and water—that is, the terrestrial globe—supply the primary material, which climbs to the heights through exhalation <note>original Greek: *ἀναθυμίασιν* (anathumiasin)</note> or evaporation. This they divide into the moist, which they call vapor, and the dry, which they call exhalation. 

But it must be understood that throughout the terrestrial globe, two types of moisture are everywhere mingled: the watery and the fatty. From these, watery and fatty—or mixed—evaporations are excited by heat and celestial rays. They may be thick or thin, coherent or scattered, abundant and continuous, or few and meager; they are separated by many differences among themselves due to the action of various causes. Indeed, for the most part, something of the strong and common substance <note>original: *hypostasi*</note> of earthly things—namely, salt—is carried upward. From these refined materials, the various apparatus of our misty sky is formed. They are refined and perfected by heat, both innate and surrounding, or innate in the mid-

### CHAPTER III.

#### On Comets.

Things that appear to men less frequently present a greater difficulty for this reason: that learned and proper observation (the law and mistress of things and sciences) cannot possibly recognize all the points of agreement and difference within just one or two centuries. Therefore, it is no wonder if Aristotle here completely falters, just like those over whom he triumphs so magnificently. Anaxagoras and Democritus report that the "hairy" appearance <note>original Latin: *crinitam*; the word "comet" comes from the Greek *kometes*, meaning "long-haired"</note> is a phantom of those stars called "wanderers" <note>The planets</note> produced by their blending when, because they come close together, they seem to touch one another. The Pythagoreans, however, maintain that one of the wandering stars is hairy, but that it appears only after a long interval of time and moves only a little distance from the Sun. This is what happens with the star of Mercury; for because it moves only a little from the Sun, it is often hidden, such that it is seen only much later. Hippocrates of Chios and his pupil Aeschylus held the same opinion, except they believed the star does not have "hair" of its own. Instead, as it wanders, it sometimes acquires it from its location when our sight is reflected toward the Sun by the moisture which the star draws to itself. Aristotle easily overcame all of these men; because he could...

Wherefore, when the principle of burning falls into this very thickness—on account of the motion of the celestial orbs—and it is neither so great that it burns quickly and intensely, nor so weak and meager that it is quickly extinguished, but rather a more ample and suitable exhalation is stirred up from the lower parts and carried on high at the same time, then a <term>hairy star</term> <note>original: *stella crinita*; this is the literal translation of the Greek *kometes*, the root of the word "comet"</note> exists, according to the shape which the exhalation has acquired. Furthermore, just as such a motion of a star appears to be a movement, so also the rest of a star appears to be a standing-still. For what occurs is similar to someone throwing a torch or a small spark of fire into a heap of chaff; for the shooting of stars also seems similar to this thing, since on account of the matter which is suited for receiving fire, it quickly creeps and flows further along in a certain sequence. But if this [fire] should remain, and not be consumed and waste away by shooting across, then the end of the trajectory will provide a beginning for the motion from that part where the material for the burning was most thick; and such is a hairy star, just like a shooting star that has a beginning and an end. But let us grant those points; let them be the distinguished foundations upon which the logic and nature of comets rest. Are those places then more suitable for matter to accumulate for conceiving and sustaining fires and blazes? Not at all; no more than wood and straw in an oven, which, if not thick enough and endowed with suitable moisture, do not know how to catch or sustain fire. For the nature of the element of fire is not flame-bearing, nor does it have a burning or devouring force; otherwise, according to the opinion of the ancients, all the other elements would have rightly perished. But how can there be fires within the orbits of the stars (that is, the Moon)? Woe to you! who again and so often bring the dangers of <term>Phaëton</term> <note>In Greek myth, Phaëton lost control of the Sun's chariot, nearly burning the Earth; the author uses this to mock the idea of the heavens being full of combustible material</note> into the heavens. But in these days, Philosophy is better served; since among so many thousands of learned men—of whom antiquity knew very few—there are always some dedicated to the study of nature, investigating all the differences and circumstances in the rarer miracles of the world. Hence frequent witnesses are present, and many agree with us: that not only the Aristotelian elements, but even the heavens are greatly disturbed and burdened by comets. And I fear that, even after all the centuries have passed, comets may not maintain their seats in the "superior Aristotelian world" <note>The author is questioning whether the Aristotelian placement of comets in the upper atmosphere matches the observed data of their paths</note>, nor their rapid positions, paths, advances, and declinations, and all the varieties of their motions.

But he says further concerning these <term>blazes</term> <note>original: *ardoribus*; referring to the fiery appearance of comets</note>, that they burn according to their matter and form, being either <term>hairy</term> <note>original: *crinitæ*; comets with a circular glow</note>, <term>bearded</term> <note>original: *barbatæ*; comets with a tail preceding them</note>, or <term>tailed</term> <note>original: *caudatæ*; comets with a trailing tail</note>. Those exhalations <note>In Aristotelian science, "exhalations" were dry, smoky vapors rising from the Earth, thought to be the fuel for weather and celestial phenomena</note> which are hotter and thinner rise higher and seem (if indeed there are any) to provide the material for comets. However, those that are hot and thin but do not rise beyond the spaces of the so-called "middle region" of the air <note>The *media regio* was believed to be the cold, middle layer of the atmosphere</note> produce the noise of thunder and flashes of lightning; once they catch fire, they are inflamed there, and are triggered and extinguished with sudden and headlong force. Indeed, we have observed with more diligent care that lightning bolts which flash from a higher place and terrify the sight of the eyes, striking more severely, vanish very quickly. However, in the lower clouds and more depressed storms, they carry a more reddish fire and linger longer. Therefore, the entire fuel of a comet would perish all at once without any delay, just as thicker materials resist fire longer than very thin ones. 

But how can a comet remain for a long time—for a three-month span or even an entire year—in the "Aristotelian air," in something so fleeting and changeable, which is overturned every single day? How can it last when the air is subject to so many changes? For it is not possible that fire, which is the most unbridled and rebellious of all bodies, should remain calm of its own accord; and that in a body [the air] that is highly wandering and fluid, the fire remains constant in a fluid fuel, while torches burn and pass away, lightning bolts explode like cannons <note>original: *Bombardarum*; an early type of heavy artillery</note>, and "falling stars" fly past and cut through the air.
