### OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

...they decline toward the South or the North, they easily escape the shadow) and then shine most brightly; therefore, its light is not borrowed from the Sun <note>original: "non est ejus lumen à Sole mutuatum"</note>: a point which Erastus can never prove by any historical records. But we, on the contrary, argue that if a comet <term>crinita</term> <note>Literally "long-haired star," the standard Latin term for a comet</note> were of a fiery and flaming nature, it would shine very little on its own when illuminated by a solar ray. This is just as it appears to us with larger flames placed in the Sun, such as when fires rage through fields or through cities.

Nor does that subtle argument of Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated scholar who wrote "Subtleties" as a critique of the scientist Girolamo Cardano</note> in his response to Cardano’s *Subtleties* stand in the way: he claims that fiery light is not hindered by the light-bearing power of the Sun, but rather that the eye itself and the surrounding medium are flooded with a more brilliant light; for this reason, the eye is moved very little by the lesser light. Indeed, those things which by their nature can reflect the light of another—whether they contain their own light, like the stars, or like gemstones—grow bright in the presence of other lights. If they are seen less clearly, it is because of the greater force of light around the sense organ <note>The eye</note>. Yet flames do not reflect the light of another, and they shine far less than those objects when under the foreign light of the Sun: for this reason, when illuminated by the rays of the Sun, they can scarcely be seen.

But a comet <term>crinita stella</term>, and most especially that immense "tailed one" <note>original: "caudata"</note> of the year 1578, which appeared immediately at the very setting of the Sun while the Sun's light was still grazing the tops of the lower clouds (which were at a distance of two miles from the earth), appeared nonetheless radiant, illustrated by a most powerful light even in the twilight itself. Furthermore, why is the light of a comet always cast out and extended from the side, when all standing flames rise upright in a pyramid shape, held together by their fuel? 

Moreover, neither the very swift daily revolution of the heavens nor the sufficiently rapid movement of the comet itself disturbs its flame; it proceeds so sedately, so calmly, as if it were composed of the firmest matter and the most robust joints. Whenever the sky "burns," a chasm <note>original: "chasma," a term used for atmospheric openings or auroras</note> is clearly seen, and raging flames are observed. ->Against REGIOMONTANUS<-

Among the other records which are for the most part published by writers out of ignorance or laziness, that History by the most learned man, Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a foundational figure in Renaissance astronomy and mathematics</note>, is most pleasing. This is because, by that single example, one may be easily persuaded that comets always turn their rays away from the Sun. The account is as follows:

"On the Ides of January <note>January 13th</note>," (he says), "in 1472, a comet was seen by us under <term>Libra</term> <note>The constellation of the Scales</note>. Its head was moving slowly until it was near <term>Spica</term> <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note>. It then marched through the legs of <term>Boötes</term> toward his left side. Departing from there, in a single natural day <note>A 24-hour period</note>, it described an arc of forty degrees of a great circle. When it was in the middle of <term>Cancer</term>, it was at its furthest distance from the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>The ecliptic, or the Sun's apparent path across the sky</note> by 67 degrees; and then, passing through the two poles—those of the Zodiac and the <term>Equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator</note>—it went as far as the middle of the feet of <term>Cepheus</term>. From there, it passed through the breast of <term>Cassiopeia</term>, over the belly of <term>Andromeda</term>, and then traveling along the length of the <term>Northern Fish</term> <note>One of the two fish in the constellation Pisces</note>, where its motion slowed significantly, it approached the Zodiac, crossing it near the middle of <term>Aries</term>, until, along with the stars of <term>Cetus</term> <note>The constellation of the Whale or Sea Monster</note>, its <term>heliacal setting</term> <note>When a celestial body disappears from view by entering the glare of the Sun</note> hid it from us in the final days of February."

By this proper motion of its own, the comet described a portion of a great circle, in which it was carried northward and, moreover, against the succession of the signs <note>This refers to retrograde motion, moving "backward" through the zodiac from Libra toward Aries</note>. At the beginning and the end of its appearance it moved slowly, but in the middle it moved most swiftly—nearly through four signs in one day, from the end of Virgo even into the sign of Gemini. According to the nature that must be ascribed to it, it ought to have continued its motion until it appeared again having returned to Libra. Perhaps it did move in such a way, since at its setting it was still of great size; however, because of its position relative to the Sun, and especially in northern regions, it was with difficulty at the end [seen]...

# PHYSIOLOGY <note>A term then referring to the study of nature and natural phenomena, rather than just biology.</note>

...of its appearance <note>Original: "apparitionis". Its tail, however, was less mobile; by continuously facing the stars of **Gemini**, it moved around them, never deviating from them during the entire time of its appearance. And so, at its first emergence, it stretched its tail toward the west, because the stars of **Gemini** were visible there. At the end, however, the comet—located under **Aries**—appeared only in the West due to its proximity to the Sun, with its tail stretched toward the East; this was because the stars of **Gemini** were positioned in that direction. In the middle of its appearance, it turned its tail toward the south. The stars of **Gemini** were there then, and it happened on that same night that, immediately after sunset, the tail faced the East. As midnight approached, it faced South, and after midnight, West.

By its own proper motion <term>Proper motion</term> <note>The inherent movement of a celestial body across the sky, as opposed to the apparent daily rotation caused by Earth's spin</note>, the tip of the tail—though moving more slowly than the head of the comet—was always carried toward the West, against the succession of the signs <note>This indicates 'retrograde' motion, moving backwards through the zodiac constellations</note>. From this it is clear that both the head and the tail of the comet moved toward the West and never toward the East, not only by its daily motion but also by its own proper motion.

On the Ides of January <note>January 13th</note>, while the Sun was in **Capricorn**, the tail was turned away toward **Cancer** and the stars of **Gemini**. While the comet was in **Libra**, the tail extended toward the West, away from the Sun in **Capricorn**. Similarly, when the comet was located under **Aries**, the tail was again stretched toward the East, away from the Sun. In the middle of its appearance, the tail was also turned toward the South, away from the Sun. A comet was seen when Aristaeus was archon at Athens <note>Aristaeus was the chief magistrate of Athens in 427–426 BCE.</note>, which Aristotle thereafter called a "great star" <note>Original Latin: "magnam stellam"</note> and a "great comet." But why do I strive so much with these examples to prove that the tail is always turned in the opposite direction from the Sun, when several more recent authors—namely Apian <note>Peter Apian (1495–1552), a pioneer in observing that comet tails point away from the sun.</note> and Gemma <note>Gemma Frisius (1508–1555), a Dutch physician and mathematician.</note>, who were permitted to see both the various writings of the ancients and the phenomena themselves with their own eyes—openly defend this opinion? For this does not happen because the part closer to the Sun solidifies more firmly, while it is certain that all things thin out <term>rarefaction</term> by the force of heat and are instead condensed by cold. Nor are the "hairs" <note>The word "comet" comes from the Greek word for hair; the author is referring to the tail/coma.</note> scattered everywhere from all sides—up, down, before, and behind—as someone less learned might insist. Rather, they are not seen toward the Sun because of the Sun's greater light, and they do not appear toward the sides because they are outside the lines which extend from the sides of the Sun to the sides of the "hairy star," following the width of the diameter, all the way into a continuous cone.

Furthermore, even that great tailed comet of the year 1578 <note>Likely referring to the Great Comet of 1577, which remained visible into early 1578.</note> did not carry its light in a sharp cone in proportion to its body, but rather somewhat reflected and wider at the ends; and how could the tiny body of a comet stretch a glowing tail to the length of two signs <note>A "sign" in the zodiac is 30 degrees; the tail therefore stretched 60 degrees across the sky.</note>, similar to the way shadows are cast? This is something we understand to have been observed quite often.

# PHYSIOLOGY

...if the fires were to burst forth in the front; nor is it [the comet] ever sent down to the depths, nor does it approach the ground. Since fire, where nature leads its own, is carried either upwards or toward the matter to which it clings and on which it feeds, and because no fires follow a curved path; then, if they are moved more quickly, the bodies of the flames are dragged along. It is clear that this is not a fire burning within a fuel source <note>original Latin: "in fomite," referring to the "tinder" or material that sustains a flame.</note>. Let us therefore set aside for a moment the Aristotelian <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) argued that comets were "exhalations" of dry gas from the Earth that caught fire in the upper atmosphere.</note> comets burning with fires—and believe me, they burn out with more than just "cometary" fires—and let us see what others have thought, such as Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE – 65 CE), who argued in *Naturales Quaestiones* that comets were permanent celestial bodies like planets.</note> and Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Myndus, an ancient astronomer who believed comets were distinct celestial bodies that only became visible at certain points in their orbits.</note>, who suspect something celestial is at work.

**Gemma** <note>Cornelius Gemma (1535–1583), a physician and astronomer known for his study of the supernova of 1572 and the comet of 1577.</note> thinks a comet is a portion of the ethereal sphere <term>ethereal sphere</term> <note>The "aether" was considered the fifth element, the pure and unchanging substance of the heavens above the Moon.</note> gathered together and condensed into a globular torch, illuminated more brightly by the Sun’s rays. For this reason, the closer it exists to the Sun, the more firmly it is compressed and glows with the appearance of a star; the further it is removed, the more it dissolves and its strength is weakened into rays. Finally, is it so absurd if we allow that, according to the nature or dignity of each heavenly sphere, a certain type of generation <note>The "generation" or "birth" of new objects in the supposedly unchanging heavens was a major point of debate in the 16th century.</note> can occur in each from time to time?

**Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a prominent scholar who frequently engaged in scientific polemics.</note> suggests that a comet is a vapor drawn by force from one of the stars into the highest region of the air. The nature of this vapor is not that of something burning, but of a mixed matter—much like smoke or soot—that receives the Sun’s rays and thus becomes visible; it transmits those rays, and therefore appears to have a tail. However, Scaliger proposes this paradox of his regarding the nature of the heavens with some hesitation; which is why he also adds: *What if stars lie hidden somewhere, which, coming forth in their own time (unknown to us), finally come into our sight, and are then taken away from our eyes once more?*

**Cardanus** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous polymath who theorized that comets were actually transparent globes that acted like lenses.</note> considers a Comet to be a globe situated in the heavens, which appears illuminated by the Sun; while the rays pass through it, they form the shape of a beard or a tail. Indeed, the tail is always turned away from the Sun. He believes the heaven is full of many stars, though not very dense ones; but...

# NATURAL PHILOSOPHY

### C H A P T E R V.

->*Against the deep-seated superstition concerning the planetary spheres—which the common crowd of philosophers calls "heaven"—as if they were a "fifth nature" and an immutable essence, serving as a dwelling place for the gods.*<-

Those who, with a certain religious mind, piously worship that Maker of the world and adore the inhabitant of heaven with palms raised to the stars; whose majesty is on high, but whose power and command endure forever everywhere, even in these misty dwellings of ours; they judge honorably regarding all the highest bodies, as if they were remote from every disaster and the supreme Governor were their near neighbor. They hold this view even though the Sacred Scriptures attest that these bodies were established to serve earthly needs, for signs, for seasons, and for every necessity. 

Concerning these matters, however, many opinions were held and debated among the Ancient philosophers, especially in those times when many were not bound, as they are now, to follow a master's every word <note>original: *in verba magistri*; a reference to the Roman poet Horace, describing someone who blindly follows authority without thinking for themselves</note>, but were philosophizing freely with reason as their guide. When **Pythagoras** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (6th century BC) who believed in the mathematical harmony of the universe and that the Moon was an inhabited world like Earth.</note> had weighed the mass of the Moon and the planets, he noted the sympathy of the Moon with earthly things and especially with the sea, the varied appearance of its spots, and the ray of the Sun, never idle, reflected upon its body. He observed that this happened by a certain fitting alternation, just as it does on this globe where we live; there likewise, every month, with the arriving rays of light, there is dawn, noon, sunset, and night. From this he concluded that there is a deprivation of light, and that the influences of the other stars are not hindered there. He did not think nature was idle there, nor that the spirit was entirely exhausted, but rather that *all things are full of Jove* <note>original: *Iovis omnia plena*; a quote from Virgil’s *Eclogues*, suggesting that the divine spirit or life-force permeates every part of the universe, even the planets.</note>.

But, though persuaded by no rational arguments, yet familiar to the opinion of the common people and most troublesome men, is that so often repeated **fifth essence** <note>term: quintessence; in Aristotelian physics, a fifth element (after earth, water, air, and fire) that was thought to be celestial, eternal, and unchanging</note>—a nature not subject to decay, but in all par-

If, he says, there were birth and destruction, growth or change, it would proceed from contrary matter; yet there is no contrary matter, because there is no contrary motion. No motion is contrary to circular motion; only the motions of the elements <note>The four terrestrial elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> along a straight line are contrary. But why, I ask, should the birth and passing away of things depend on local motion? <note>Local motion refers to movement from one place to another.</note> We have already sufficiently refuted the idea that elements and simple bodies in nature are distinguished by simple and contrary motions. Yet, if you consider the force and efficacy of motions, there is no less hostility in circular paths—which are driven in contrary courses from contrary positions in the heavens—indeed, much greater hostility than in straight lines. This is especially true since celestial bodies are carried by the most rapid and swift motions. But Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous Italian scholar and physician who was a staunch defender of Aristotle.</note> urges with Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A term for followers of Aristotle, referring to his habit of walking while teaching.</term> subtlety that the contrariety comes from places which are most distant, from the center to the concave surface. For why does that learned man press that more than nauseating "contrariety of places," when no place is contrary to another? There is a dissimilarity in the positions of bodies in the nature of things, not a logical contrariety of locations. These notions are drawn from that "workshop of the Greeks," in which they wish for the things themselves—and all philosophy—to be demonstrated and contained by the logical rules of certain words and idioms; whereas the entire power of words and all idioms are hardly sufficient even to illustrate the works of nature. ## CHAPTER VI.

->*Bodies are created and changed above the orbit of the Moon.*<-

**S**irius <note>original: "Canis major," the Dog Star</note> seems to be changed very much from the nature of Mars <note>original: ♂</note> and Jupiter <note>original: ♃</note>; the other fixed stars are also judged by their appearance and colors, as well as by their effects; and it [Sirius] has now clearly shifted into the appearance and influence of Venus. ## CHAPTER VII.

->*Comets sometimes exist below the Moon.*<-

**J**ohannes Voghelin [Voghelinus], the most celebrated mathematician, discovered a comet in the year 1532, the parallax <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different perspectives; used here to calculate distance.</note> of which was a full sign, two degrees, and 27 minutes. If that had ever been the case, the planet would be ruled by the comet; or rather, the comet would follow the planet like a handmaid. How harsh is that opinion: that exhalations are compressed by the motion of celestial bodies to the perpendicular of some specific star? By the motion of the heavens, they would instead be scattered to uncertain places through the vast and thinnest spaces of the air. It is even more thoughtless to suggest that "hair" is seen near stars just as a corona is seen near the Sun—except that a corona is merely a reflection, and coronas and halos <note>original: "halones"</note> are like rainbows <note>original: "Irides"</note>, resulting from the conditions of the surrounding air.

...[Swabia]ne, not of some body growing together into a specific form. Furthermore, the fixed stars have no motion beyond the common movement of the daily revolution, which they share with comets. Therefore, the constellations would have to be disturbed by a miraculous force, and the very fabric of the firmament and the fixed stars would have to be shaken; yet it has never been recorded in memory that any of the fixed stars held a comet clinging to itself.

It remains for us now to set forth the causes, locations, and natures of comets with greater certainty. And first, we must utterly cast off the old and deep-seated superstition of the Aristotelian heavens and elements. We must no longer believe in those boundaries so often chanted about—those extending to the hollow of the Moon <note>In the traditional Aristotelian view, the universe was divided at the Moon: below it was the "sublunary" sphere of change and decay, and above it were the unchanging, eternal heavens.</note> in this dark sky of ours—as we have already sufficiently proven through various arguments when we disputed the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic|Followers of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about the Lyceum in Athens.</term> elements. We will judge what a comet is far better and more surely once all the evidence has been gathered from their distances, locations, rays, lights, and sizes, as well as their timing, motions, increases, decreases, and even their effects.

One comet may be in the middle of the air, or within the sublunary space; another is very close to the hollow of the Moon; another is above the Moon in the sphere of Mercury; another is in the sphere of Venus; and some even surpass the higher planets.

They appear in the Southern region as they do in the Northern and the Zodiac; they incline toward the poles themselves and move through the stars of every constellation. No region of the sky rejects them.

They have longer rays, which are always turned away from the Sun. These rays may be straight or curved, shaped like pyramids, or equally wide throughout; they may be wider at the tip, or dispersed, and some comets are even found without rays.

Some are luminous, while others are quite dark. The variety of colors is for the most part determined by the condition of the region and the state of the lower atmosphere.

The small ones measure two or three degrees <note>Degrees are units used to measure distances across the sky.</note>; others are massive and terrifying, spanning two signs <note>A "sign" refers to a 30-degree segment of the Zodiac; thus, a comet of "two signs" would stretch across 60 degrees of the sky.</note>, though most are of a middling size.

### BOOK III ###

Some [comets] last for a few days, others fulfill a span of weeks; some are visible for two or three months, while others appear for an entire year.

They possess a wandering and uncertain motion, moving both according to the order of the signs of the Zodiac and against it. At times they travel with a swifter course, at other times slower; occasionally they wander and stray without any motion at all beyond the daily revolution of the sky. Yet they do not move like the <term>errant stars|The planets, which follow predictable paths along the ecliptic.</term> within the Zodiac, but throughout the entire sky, and with an irregular pace—much like that greatest comet described by <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), known as Regiomontanus, was a celebrated mathematician and astronomer whose observations of the comet of 1472 helped pave the way for modern cometary study.</note> Regiomontanus. Furthermore, they ascend from the center of the earth and then fall back down toward it again.

When comets are observed within the spaces designated for the celestial spheres, they do not move with the motion of those spheres, nor are they urged on by any planet. For this reason, those <term>real orbs|The traditional Aristotelian belief that planets were carried on physical, crystalline solid spheres.</term> do not exist; if they did, the comets would be moved by them.

Tycho Brahe <note>A Danish nobleman and astronomer (1546–1601) known for his incredibly accurate astronomical observations.</note> maintains that a comet sometimes extends its tail toward Venus rather than away from the Sun. This may indeed happen occasionally, and yet the cause can still lie in the solar rays when the material of the comet diverts the light slightly—just as we often see in the evening rays of the sun passing through clouds. However, it must be investigated whether a comet ever faced Venus in other positions. It is believable that this was a chance occurrence, happening once due to a deviation of the rays.

Comets, being wandering and newly formed bodies, do not possess <note>original: "politatem." The author suggests comets lack a fixed axis or magnetic polarity, which is why their movement appears erratic compared to the "polarized" planets.</note> polarity; for this reason, they wander and stray.

They shine with a wider <term>coma|The "hair" or atmospheric envelope surrounding the nucleus of a comet.</term> for the most part shortly after their beginning, and they also gradually fade away near their end and disappearance; sometimes shrinking from a very great mass to a tiny one, though occasionally—though more rarely—their disappearance is more sudden.

Droughts are often known to follow them.

It has always been established for me by numerous arguments—both through proofs and through certain natural instruments—that (whether it remains immobile as the center of some circumference or not) [a celestial body] acts in concert through a wonderful bond of motions and positions, as well as by a <term>sympathy of natures|A Renaissance concept where celestial bodies affect one another through shared qualities or "affinities" rather than just physical contact.</term>, beyond that which emanates from the ray of light. Each is moved by the other, and they harmonize together both in their distances and their motions. There are internal <term>hypostases|The underlying substances or essential natures of things.</term> of the world; from some of these—sometimes many, sometimes few—the resolved proportions of substances flow out through the vast spaces of the <term>ether|The material that was thought to fill the region of the universe above the terrestrial sphere.</term> due to their configuration, position, and motion. These substances flow together and are massed together in various ways, like clouds, which the Sun's rays immediately illuminate and strike, presenting a variety of forms from the variety of the matter.

And although the more constant and bright planets, such as the Earth or the Moon, do not accumulate so large a mass of matter, they nevertheless release <note>original: "fluores"</note> fluids from their bodies, flowing out like <term>spirits|In early modern science, 'spirits' were subtle, invisible fluids believed to carry life, heat, or celestial influence.</term>. Thus, comets are formed as if in a general refuge within the ether. When they are joined together in <term>syzygies|The alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the Sun, Earth, and Moon, in a straight line.</term>, they are again dissolved and flow apart by contrary motions. And if any parts of them fall down to the Earth, either a great force of winds or massive droughts usually follow.

That the planets pour out and release their substances is manifest to our senses in the case of the Moon, mediated by its "spirits," which are the substances themselves. These spirits become incorporated among us, and that is the "impregnation" of all growing things by the Moon. This does not happen by bare light or some <term>imaginary ray|The author is arguing that the Moon's influence is physical and material, not just a visual or "phantastic" effect of light.</term>; it even pushes the seas toward the "corner" of the Earth, both when it is above our <term>horizon|original: "Finitorem"</term> and from the highest point of heaven. Indeed, when it has descended to the limit of its <term>perigee|The point in the Moon's orbit where it is closest to the Earth.</term>, it has wonderful effects, quite different from those at its <term>apogee|The point in the Moon's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth.</term>, as is clear to those who contemplate nature more diligently.

BOOK III.

If an imperfect substance were moved at the swiftest speed, it would immediately be scattered. For even whole clouds sometimes persist for quite a while in our own gloomy sky (within the sphere of the air), moving quickly by the force of the winds. But in the <term>ether|The subtle, pure substance believed by early scientists to fill the heavens above the Earth's atmosphere.</term>, there is nothing—or very little—that offers resistance. In that realm, bodies set in motion are not carried along by a vacuum, nor are they stopped or pulled apart. 

Here on Earth, projectiles fly much more slowly when the south winds blow and the air grows thick; they fly much more freely when the north wind clears the sky. But there, the ether is naturally clearer than any northern breeze, unmixed with any impurity. Therefore, these bodies flow and fly, becoming more stable with every increase in speed. We have often observed illuminations of the cloud-bearing region by the Sun, an hour or two after sunset, which mimic comets with their rays. For example, on September 9, 1580, because of the state of the clouds between seven and eight o'clock, various colors were seen. And while I was writing this and dealing with the matter of comets, a <note>original: "pseudocometes"</note> "false comet" appeared in one place—acting like a mimic—with its tail, as is expected, turned away from the Sun.

...they constantly affirm. Anaxagoras believed that the Milky Way is the natural and peculiar light of those stars which do not receive their light from the Sun <note>Anaxagoras suggested that the Milky Way was the shadow of the Earth falling on distant stars, allowing their own dim light to be seen.</note>. The fiery Aristotle, after he had "kindled" the comets in the upper air, also considered the Milky Way to be a smoky circle, glowing in the dense air; he thought that just as a halo forms around a single star, this Milky Way does the same around the orbits of many stars. For this reason, he claimed it is the radiance of a great circle and a vast space, which appears because of perpetual exhalations <note>original: "exhalationes," referring to vapors or dry fumes thought to rise from the Earth and ignite in the upper atmosphere.</note> running together. 

But this opinion is marked as quite absurd by all learned men, and even by some of Aristotle's own commentators. For the appearance of the "Milk" does not always appear the same, nor is it always positioned in the same place—no, it appears as a whole, intact, and enduring in all its parts, as much in its length and width as in its brightness and dark parts, its densest and thinnest sections, and even in certain breaks, bends, and intervals, as well as in its division and doubling. Furthermore, since the air itself is subject to many changes and is fertile with various "impressions" <note>In this context, "impressions" refers to atmospheric phenomena like rainbows or meteors.</note>, and since that upper air is moved by the rush of the daily revolution, such inconstant material cannot remain permanent. 

Therefore, in no way will the same form remain in such fluid material, in an uncertain and wandering exhalation, so that it would continue along with the stars without change; this is something that has never happened to any <term>sublunary|Refers to the region "below the moon," which in ancient science was the realm of change, decay, and weather, unlike the "unchanging" heavens.</term> formation. For just as comets are wandering and undergo perpetual changes, and all things that appear in the air vanish soon after being fused and dispersed, the fact that no variation in perspective or <term>parallax|The apparent shift in the position of an object when viewed from different locations. A lack of parallax indicates the object is very far away.</term> can be recognized is the greatest proof of its more sublime and eminent nature. Nor is the visible circle cut off in Gemini and Sagittarius where it intersects the <term>Zodiac|The band of the sky through which the Sun, Moon, and planets move.</term>; although by Aristotle’s reasoning, the Sun moving in the <term>Ecliptic|The Sun's apparent yearly path through the stars.</term> would dissolve all the power of that material throughout the spaces of the Zodiac. But neither in those...

<summary>This page refutes Aristotle's theory that the Milky Way is a temporary atmospheric phenomenon caused by burning vapors, arguing instead that its permanence and lack of parallax prove it is a distant, celestial feature.</summary>

parts. Nor does the Sun, by its approach or withdrawal, bring about even a slight change in the Milky Way, not even in its smallest parts. That opinion is not true—that the "Milky" circle is created by some great force of light from the star-bearing sphere; for if that were so, it would pass through the more luminous parts of the sky and the most crowded and largest stars. But the part of the sky studded with the greatest lights, passing through Orion and Taurus, does not have the "Milk"; instead, it is seen in the sky from the Greater Dog <note>Canis Major</note> toward the east, where no star appears. Indeed, in the Milky circle from the stars in the stern of the Ship <note>The constellation Argo Navis, which modern astronomers have since divided into Puppis, Carina, and Vela.</note> all the way to the feet of the Twins <note>Gemini</note>, across a space of nearly thirty degrees, only a single star has been observed between Cassiopeia and the tail of the Swan <note>Cygnus</note>, where the circle is at its widest. The bright star in the breast of the Swan <note>Sadr</note> is seen in a certain separation of the Milk, where it even split into two parts; it is dense from the top of the Archer <note>Sagittarius</note> to the tail of the Eagle <note>Aquila</note> without stars. A branch descending from the mouth of the Swan proceeds without lights to the stars near the shoulder of the Serpent-Bearer <note>Ophiuchus</note>, where it ends, and terminates right at those lights; whereas, if the theory were true, it would rather proceed *through* those lights. Therefore, it is not caused by the light of the fixed stars <note>original: "stellarum inerrantium," literally "unwandering stars," used to distinguish them from planets.</note>; nor does it seem to be any relation of the Sun or the planets, since the stars that move perpetually would also cause a change in that relation. 

Someone might perhaps wonder whether it is a substance poured out into the upper ether <note>The "aether" was believed to be a fifth element, distinct from the four earthly elements, making up the heavens.</note> of the heavens, firmly placed and established beyond the harms of other natures. Nor, however, is it evident that the Milk is scattered within the orbits of the wanderers <note>original: "orbes erronum," referring to the planets, whose name comes from the Greek word for "wanderers."</note>; for if it were of a slightly denser essence, it would either obscure their lights or at least, as they pass through the Milk, change their light and vary their splendor. But neither do we see any great difference in the heavens or the light among the fixed stars in the Milky circle; they shine, glow, redden, and sparkle with clear lights just like the other fixed stars. For which reason, it must exist even above the fixed stars (especially some of them)...

# PHYSIOLOGY

...is consistent. For it is only through the vacuum of the ether <term>aether: the substance once believed to fill the upper regions of space beyond the Earth's atmosphere</term> over the longest distances that lights reach our senses in an uncorrupted state. Therefore, it must be observed above the fixed stars, or at least above most of them. If it belongs to the framework of the starry heaven, and if all those stars were fixed in a specific sphere whose motion from west to east were slow—by which the stars precede the equinoxes <note>A reference to the precession of the equinoxes, the slow shift in the orientation of Earth's axis over thousands of years</note>—it would certainly be necessary for it to be attached to that sphere, specifically in its upper part. 

But if that motion and apparent change of the fixed stars arises from other causes, and the fixed stars are not moved by a single mobile system, and the stars themselves, while fixed, are separated from one another by vast and incomprehensible distances in the world, then the "Milk" will be a substance existing in the most remote ether. This substance is such that it can catch and reflect the light of the Sun and the stars; likewise, it appears to be poured around certain stars like clouds. For this reason, they are called "nebulae" <note>original: *nebuloſæ*</note> by astronomers, not only because they possess a dim light, but also because a certain mist seems to surround those stars, such as in the Manger <note>The Praesepe star cluster in the constellation Cancer</note> and in the hand of Orion. For in this way the material ether, when it is situated somewhat lower and spread around the stars, creates nebulae, just as when a mist covers the full Moon or the Planets <note>original: *Errones*, literally "wanderers," the ancient term for planets</note>. And for that reason there are fewer stars in the milky circle, because some stars, which are above the material and resistant nature of the Milk, cannot be seen by our eyes at all; whereas those that are below—and they are few—pour forth their own lights, which are clear, primary, and sparkling, through the vacuum of the world.

Democritus <note>Greek philosopher (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) who famously hypothesized that the Milky Way consists of distant stars</note> thinks the milky circle is the collective glow of stars, caused by the crowding together of many small stars that are near each other and illuminate one another. It could also be a physical effect within us and our eyes, when tiny lights produce only a diffuse glow in the organ <note>the eye</note>, rather than a distinct point like the stars.

<header>BOOK III.</header>

# CHAPTER IX.

## Concerning clouds.

How great the height of clouds is from the earth is thought by some to be impossible to easily understand, due to the fluid and inconsistent nature of their matter. Because such a demonstration is very useful to this natural philosophy, we shall teach how to investigate this very thing more reliably. Let there be a clear day, in which only thicker masses of clouds are moving—those which cast a shadow—and let the observer stand atop a tower so that he can look out over the fields at a distance and see the shadows of the clouds on the ground. If the Sun is visible to you and distant by six or eight degrees from the nearest side of a cloud, it is obscured on the fields at a distance of one or two miles from that cloud. It is clear that things higher up have less variation in appearance <note>This refers to the concept of parallax: higher objects move less relative to the background than closer ones</note>, while those closer have more.

The height of clouds is revealed from the parallax <term>parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different positions</term> of a solitary cloud. When someone is able to look down upon the level of a region, it shows that there is a great variation in our view toward the Sun and the shadow of the cloud above the level of the earth, such as a distance of four stadia <term>stadium: an ancient unit of length, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters</term> or one mile.

Height also appears from the sound of thunder and from the sound of a cannon <term>bombarda: an early type of firearm or cannon</term>. For example, if a piece of artillery were fired at a distance of two miles, we see the fire at the mouth of the machine at the moment of the strike, yet the sound reaches our ears after the sixth or seventh beat of a healthy person's pulse <note>Before the invention of reliable stopwatches, scientists often used the steady rhythm of a human heartbeat to measure short intervals of time</note>. In the same way, the sound of thunder arrives after the visible flash of lightning—sometimes more quickly, rarely more slowly. Therefore, the clouds are not sent far away from our senses, but hang nearby, within one or two miles.

## CHAPTER X.

->Why clouds hang in the air.<-

Many philosophers greatly wonder at the way clouds roll through the air without sinking down toward the mass of the earth. It is easy for anyone to see that clouds are heavier and thicker than the air itself; therefore, it will not be out of place or superfluous to philosophize a bit on these matters. Water and the moisture of the earth are dissolved by heat into vapors which, by the force of their expansion and the nature of their thinner substance—with the air itself lifting them—rise on high. They continue to rise until either that initial force ceases, or the air at that height becomes too thin to carry them further, or the heat (having now almost died out) allows them to turn into a cloud. 

Indeed, although clouds are opaque <note>meaning they block light</note>, they are not necessarily that heavy. Many opaque things are much lighter than transparent things that allow light to pass through: for instance, feathers and thistle-down weigh much less than glass or specular stone <note>original: *specularis lapis*, a translucent mineral like mica or selenite used for windows before glass became common</note>. Similarly, in water, wood weighs less than the water itself; it is lifted to the surface by the water and floats, yet it is not more transparent than the water, but entirely opaque. 

Likewise, the smoke stirred up from burning wood hangs and floats in the air within a stone's throw once it has risen a little higher; it does not immediately fall downward, and yet, like a cloud, it can block the sun’s brightness from us. When many bronze cannons <note>original: *tormenta ænea*</note> are fired at once, especially when aimed upward, a mist arises which wanders through the calm air with the wind. In mountainous regions, we can very often see clouds running across below the peak of the mountain by the force of the winds, rather than being carried downward. For the height of clouds is varied and very different: some are scarcely two stadia <term>stadium: an ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters</term> distant from the surface of the earth, while others are a mile, or two, three, or four miles away.

<header>B O O K  III.</header>

Heavier clouds are sustained by lighter ones with air mixed in at high altitude; this is no different than how a lead vessel floats on water when it is filled with air. And just as cork does not sink to the bottom of the water because of the air trapped within its porous passages <note>original: *rarioribus viis*, literally "rarer ways" or passages</note>, so too clouds are not carried downward because of the thinner air mixed into them, and because the air in the place where they were created is thinner <note>or less dense</note> than the air found near the earth.

# METEOROLOGY
## BOOK FOUR.
### CHAPTER ONE.

->*Wind is not created from a hot and dry exhalation.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring foliate motifs and scrolled leaves.</image-desc>
The powerful nature of winds is often stirred up by the fury of lightning; but it also purifies the air with a calm motion, without force or rage. It is clear that this material originates from the earth, and not so much from the surface and circumference of the lands, as from its deeper bowels. We see this since even the deepest seas swell and are greatly agitated before heavy storms by <term>vapors</term> <note>original: *halitibus*, refers to breath-like steam or gas rising from the earth</note> rising from the lowest depths; just as when regions are shaken by an earthquake, the seas also tremble with wild blows. Yet in hotter regions and seasons, the air is more still, just as it is in the coldest ones: it is in temperate regions that <term>stormy battles</term> <note>original: *nimbosa prælia*, a poetic way of describing colliding storm fronts</note> grow strong. Therefore, as winds perish from heat and dryness, they are not entirely of that same nature <note>The author is refuting the traditional Aristotelian view that wind is merely a "dry exhalation."</note>. Spring, middle climates, dawn, and sunset foster winds; humid air and rain extinguish them—although quite often a very rapid wind mixed with rain levels everything in its path. What then? Is it a thick vapor? Such a thing is more prone to becoming a cloud; and it produces waters, or mists, and fogs; and by winds alone the air is not thickened, but sometimes becomes clear.

Therefore, the origin or movement of winds is merely a fluctuation of the air, just like the rush of rivers, driven by its own force and the succession of its generation, as well as by the courses and rays of the stars: or it is a force brought about by <term>dissolution</term> <note>original: *resolutione*</note>, when moist and solid things are dissolved by new heat, and once dissolved...

...they seek more spacious locations. Nor does this happen because the material is hot, or dry, or moist and hot, but it is purely an act of <term>resolution</term> <note>original: *resolutionis*; in early science, this refers to the process of a substance breaking down or changing state, such as a solid turning into a gas</note>, and specifically of something that has been condensed. Truly, what is condensed is contained by moisture, just as <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: *halinitrum*; also known as nitre, a key ingredient in gunpowder known for its volatile nature</note> in a fire, or gunpowder when it has already caught fire; those things which are endowed with "aerial salt" in their mixture pass most easily of all into wind and blast. For that reason, a more intense wind immediately precedes rain, when the thinner substance, having been <term>resolved</term>, is carried more quickly after being separated from the thick matter, with the mass of rain following after. Therefore, the force of the winds breaks out from the inner recesses of the earth, from condensed humors and—so to speak—salts, which have been broken down by the Sun and the stars; for salt is the <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: *hypostasis*; the fundamental underlying substance or essence of a thing</note> of such concretions. Such spirits <note>original: *spiritus*; here meaning gaseous breaths or vapors</note> break out everywhere; they do not always fly in from afar, as most people suppose. This can be seen in the example of **A**, the furthest northern limit of the Island of Britain—the Scottish kingdom—and **B**, the southern limit of the English kingdom, a distance of five hundred miles.

A wind presses from the north at **A** toward the south at **B**; it arrives not as one continuous body, but as bodies variously divided into different and dissimilar blasts. For the locations at **B** are shaken by a force emerging and breaking out of the earth at **M**, or **L**, or **I**, or **H, G, F, E, D, C**. And indeed, the forces of the winds arrive at those places in various ways, either because of the distance, or the nature of the locations, or the material, or the region, and the position of the mountains. In the sea, however, the stirring of the waves and the fluctuation of that restless nature increases the motion.

The generation of winds is from moisture; the true substance of winds is a breathing or a thick vapor, fleeing from an aqueous nature. A cloud, however, is a thick vapor, just as it is dense...

It may be asked why winds are carried obliquely <note>sideways or horizontally</note>, and do not seek the higher or supreme regions, but are carried most rapidly at a height of perhaps only one mile, as if restrained by boundaries and narrow straits? And this too may be observed quite often: that clouds in the upper altitude seem to rest, and are neither pulled apart nor moved forward by the force of the winds; yet the lower clouds, near the earth—distant by perhaps half a mile or three <term>stades</term> <note>A classical unit of distance; three stades is roughly 600 yards</note>—are stirred up and hurried along in frantic courses. Does the mist or the cold of the <term>middle region</term> <note>In Aristotelian meteorology, the "Middle Region" of the air was thought to be perpetually cold, preventing vapors from rising further</note> prevent them from climbing further into the more spacious areas, as it seems to our <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note>? Or is it rather because they lean more on their "offspring" <note>their source material</note> in their earthly course, and recognize in their full flow the breaths even now flowing out of the earth? They snatch these up for their own support and pass through them most eagerly, not unlike a liquid poured out on a flat surface: it moves toward the place where the surface is marked by some track of moisture, declining the dry parts entirely. Nor can it be raised directly away from the earth, because it follows its common mother like a shadow...

...is united <note>The OCR "cillio- mitatur" likely represents *conciliatur*, meaning to be joined or united</note>, and is bound to the terrestrial globe as if to a parent; just as all the air within this circumference, and the clouds at a small distance, adhere to the earth like garments, and are not carried away by the daily revolutions. But why are some clouds carried above others at different heights? It is because those which have their origin nearby, or in the same region through which they are carried, fly through the lower altitudes; those from a distance fly through the higher regions. This is not unlike the sea tides and certain rivers, where wave passes over wave, and the waters are carried more quickly at the bottom than on the surface in a diverse course, as new springs burst forth or a tide of waters arrives from elsewhere.

Usually, those winds that are brought in below pass through more quickly if two contrary or sub-contrary winds blow at the same time; this is indicated by the clouds which are moved by them. This happens because they are in a narrower space, and also because they complete their journey in a smaller circle; but especially because these lower winds grow and gather force and collect supplies of exhalations <note>original: *halituum*; in early science, "exhalations" were dry or moist vapors rising from the earth thought to produce weather</note>, while the others languish for opposite reasons. They even cease, settling into clouds and rain when they are condensed by the cold.

And although Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose *Meteorologica* was the standard textbook on weather for centuries</note> teaches that contrary winds cannot blow at the same time, we have certainly discovered that not only contrary, but sub-contrary, and all sorts of winds can blow together. As Virgil wrote: *“He saw all the battles of the winds clash together”* <note>original: *Omnia ventorum concurrere prælia vidit*; a reference to Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 1, line 318</note>. This occurs not only at different points on the horizon, but also at vastly different distances from the earth. For we have very often seen the South Wind <note>original: *Austrum*</note> leading clouds in the lower parts of the air, while the North Wind <note>original: *Aquilonem*</note> carries others in the opposite direction above. 

I myself have seen, as indicated by the masses of clouds, five different winds at once, varying in height in the air and in position from the horizon. Indeed, before oncoming storms, contrary winds clash at the same altitude and region; not otherwise than opposing wings of cavalry, when they charge in squadrons with loosened reins, and the stronger sweeps along the weak...

There is also a great dissimilarity—and even opposition—of winds in different places, due to the positioning of mountains, the sea, plains, and headlands. For this reason, sailors very often feel changes in the winds (as if they were the various and distinct kingdoms of Aeolus <note>In classical mythology, Aeolus was the keeper of the winds. For after they have sailed for a long time with a favorable East Wind <note>original: *Euro*</note> and full sails, they suddenly encounter a South Wind <note>original: *Austrum*</note>, or whatever other wind chance provides. For they do not always arise from far away, but close at hand within a distance of ten, twenty, or sixty miles, and then they cease; although more often they are more universal, and many breathe together into a single gust and wander far and wide. This dissimilarity occurs in maritime places and near headlands, where the wind runs along the edges of the land over flat stretches of water; thus various winds sometimes clash. For example, those sailing along the English shores of Cornwall <note>original: *Cornubiæ*</note>, after they have passed the final cape <note>Likely referring to Land's End</note>, often catch new incursions of wind in their sails from either the bay between Wales <note>original: *Walliam*</note> and Cornwall, or from the Irish Sea, as the previous winds cease or give way.

### *The origin of the motion of winds does not occur from a higher place.*

Winds arise from the earth and waters; winds, bursting forth by their own nature, shake the waters and the seas, and that very exhalation <note>original: *exspiratio*; according to the Aristotelian scientific tradition, "exhalations" were dry vapors rising from the earth that were thought to be the primary matter of wind</note> is in motion. Wind is what we define as the movement of our misty sky, usually resulting from the swift generation of newly born air. However, they gather greater strength in the atmosphere as reinforcements arrive from all sides, with matter flowing together from longer distances. For in the County of Derby <note>Derbyshire, England</note>, a mountainous and stony region, such violent eruptions of wind emerge from certain caverns that clothing and cloths thrown in are blown out again with great force and carried higher into the air. Hence the seas roar before storms and are raised up by insane waves by the winds carrying them along, which emerge from the deepest parts of the earth, the very foundations of the seas.

The cessation and death of the winds occurs either by the heat of the Sun and the mid-day glows, by which that vapor <term>halitus</term> <note>Vapor or "halitus" was considered the "material" cause of wind in early modern science—a dry exhalation from the earth.</note> is dissolved into thinner air, or by intense cold, when all things grow stiff with the excessive inclemency of the heavens. And thus the names of the winds are established and assigned according to the fixed order and arrangement of the regions of the heavens.

The qualities of the winds correspond to the nature of the places from which they originate. Therefore, the northern wind <note>original: *septentrionalis*</note> is cold by nature, while the south wind <note>original: *auster*</note> is hot; the former blows from colder climates, the latter from warmer ones; and those winds nearest to them imitate that same nature. However, a different reasoning must be applied to the eastern winds and those that blow from the west. Aristotle argues that those blowing from the East <note>original: *Ortu*</note> are hotter than those from the West <note>original: *Occasu*</note>; he adds the reason that those blowing from the West are positioned under the Sun longer, and because the Sun then recedes more quickly from the place where it sets, and approaches it more slowly. But for us English <note>original: *nobis Anglis*</note>, these winds are much colder, so much so that those blowing from the midpoint between the East and the North are the coldest of all. Nor does it matter that they remain a little longer with the Sun. This is of little consequence, since those winds also have a Sun that grows hotter through the contrary stimulation of its rays; at which time, because of that very heat, they are mostly dissolved and dissipated. But as is his habit, Aristotle invents his "Problems" to suit his own Greece, not because he is knowledgeable about other regions. ## CHAPTER V.
->*On the Eastern Winds.*<-

East winds, among us English, are colder because they blow thin and piercing—not so much because of their time spent with the Sun, but because they originate from the continent of Germany <note>In this period, "Germany" often referred broadly to the Northern European mainland</note>; where the winds are much thinner than in our Island, which is for the most part covered in mists and fog. Those winds are cooled or tempered in the summer by the nearby German Sea <term>German Sea: The historical name for the North Sea.</term>. But in winter they are inherently much colder, since the mainland is much colder in winter than our Island, even when located on the same latitude <note>original: *parallelo*</note>; (for great vapors <note>referring to maritime moisture</note> temper both the winter cold and the summer heat). They are mostly clear, provided they have not been mixed with others. They damage budding fruits beyond measure, especially in coastal places situated to the East; however, in inland <note>original: *Mediterraneis*, referring here to landlocked areas rather than the Mediterranean Sea</note> places, they are transformed by the local mercy of the sky and the customary breezes; they are not so hostile in other regions.

## CHAPTER VII.
### On the Northern Winds.

North winds are fair and clear because they are born in colder places where, being stirred by less heat, they possess an overly thick nature. But when they penetrate further into warmer regions, the heat thins them more, and does not condense them into mist, or cloud, or water.

## CHAPTER VIII.
### On the Western Winds.

West winds are colder and more humid for some regions due to the geographic position of those regions, and because—running in a course contrary to the daily revolution <note>The author refers to the Sun's apparent movement from East to West; winds moving West to East "meet" the sun for less time</note>—they linger less with the Sun. To us English, however, who inhabit the southern part of the Island, they appear clear and are most frequent; so much so that they arrive more often and more frequently from the West and its neighboring quarters than from the other three directions. They are clearer because they are strong; for they are the strongest of all winds among us. They are more frequent and strong because they come from the mountains of Wales <note>original: *Walliæ*</note> and the shores of the stormy Irish Sea, as well as from the vaporous region of the Island of Ireland <note>original: *Hiberniæ*</note>.

#### *On the State of the Air and its Secret Foreknowledge.*

You shall consider the primary qualities, <note>In traditional physics, these are heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> first and especially concerning secondary effects such as hail, thunder, and hourly rains; because these occur in various and uncertain ways according to the positions of certain winds and regions, they can be predicted with less certainty at their specific times.

#### *Heat: The Sun approaching the Tropic.*

**Mars (♂)**
- 1. When it is in the lower part of its epicycle <term>Epicycle: In the older model of the universe, this was a small circular orbit that a planet followed while its center moved along a larger circle around the Earth.</term> or in retrograde <note>original: *retrogr* — appearing to move backward in the sky</note>; and in that place where you should look for the sextile <term>Sextile: An astrological aspect where two celestial bodies are 60 degrees apart, often considered a harmonious influence.</term>.
- 2. In its approach to the Summer Tropic <note>The Tropic of Cancer, marking the height of summer.</note>. However, this has no effect when the planet is at apogee <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit where a planet or the Sun is furthest from the Earth.</term>.
- According to observations: 56 degrees from the Sun.

**Jupiter (♃)**
- 1. In its approach to the Summer Tropic.
- 2. When it is in configuration with hot fixed stars.
- 3. When it is at perigee <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit where a planet is closest to the Earth, increasing its perceived influence.</term>.

**Venus (♀)**

You will compare the year 1540—which was very hot and dry—with the year 1574. You will see that Mars and Jupiter were positioned in the same perigees. Look at the comparison of those years regarding Venus, Mercury (☿), and the Moon (☽) at perigee; during opposition <term>Opposition: When two celestial bodies are on opposite sides of the sky as seen from Earth (180 degrees apart).</term> or conjunction <term>Conjunction: When two celestial bodies appear close together in the sky.</term>, it increases moisture.

Observe the sextile aspect (⚹) to the Sun (☉), Saturn (♄), Jupiter, and Mars for clouds and rain; Jupiter and Mars always bring heat. The Moon’s perigee during an opposition brings rain. Look for conjunctions or oppositions at maximum latitude <note>The distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic, or the Sun's path.</note>.

From the North, out of Leo (♌), come rains; Mars (♂) in the west brings cold. Mars (♂) near the Sun or further from the North in winter brings cold. Saturn (♄) ascending during a new moon brings cold.

In the year 1540, there was a Solar Eclipse at the 28th degree of Aries (♈). The summer was dry and hot beyond measure; likewise, in the year 1567, there was a Solar Eclipse at the 28th degree of Aries (♈), and the drought lasted through the three following months. The cause of the great cold of 1572:

In the 24th degree of Scorpio (♏), Mars (♂), the Sun (☉), and the Moon (☾) were with Saturn (♄); no planet either held a cardinal point <term>Cardinal point: The four most powerful positions in an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli.</term> or looked toward the Sun (☉). Mars (♂) was positioned shortly after sunset in the "angle of cold"; Venus (♀) followed also in the west; the Moon (☾), at a proper latitude, was joined to Saturn (♄). Neither fast nor slow in its course, Mercury (☿) applied its influence to Saturn (♄). Mars (♂) was at its furthest point from the North and at its apogee <term>Apogee: The point in an orbit where a planet is furthest from the Earth.</term>. Venus (♀) and Mercury (☿) were moving toward the upper parts of their epicycles <term>Epicycle: A small circular orbit centered on a larger one, used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary motion.</term>. Mars (♂), Saturn (♄), and the Moon (☾) were in the Meridian <note>original: *Merid.*; the highest point of the sky.</note>.

## The Cause of the Great Cold of 1564.

First, the conjunction <term>Conjunction: When two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky.</term> of the Moon (☾) and the Sun (☉) occurred after sunset; likewise, Venus (♀) following Saturn (♄) in both cases ascended strongly toward the North in perigee <term>Perigee: The point in an orbit where a planet is closest to the Earth.</term>. Mars (♂) was at its furthest distance. No configuration <note>original: *figuratio*; the angular relationship between planets.</note> occurred with the Sun (☉) except for a trine (△) <term>Trine: An astrological aspect of 120 degrees, usually considered beneficial or strengthening.</term> with Jupiter (♃), because the North Wind, while clearing the air, greatly increased the cold. The Moon (☾) was neither fast nor slow; Venus (♀) and Mercury (☿) moved toward the upper part of their epicycles. There was a trine (△) between Saturn (♄) and Venus (♀), a trine (△) between Saturn (♄) and Mars (♂), and a conjunction (☌) of Saturn (♄) and the Moon (☾) in the upper region.

## Great Weather Conditions in the Year 1564.

At the beginning of December, and from the 17th to the last day and beyond, there was a maximum frost. From the first of January until the feast <note>Likely the Feast of the Epiphany, January 6.</note>, there was heat. From then, maximum frost again. Again from the 12th to the 24th of February.

## 1565.

From the 6th to the 15th of May, it was hot. From the 23rd of June to the 3rd of July, the North Wind blew. 
From the 28th of July to the 5th of August, there was rain every single day. 
In September, from the 3rd to the 8th, rain; then until the 21st, clear weather. On the 20th of November, there was a great, continuous rain.

## The Winter of 1566 was Warm.

February 3rd to the 17th, very windy. From the 27th of May to the 5th of June, hot. From the 28th to the 31st of August, rain.

# CHAPTER X.
## On the Rainbow.

The lighting of the Rainbow <note>original: *Iridis*</note> is conceived from the vaporous air <term>Vaporous air: the Latin *vapido* refers to the moisture or mist in the atmosphere that captures light.</term>, and is reflected or held in place by a dark object; just as in mirrors, an image <term>Image: the original *idolum* (from Greek *eidolon*) refers to the optical reflection or phantom appearing in a mirror.</term> is not reflected unless you place tin or something of that sort behind the glass. In this same way, the Rainbow—a solar image—is not reflected to the sight without an underlying subject, such as a cloud, a rock, a mountain, or a building.

The primary Rainbow is conceived from the vaporous air that is adjacent to and surrounding us, and is reflected by a dense cloud or a high cliff. However, the Rainbow is not "conceived" within the cloud itself, in the same way it is in glass mirrors. The form or light is reflected by the glass, yet it truly comes from the tin or pitch <note>original: *bitumine*</note> placed beneath it; yet the light itself is not *in* the tin or pitch.

The second Rainbow is conceived from the vaporous air near or within the cloud, and is sent back from the darkness present there, just as is fitting, with the brighter colors of the first concave <note>The author is discussing the "inner" arc of the rainbow.</note>. But the primary rainbow is reflected from a distant cloud, which is why the color is inverted and luminous on the convex <note>The "outer" side of the arc.</note>. From smaller lights, with the rays being more refracted, a lesser light is produced, yet the luminous color is more intense.

A likeness of colors and light exists as the Rainbow conceived in the mist; however, it is not reflected to the eye unless by a preceding dense object. It does not matter how far away this object is placed, provided it can be seen at all, or it may be near if the temperature is suitable enough; thus, we have sometimes seen one within twenty cubits <term>Cubit: original *ulna*; a unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18–22 inches.</term>.

## CHAPTER XII.

### *On the arc or the Rainbow.*

The Rainbow <note>original: *Iris*</note> is a sort of reflection, not of the Sun’s form, but a representation of the illuminated air brought back to the eye by the opposite air. If this air is dense and smooth enough, and positioned directly opposite, it will reflect the entire form of the Sun (as glass mirrors usually do). But the light does not stay in the opposite place; it is diffused in the vaporous and bright air, with its sensible vigor increased and gathered into a sphere—both because it is light, and because it comes from a round source. The image and the variety of colors are reflected when the luminous rays passing through the moist vapor grow weak at the sides, if something thick—whether a cloud or a mountain...

### CHAPTER XIII.

#### *On the colors and positions of the Rainbow.*

That variety in the reversed position of colors <note>The author is referring to how the colors of a secondary rainbow are in the opposite order of the primary one.</note> occurs because things that are reflected from waters appear reversed. For example, if the point of a knife is turned toward the water and the handle toward the sky, in the water the point and the iron of the knife will appear above, and the handle will appear below. # METEOROLOGY
## BOOK FIVE.
### CHAPTER ONE.
->*On observations of springs.*<-

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'I' containing complex scrolling foliate and floral motifs.</image-desc>
IN our Britain, in the Forest of Knaresborough <note>original: *Knaresborn*; a historic town in North Yorkshire famous for its "dropping well."</note>, there is a spring whose water turns wood, meat, and the leaves of trees into stone after they have remained in it for some time. Near the river Nidd <note>original: *Nydd*</note>, there are cold waters that drip from hanging rocks; whatever is placed in them, after an interval of time, turns to stone <note>The author is describing the process of petrification, where minerals in the water (calcium carbonate) coat objects in a stone-like crust.</note>. There is a grove in Ireland <note>original: *Hibernia*</note> which Boethius <note>likely referring to the Scottish historian Hector Boece (Boethius), known for recording regional marvels.</note> claims to have seen, around which neither grass nor any tree grows for a very large space all around. If you drive a stake of wood into the ground there, within about the course of one year, that part which was fixed in the earth will be turned into stone; the part that is covered by water will turn into iron; and the remaining part standing out from the water will keep the form and nature of wood. Thus, stone, iron, and wood are seen combined in the same trunk with an unheard-of novelty.

The river flowing past Dublin in Ireland, called the Liffey <note>original: *Lyffie*</note>, has a marvelous property: while it rains heavily for five or six whole days, it does not swell very much; but after the rains have ceased, the springs suddenly burst forth so that the river can hardly be crossed by a ford in any place.

In Ulster <note>original: *Ultonia*</note> in Ireland, if someone washes with water drawn from a certain spring, it prevents gray hair.

In Munster <note>original: *Momonia*</note> in Ireland, there is a spring by whose bath gray hair arrives very quickly.

In the same region, a spring gushes forth which is beneficial to humans but fatal to livestock.

There is an underground passage, or rather a monstrous cave, in the English county of Somerset, which is called the "Prison of Aeolus" <note>Aeolus was the Greek god of the winds; this name suggests the cave was known for its drafts or echoing winds.</note> and by the locals *Chedderhole* <note>original: *Chedderhole*; referring to the famous Cheddar Gorge and its cave systems.</note>. It stretches far and wide: those who explore it, passing through very long distances, find various streams and springs.

### CHAPTER II.

->*On springs.*<-

We must now speak of springs—from where such a great and perennial flow of water originates. Aristotle thinks that water arises in them for the same reason it arises in the air above the earth <note>Aristotle's theory of "meteorological" origin suggested that just as rain condenses from air in the sky, water condenses from air trapped in the cold earth.</note>. Thus, if the air there is condensed into water by cold, it must be thought that this very thing happens because of the cold hidden within the earth; and that not only does the water already hidden there flow out, but it is continuously being created. 

How can this opinion be held as true? For a vaporous breath within the earth is also changed into water, not so much by the cold itself as by being held within a thicker container, such as when it encounters more porous rocks or moist sand. Nor is it required (as some claim) that there be large and spacious caverns to contain a huge force of air to be turned into water. Nor is the air so thin as it is among us; it nevertheless permeates the masses of moist sand and, turning into moisture, gushes out through many small veins into channels carved by the flow itself, as occurs in underground rocks and firmer earth. In sand, however, it is strained <note>The author is describing a process of filtration or percolation through the earth.</note>, with the material mostly being absorbed from nearby places. In the deepest parts of the earth, and (so to speak) closer to the center, there must be a vast force of waters. For there are such great and perennial whirlpools, as if reaching to the very [realm] of Pluto <note>original: *Plutonis*; Pluto was the god of the underworld. The text cuts off here, suggesting the depths of the earth are connected to a massive subterranean reservoir.</note>—

...into the inner recesses; just as the horrific whirlpools <term>charybdes: great vortexes or whirlpools, named after the Greek mythological sea-monster</term> of the sea near the pole, as well as in the Northern and Western Oceans, and in many other places, through which undoubtedly a great force of water—which is carried by rivers into the sea—is brought back again to the first beginnings of springs. There, worked upon once more by the spirit and heat of the terrestrial globe, it is carried up to its surface. 

For that Peripatetic <note>original: *Peripatetica*; referring to the followers of Aristotle, who taught while walking in the "peripatos" or colonnade of the Lyceum.</note> vanity in the classification of elements must be entirely rejected: neither should the earth be separated from the waters, nor the water from the earth, nor should they be distinguished by location. For they merge with one another by mutual necessity; and the waters irrigate the inner recesses of the earth, just as blood flows through the human body, its bones, and its flesh. 

And from here, by the heat of the terrestrial globe, vaporous breaths are diffused to the extremities; these flow out due to the tempered heat of the Sun, and indeed the rays and physical sympathy of the Moon, as well as the other stars. This is why the caverns of the earth are felt to be more humid a day or two before our sky darkens; these are indeed fitting signs of a coming change in the weather or a storm, as is apparent to those who enter caves and mines <note>original: *cuniculos*; literally "tunnels" or "burrows," frequently used to describe man-made mine shafts.</note>. Therefore, rivers do not grow so much from the air or vapor entering from outside, as they do from that which is implanted and innate within, before it bursts forth into the open air. For there are found not only the origins of springs, but also the generation of vapors, and the first and primary workshops of these breaths.

There are also, in the judgment of Aristotle <note>original: *Aristotele judice*</note>, and as daily experience testifies, lower places of such a kind that they contain within themselves as great a force of water as lakes or ponds. Rivers declare that the maws and chasms of the earth, which hide themselves underground, are of this sort; this happens in many places, just as many parts of the Peloponnese <note>The large peninsula forming the southern part of mainland Greece.</note> in Arcadia <note>A mountainous region in the Peloponnese, famous in antiquity for its "disappearing" rivers and sinkholes called *ponors*.</note> are like this, because they have no flow from their riverbeds. For rivers that are full, and have no place into which they may pour out, find an exit for themselves in the depths

Aristotle believes that no mass of water is so great, nor can it be contained by the earth, as to be constantly drawn from what exists in the nature of things; therefore, he thinks the beginnings of rivers cannot arise from defined and fixed channels. This would be true if new material did not flow into those channels, and if the veins of the earth did not conceive new moisture from its own vitals—just as the veins from the intestines of the human body—and if that flow and consumption were not restored by a reciprocal nature. 

Therefore, springs can emanate from their own more abundant internal stores, and they also arise from the transformation of vapors ascending within the earth, as well as from the "sweating out" of moisture and water from sandy soil. These sandy soils—especially those we call "living sands" <note>original: *vivae*; likely referring to quicksand or porous coastal shoals</note> in the sea—soak up the moisture of the seas, which becomes fresh through long filtration; and the whirlpools <term>charybdes: great vortexes or whirlpools</term> of the sea in many places absorb a massive force of water through open chasms. By this means the seas are unburdened; for although they receive an immense volume from rivers, they nevertheless [do not exceed] their limit...

...they preserve, nor do they cross their accustomed limits. And although we cannot observe this so exactly in the great sea and the Ocean, let us consider that Hyrcanian or Caspian Sea <note>The Caspian Sea was frequently referred to as the Hyrcanian Sea in ancient and early modern geography</note>: into it the Volga river and many others flow with such an abundance of water relative to its basin, that if one were to imagine the entire sea boiling—much like a furnace with burning fires placed beneath it—even such a fiction would not allow that it could be emptied by so rapid a transformation of water into vapors <note>original: *halitus*; literally "breaths" or "exhalations"</note>. Similarly, many rivers in Africa are hidden in lakes. For it would be foolish to think that these are emptied only by the rising of vapors. 

First, because the entire volume of rain that falls during the whole year across the entire world by no means equals the abundance of the rivers. Add to this that the land and terrestrial regions themselves supply the greatest amount of material for vapors; and the rains themselves, which fall upon the lands, for the most part return <note>that is, evaporate back into the atmosphere</note> before they are collected into streams and enter rivers and seas. Rain also falls back into the sea; I would not say in as great a quantity as was raised from it, but nearly equal, or not far different, for it often rains at sea. Also, certain humid meteors <term>meteor: in this historical context, "meteor" refers to any atmospheric phenomenon, such as rain, snow, or lightning, rather than a space rock</term>, by a natural sympathy, seek the seas more than the land, as is shown by those sudden downpours of water falling in great mass like rivers, which have been observed by sailors. 

But if, according to their opinion, water originated in the earth from vapors entering from the air, a much greater volume of vapors would enter than would exit—not to mention those vapors which turn into clouds and rain. Otherwise, the entire Aristotelian element of air would surely have perished many centuries ago through such rapid depletion. Therefore, those absurdities regarding the origin of springs—which they claim are summoned from the air into the mountains—ought to be utterly driven out of Philosophy.
