### CHAPTER III.

->On the disappearance of springs, their various differences,<-
->and the transformation of lands by waters.<-

Just as there is a cycle of change and turnover in all things, so it is with springs. Seas change, the borders of lands are altered; where once there was dry land, there is now the deep sea, and the seas in turn give way to land. Likewise, in the deepest hidden recesses of the earth, the veins <note>Subterranean water channels were often compared to the veins in a human body.</note> change, dry up, become blocked, grow dense, turn to stone, liquefy, gape open, or are newly uncovered. For this reason, after several centuries, springs are changed, and even the rivers that bubble forth from certain specific springs. However, those rivers that have more frequent beginnings, and are filled by many various streams and springs—where as some dry up, others burst forth and flow more abundantly—remain in the natural order and are celebrated throughout many centuries in the long memory of man, such as the Ganges, Indus, Euphrates, Nile, Danube, Rhine, Rhône, Tigris, Ebro <note>original: *Iber*</note>, and Thames. Although great changes occur in all of these, appearing differently than they did in a previous age, they nonetheless persist and, for the most part, retain their ancient channels.

Yet some of them have dried up because the lands themselves occasionally dry out; from this, it is inevitable that those beginnings and spring-heads <note>original: *scaturigines*</note> are buried. Lands that were once wet and swampy become firm and solid plains; and so, where Troy once stood, there is a crop <note>A reference to the Latin poet Ovid: "Jam seges est, ubi Troja fuit," meaning that time eventually erases even the greatest cities.</note>, and where there was a crop, there is now a swamp. Egypt once seemed to be an alluvial deposit of the Nile; but slowly and step by step, as the swamps dried out, people began to inhabit the neighboring places. Therefore, all the mouths of the Nile, even in the era of Aristotle, appear to have been made by the labor and art of men, except for the Canopic mouth <note>The Canopic branch was the westernmost mouth of the Nile Delta in antiquity.</note>, rather than by the river itself. In this way, humid places are restored to a better state; however, those which were previously fertile, unless...

### CHAPTER IV.
#### Concerning certain temporary springs.

Temporary springs also exist, which are not of a perpetual flow, but rise and fall at certain fixed times of the year; such as those in England, near Chichester, which break out at the roots of the mountains (and are called "the washing ones" <note>original: *lavantes*; this refers to the River Lavant, a "winterbourne" or intermittent stream that flows through Chichester after heavy rain in the chalk hills.</note> by the inhabitants). These flow with such force that within a distance of two or three stades <note>A "stadium" was an ancient Greek measurement of distance, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters.</note> from their first source, they are able to power one or another wheat mill; they flow until midsummer, and then they are completely dried up. It is believable that the winter rains, absorbed by the sand, generate these very springs. In Kent <note>original: *Cantium*</note> indeed, at the village of Orpington <note>original: *Orpingdow*; likely referring to the intermittent springs that feed the River Cray.</note>, sometimes in the tenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth year, springs break out from the earth in very many places at the beginning of summer—in the streets, in the fields, and in houses—even when neither the winter nor that year has been excessively rainy beyond the usual custom, nor has such a year preceded it.

### CHAPTER V.
#### Springs from mountains, and why.

Aristotle shows that most rivers arise from mountains, and the greatest and most massive from the highest ones. In Asia, many of the largest rivers glide down from Mount Paropamisus <note>The Hindu Kush mountain range in Central Asia.</note>; from which flow both the Bactrus <note>The Balkh River in Afghanistan.</note> and the Choaspes <note>The Karkheh River in modern-day Iran.</note>, as well as the Araxes <note>Likely the Amu Darya or the Aras River; ancient geographers often conflated these.</note>, a part of which, the Tanais <note>The Don River.</note>, flows into Lake Maeotis <note>The Sea of Azov.</note>. The Indus also, the greatest of all rivers, glides from that same mountain. Moreover, from the Caucasus, many other rivers of incredible height and magnitude flow together, including the Phasis <note>The Rioni River in the nation of Georgia.</note>; for this mountain is the largest of those that look toward the summer sunrise <note>The Northeast.</note>. And such is the nature of subterranean springs: mobile, lifting itself up in the womb of the common mother <note>The Earth.</note>; such is also the nature of hidden rivers that break out again, which open rivers flowing far distances also imitate. For one ought not to think that rivers are further advanced and continue their course only because they always flow into more downward-sloping places. along a straight line, nor falling down toward some slant into lower places; but the surface of the Nile is circular, provided that the terrestrial globe is in some way round. Just as a quadrant of a circle **a c b** is formed, with the sources of the Nile **d** being fifty degrees distant from its mouths **b**, it is clear that the waters are carried along the arc **d b**, not along the straight line **d b**. For if they flowed down because of higher ground <note>The author is refuting the idea that the source must be physically "higher" in a flat-earth sense for water to flow; he argues the water follows the Earth's curve.</note>, the sources **d** would have to ascend to the boundary **f** on line **d f**, or even higher; than which nothing is more absurd. Therefore, the Nile flows in a circle; not because of a perpetual tilt of the lands and the falling of waters, but by a general nature and the cooperation of the whole—namely, when it finds a smooth path <note>original: *æqualem*</note>, not heavily obstructed by mountains and valleys.

But if the waters in the earth's innards did not ascend from the center toward the surface, where would the forces of the waters descend into so many and such horrific abysses <note>original: *voraginibus*; the author imagines the Earth having internal cavities where water is recycled.</note> that penetrate to the interior? Although they descend salty, they lose their salt through separation, and become fresh by filtration <note>original: *colatura*</note> through the passage of sands and earth. Therefore, fresh veins of water are carried both to the mountains themselves and from the depths of the earth to the plain. # PHYSIOLOGY

[Pli]ny, in his fifth book, wrote that between the island of Arados <note>Arados, or Arvad, is an island off the coast of Syria. Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD) was a Roman naturalist and author.</note> and the mainland, a spring is drawn out from the very bottom of the shallow sea through leather tubes. In some tiny islands as well, very abundant springs gush forth. They exhale, therefore, from the inner recesses of the earth as nature carries them out, and for the same reason they ascend into the mountains.

And that statement of Solomon <note>Referencing King Solomon as the traditional author of Ecclesiastes.</note> is true, who said that rivers are generated from the sea; "All rivers," he says, "go to the sea, and the sea is not filled: to the place from which the rivers set out, there they return, so that they may flow back again." <note>A translation of Ecclesiastes 1:7. This was a central text for early modern thinkers trying to explain the water cycle.</note>

For the Earth drinks in the moisture of the seas, either through open mouths, as in whirlpools, or when sand and porous earth catch it and lead it to the innermost parts—to wide, spacious, and internal sources to which the sea sends back its waters, from which rivers are born. This does not happen, however, at some "Tartarus" <note>original: *tartarum*. In Greek mythology, Tartarus is a deep abyss; the philosopher Plato used it in his work 'Phaedo' to describe a central reservoir of water within the earth.</note> in the midst of the earth's bowels, as if it were the parent of all rivers, as Plato wished.

Nor are those arguments opposed to our view which we have proposed to challenge in order: First, the objection that water cannot ascend to such a height as the peak of mountains, and that it would break out everywhere just as it does in mountains. Likewise, the objection that rivers would never decrease. Furthermore, that the sea itself would not suffice for so many rivers, since the greatest part of the waters evaporates because of the Sun. Also, that such movement under the earth would shake it, and there would be no reason why water should flow from one mountain and not another; and finally, that the water is made so pure from all saltiness <note>original: *salsugine*</note> seems hardly likely.

But these subtleties of Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576) was a famous Italian polymath who wrote extensively on physics and natural history.</note>, being of little weight, are dissolved in reverse order. It has been demonstrated before that salt is cast off; and in daily experience on the shores of Africa, near the sea, they draw fresh waters from a pit that has been dug. But to the next reason—namely, why they would flow from one mountain rather than another—I respond: some mountains have caverns and porous sand <note>original: *arenam fistulentam*</note> that draws in and absorbs moisture, while others are solid,

...are earthy, stony, made of tufa, chalky, or gravelly. His **fifth argument**, that such motion beneath the earth would shake it, is ridiculous; as if it were necessary for the mass of the earth to be agitated simply because the flow is steady and the path unobstructed. Even where a path is blocked, it does not necessarily follow that a shaking of the ground occurs; indeed, the earth is not jolted unless it is agitated by a blast of air <note>original: *flatu*. The author follows the Aristotelian view that earthquakes are caused by trapped wind or vapors rather than moving water.</note>.

**Fourth**, he argues that the sea would not suffice for the rivers, for the greatest part of the water is consumed by the heat of the Sun. But matter is not destroyed; if it were, the sea would have been consumed by now, along with its rivers. In truth, the sea suffices for the rivers by a mutual exchange of favors; for it receives what it gives. Thus, both the sea and the rivers are contained within a single body of water, and there is a mutual recirculation of moisture, just as occurs in the **vessels of the chemists** <note>This refers to "circulatory" distillation in alchemy and early chemistry, where a liquid is evaporated and condensed back into the same vessel.</note>; that which is exhausted by the power of the Sun is restored by the transformed air.

The **third objection** is this: that rivers would never decrease in volume. Certainly, that quantity which is supplied by the sea undergoes little or no change; however, variation occurs in those internal vapors that rise from the depths of the earth due to the varying intensity of terrestrial heat, as well as from the melting of snow and the addition of falling rains. Indeed, those torrents that do run dry receive no supply from the sea.

The **second objection**: that the waters would burst forth along their journey. Yet, in certain places, they do indeed burst forth even on level plains, forming pools; sometimes new springs arise and older ones cease. Nevertheless, the foundations of the earth are so placed that they do not easily collapse or break apart from every slight pressure.

There remains the **first argument**, in which he denies that waters from the sea can be drawn up to the summits of mountains. His reasoning is based on the level <note>original: *libella*</note> used by **water-engineers** <term>Aquilegum: Specialist craftsmen or engineers in the Roman tradition who sought out and managed water sources using leveling instruments.</term>; for water cannot be moved higher than the surface from which it is derived. The earth is permeated by many caves in those locations where water was once present, but which are now occupied by earth; the water has moved into the hollow places of the earth. 

Since these spaces are narrow and cannot hold such a vast mass of sea, that portion of water—compressed by the sea lying upon it from the outside and seeking to reclaim its rightful seat—seeks a way to exit wherever it can, just as that water did through the small tubes. From this pressure come the exits and leapings-forth of water, which are called **bubbling springs** <note>original: *scatebrae*</note>, a word of Greek origin derived from <term>σκάπτω</term> <note>original: *skaptō*, meaning "to dig" or "to hollow out"</note>; and because these are not in their proper place, they flow downward.

...[tun]nels they thrust and hide themselves everywhere in the sea (although in some places they enter through wider passages), nor are all internal water courses so violent. Therefore, it must be concluded—following the true ancient philosophy, which was poorly understood by the Greek philosophers, but which the most wise **Solomon** <note>A reference to King Solomon, traditionally the author of the book of Ecclesiastes.</note> demonstrated in this controversy when he said, *All rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is not full; to the place from which the rivers come, there they return* <note>original: *Flumina &c.* (Ecclesiastes 1:7)</note>—that the terrestrial globe is a single body. It is bound together by the mutual connections and harmony of lands and waters, so that the moisture in the earth naturally flows through its **springs** <note>original: *scaturiginibus*</note> upward, downward, and in a circular fashion among the "entrails" <note>The author uses *viscera* to describe the internal depths or "guts" of the earth.</note> of the world. One must not overlook (says **Scaliger**) what was once said by a **"half-monk"** <note>Scaliger’s derogatory nickname for his rival, Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), implying he was a superstitious or failed cleric.</note> among dinner guests: that there are veins in the earth from which water is drawn, just as blood is drawn from the veins of animals. Scaliger presents this as a joke against **Cardano** to serve as **dessert** <note>original: *bellariis*—literally sweetmeats served at the end of a meal; here meaning a light, mocking anecdote for the entertainment of the guests.</note>. 

But our own gardeners laugh at Scaliger. To irrigate delicate plants with constant moisture, they make water ascend by simply placing wet linens into vessels of water. By this art, the water climbs and falls over the herbs in the manner of a **water-clock** <note>A *clepsydra*, an ancient device that measured time by the regulated flow of water.</note>. This one piece of practical ingenuity surpasses all of Scaliger’s most subtle refinements regarding the sea and its waters. For in this same way, water also passes from the sea into various regions and mountains: just as it happens in the pot **a**, which is full of water up to the line **b**, with a wet linen or a strip of cloth **c**, which is inserted by one end into the water...

Everywhere on earth, water is dug out through wells; however, this occurs in deeper places that are gypsum-like, hardened, and limestone-heavy, which release water less easily. Therefore, moisture is found everywhere except in the hardened heights of the earth that are greatly dried out by the Sun, or in other places that are unnaturally dense; thus, moisture is not so diminished that it would dry up, because of the eruptions of springs and the moisture following from the lowest and deepest hidden treasures of the waters, and from the sea itself.

## CHAPTER VI.
### *On the causes of mountains.*

It seems very appropriate to this discussion to say something about the causes of mountains, which arise from the same causes as lands, regions, and seas. For they piously wander in their logic <note>original: *pie delirant* — literally "they rave piously." The author is gently mocking those whose religious convictions lead them to unscientific conclusions.</note> who have claimed that the earth was torn and pulled down by the **Great Flood**, and that mountains were merely exposed by the waters rushing headlong into the sea. This is such a great folly that they are ignorant of the fact that if the summit of the highest mountain were to be leveled with the surface by a new placement of earth, the entire world, torn from its own seat and pulled away from its center point, would be exhausted. Indeed, mountains are not made by the work of the stars; for why would there be more mountains in the **Alps** than in the **Low Countries** <note>original: *Belgis* — referring to the region of modern-day Belgium and the Netherlands, known for its flat topography.</note>?

<summary>The author explains how water reaches great heights through capillary action, citing the deep well at Dover Castle and mining observations by Agricola, before refuting the idea that mountains were formed solely by the Great Flood.</summary>
<keywords>hydrology, Dover Castle, Georgius Agricola, fathoms, geology, mountain formation, Great Flood, Alps, Belgium</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author’s discussion of the physical transformation of the earth, moving from the growth and decay of mountains to the origin of the world's water systems.</meta>

# BOOK V.

...in the land of the Pyrenees, or in Campania? <note>original: *Campania* — a fertile region in southern Italy, famous for its volcanic landscape and mountains like Vesuvius.</note> Yet mountains undergo their own transformations, just like all other things. Some are larger than they were in the previous century, many are even smaller, and some have even newly emerged. However, because these great changes happen over such vast durations of time, and because their exact dimensions were never accurately measured or recorded in writing, they escape our perception and judgment. Sometimes they collapse or split apart due to earthquakes and fissures, as seen in the Alps. They also grow, as can be seen in their very "innards": when tunnels excavated by miners—wide enough for entry and passage—are found after several years to be so tight and narrow that a person can hardly enter, or cannot enter at all. <note>This reflects a common early modern belief that the Earth was a living organism and that rocks and minerals could "grow" or regenerate over time.</note> In many places, sands are carried down by mountain streams and accumulate, or they harden into stones and cliffs from firmer soil. In other places, aging cliffs dissolve, and the higher parts are carried down to the deep valleys by the flow of water. Sometimes the earth subsides, as happened in recent years in the Western part of our Britain, where huge trees fell and the ground was swallowed up to the very peaks.

Such changes happen gradually and go unobserved; or, if great changes did occur, they have not reached our knowledge because of the vast passage of time and the negligence of men.

Some also attribute this opinion to Moses, since in Genesis, when describing the flood that occurred in the times of Noah, he mentions the "great abyss." <note>original: *magna abysso* — referring to Genesis 7:11, "the fountains of the great deep were broken up."</note> But "abyss" is also used in the Holy Scriptures to mean the depths of the sea; and just as the tides of the sea now rush toward the lands from the deep oceans, so they then burst forth from the depths onto the lands, and were carried everywhere for the destruction of a world stripped of its form. However, Aristotle sufficiently refuted that opinion. <note>Aristotle argued against the idea of a vast underground reservoir (Plato’s Tartarus), believing instead that water was generated within the Earth from condensing air.</note> Furthermore, magnetic rotations are constant and proportionate when produced by a solid earth, except for minor defects on the surface. If there were a huge cavity within the earth serving as a source for the waters, all magnetic motions would be crippled and useless, or would hardly exist at all. <note>The author is likely drawing on the work of William Gilbert (1600), who proposed that the Earth acts as a giant solid magnet.</note> It is also necessary for the source to be near the center, since springs flow out everywhere across the entire globe. Moreover, the idea that the base and foundation of the earth consists of a vast quantity of water—a fluid and uncertain consistency—does not agree with reason at all. For the globe of the lands would rest upon an unstable seat and support, and would eventually have to burst, break, and settle in a massive ruin. Likewise, such a great mass of water would constantly emit a perpetual and immense vapor, which would necessarily rupture the arched vault of the earth. We do not, however, deny that in this earth which we inhabit, there are large caves in certain places filled with water and air; because of these, it occasionally happens (though rarely) that lands subside in the sea, islands are submerged, and others emerge and are born.

But what fervor of the Sun exists there, either to draw out sweet moisture or to scorch the terrestrial <term>exhalation</term>? <note>In Aristotelian physics, "exhalations" were dry or moist vapors rising from the Earth that produced weather, minerals, and, as some argued, the salt in the sea.</note> This is especially true in winter, during the Sun’s greatest retreat, when even in midsummer the sun can in no way melt or liquefy the mountains of ice. Indeed, those who have passed the Tropic of Capricorn and direct their course toward the Southern circle, along the very long and not yet well-explored shores of the Southern hemisphere, find the sea salty and poorly suited for human use; yet there, as in the North <note>original: *Arctos* — literally "the Bears," the constellations used to denote the North Pole.</note>, the fervor of the Sun ceases. 

To claim that the sea is salty because of the Sun's heat is false; for those same forces are perpetually constant: as much as they are intensified on this side of the equinoctial line, they are diminished on the other, and vice versa. Why, then, does the sea not eventually become the saltiest of all, or, so to speak, salt itself? They say salt does not settle in the sea, and they claim that the bottom depths are fresher, based on the experience of divers <note>original: *urinatorum* — professional breath-hold divers used in antiquity and the Renaissance for salvage and scientific observation.</note> and of vessels that are lowered into the deep while closed, and then opened by some artifice in those deep places. ...continuously shut off. Indeed, rivers and rains only dilute the saltiness <note>The OCR reads *falsuginem*, but this is a transcription of the Latin *salsuginem* (brine or saltiness), where the early modern "long s" (ſ) was often mistaken for an "f".</note> of the sea; they do not diminish it. But if the salt were to increase day by day, and were not hindered by anything other than the dilution from these sources, it would undoubtedly become saltier <note>OCR: *falsius* for *salsius*</note> every day, and eventually reach a state of extreme salinity.

The entire crowd of **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, who often walked while discussing logic and nature.</note> follows the opinion of **Aristotle**; namely, they say that the saltiness <note>OCR: *falsedo* for *salsedo*</note> of the sea is produced by the admixture of some scorched terrestrial matter, exhaled by the subtle heat of the Sun. They claim the sea is salty because the Sun’s heat mostly draws upward that which is "sweet" <note>Fresh water was referred to as "sweet" (*dulce*) in contrast to "salty" or "bitter" water.</note>, for sweet waters are lighter; thus, the heavier water sinks in the sea, mixed with dry and scorched terrestrial <term>exhalations</term> <note>In ancient physics, these were dry vapors rising from the earth, thought to be the "fuel" for salt and minerals.</note>, which render it salty. 

But how are these terrestrial exhalations scorched, or how do they rise scorched from the earth in the deep sea with the sea itself positioned in between? Or do the seas grow so hot that the foundations beneath them remain scorched as a result? Look at the entire surface of the lands; one may survey the fields and open plains, heated much more intensely by the Sun, from which huge quantities of breaths <note>original: *halituum* — vapors or "exhalations"</note> rise: yet those lands are not notorious for saltiness, while in the meantime the sea becomes salty. 

Furthermore, as for what exhales as sweet from the sea and is converted into clouds and rains by means of vapors, does it not descend in rains and showers just as sweet as it ascended? What, then, is that separation of the sweeter moisture from the thicker moisture (polluted by a "stain" <note>The author uses *labem* (stain/defect) to describe the impurities Aristotelians believed were left behind during evaporation.</note>), such that what remains behind becomes saltier? Rain flows down from the air just as sweet as the matter from which it ascended, as is also manifest in **alembics** <note>A chemical apparatus used for distillation, consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</note> and the instruments of distillers. Therefore, it is evident that neither the separation of a "sweeter nature," nor the stain conceived from those breaths, is the cause of the taste in the sea.

<summary>The author critiques the Aristotelian view that sea salt is caused by "scorched exhalations" and the evaporation of fresh water, pointing out that distillation in both nature and chemistry produces pure water without leaving the remaining liquid increasingly scorched.</summary>

# BOOK V. CHAPTER IX.

->*What the true cause of the sea's saltiness <note>The OCR reads *falsedinis*, but this is a transcription of the Latin *salsedinis*, where the early modern "long s" (ſ) was mistaken for an "f".</note> is.*<-

We previously stated that there is a dual moisture <term>humor</term> <note>In early modern science, "humors" referred not just to bodily fluids but to the fundamental moistures of the earth that determined the properties of minerals and water.</note> in our globe: the watery and the fatty. The fatty moisture is mixed with the earth in more elevated places and within certain boundaries of the surface. For this reason, the water of rivers flowing past it in their descent, or water standing still in inland places, does not take on salt, because the fatty substance resists it, even though salt is perpetually implanted throughout all the earth. But the "lean" sands of the sea <note>The author contrasts the "fatty" soil of the mainland with the "lean" or "hungry" (thin) sands of the coast which do not have the same protective oily coating.</note> yield their salts when mixed by the motion of the waves; these sands also reclaim those same salts, absorbing and filtering the sea as it penetrates into the inner recesses.

Neither the lowest parts of the earth, nor its deeper bowels, change the waters or make them salty, even though they contain a great force of salt everywhere. Some believe this necessarily happens because the nature of salt in those deep places is sufficiently fixed and coherent, and does not flow away when touched by moisture; this is much like many types of stones which contain a very large and abundant nature of salt. However, where the salt is not made firm and the earth is not fixed, salty waters gush out—sometimes even the saltiest waters—namely in the salt-pans <note>original: *salinis*</note>. These salt-works are granted to almost every province of the world because of the "nobility of the profit" <note>This refers to the high economic value of salt, which was often a state-controlled monopoly and a major source of tax revenue (the "gabelle").</note>; these are salt springs, and they sometimes flow quite far from the sea. Although there are great heaps of sand in rivers, these are either fixed or "fattier" <note>meaning more bituminous or oily, preventing the salt from dissolving</note>, or the perpetual succession of flowing water dilutes any taste of salt. There are also certain rivers that are less "tasty" <note>meaning they have a slight mineral or brackish flavor</note> than others because some salt has been conceived and mixed into them; just as there are lakes that are salty like the sea. For example, there is the so-called Sea of Galilee; while the Syrian Sea <note>The Dead Sea, often called the "Syrian Sea" or "Lake of Bitumen" in older texts.</note> even grows bitter with a bituminous salt. Indeed, it was possible in the past, as it is now, to see many masses of salt and bitumen within its borders. And you will not easily find a spring, but that some...

## CHAPTER X.
### On the tide, flow, and ebb of the sea.

Aristotle was indeed cautious to overlook this entire branch of philosophy. For since he could barely disentangle himself from other difficulties concerning the sea, he would undoubtedly have been overwhelmed by these waves <note>The author uses "waves" metaphorically to mean the difficult problems of tidal theory.</note>. When other Peripatetics <term>Peripatetici</term> <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> sought light from him, they too left frustrated and deprived of their own vision. For nothing exists in the writings of the Ancients regarding the sea tide except for passing and ill-considered remarks. More recent authors have tackled the subject, but unsuccessfully; such as Federico Delfino <note>original: "Fredericus Delphinus", an Italian mathematician who wrote on the tides in 1559.</note> and Jean Taisnier <note>original: "Iohannes Tayſner", a Belgian author of the 16th century.</note>. They do not touch the heart of the matter; they describe the sequence of events but do not offer the underlying reason. Levinus Lemnius <note>A Dutch physician known for his works on secret wonders of nature.</note> performs very poorly, and Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a prominent Renaissance scholar.</note> most absurdly attempts to reveal the causes through reasoning; but he does not reach the primary causes, getting stuck on trifles and falling into error. For in this branch of philosophy, it is difficult to know even a few things if one does not know most or all of them. Therefore, since—as far as I know—this has never been committed to writing or truly understood by anyone, we shall attempt with greater care and diligence to aspire toward such hidden causes, guided by reason and the rules and directions of observation, starting from the effects themselves. The sea moves toward the lands,

lands, and from those same lands again by flow and ebb <term>fluxu & refluxu</term> <note>The rising and falling of the tide.</note> it follows the daily revolution of the Moon; so that the sea flows when the Moon occupies a certain point in the heavens, and again ebbs when it is positioned at another certain point. Thus, because of the Moon's own motion, by which it is carried toward the East, the times change both by day and by night, since with each 12-hour approach <term>accessibus</term> there is an alteration of nearly half an hour <note>The author is describing the "tidal lag," where high tide occurs about 50 minutes later each day.</note>, as the motion of the Moon intensifies or slackens: or as the tilt of the Zodiac and the latitude of the Moon align with right ascensions <term>rectis adscensionibus</term> <note>A coordinate in astronomy used to chart the positions of celestial bodies.</note>. But because this occurs on all our British shores, let us begin with them—as they are especially suitable above all others for investigating the variety and science of this matter—having first established all the differences on every shore and at the mouths of rivers.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *Which Moon, or what point in the heavens, causes the flood tide, and which the ebb.*

<margin>Exercise 52 in Scaliger’s critique of Cardano. <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558) was a famous scholar who wrote a series of "Exercises" critiquing Girolamo Cardano’s work on natural philosophy.</note></margin>
It is not always to be held as a law that the Moon causes the sea’s flood tide at the exact point where it is located when it flows—whether at its beginning, middle, or end. Therefore, many "know-it-alls" <note>Original: "scioli" - used mockingly for those with superficial knowledge.</note> are deceived; having not observed the tides in many different places, they most foolishly judge the Lunar power from the Moon's less consistent movements across the heavens, and are (as the saying goes) as far off as the whole sky. Federico Delfino <note>A 16th-century Italian mathematician who studied the relationship between the moon and tides.</note> established a middle point between the ascending point <note>the eastern horizon</note> and the Meridian <note>the highest point in the sky</note>, in which, when the Moon is placed, it drives the waves toward the land; and likewise again between the Western boundary <note>the horizon</note> and the angle of the mid-heaven. Scaliger divides the entire hemisphere above the horizon—which consists of twelve hours—and claims the course of the Ocean is bounded by half of that time. He argues that the Moon "pulls" the Ocean, and does so in a twofold way at the mouths of the Garonne <note>A river in southwest France.</note>: namely, when the Moon travels from its rising to the Meridian, the seas are summoned. This is indeed a clever and subtle argument; however, he does not offer even a single word regarding the second tide, or that arrival of water that occurs when the Moon is hidden beneath the earth. Nor does he see that the Moon sometimes consumes only three hours in its entire journey from the horizon to the Meridian circle; it does not reach and does not know that terminating line of the sky, which it passes by untouched most subtly. Thus, he wastes his time and effort <note>Original: "oleum & operam perdit" - literally "loses his oil and labor," an ancient idiom for working in vain by lamplight.</note>.

Lemnius <note>Levinus Lemnius (1505–1568), a Dutch physician and author.</note> teaches that the port upon which the Moon "looks" is filled, and he describes this in relation to certain ports of Flanders, how in...

<meta>This page continues the critique of Renaissance tidal theories. The previous page ended while discussing how Julius Caesar Scaliger divided the sky into segments to track the Moon's influence. This page concludes Chapter XIII by refuting the theories of Johannes Hagius and others who relied on the Moon's visible presence or the horizon, and begins Chapter XIV by challenging the widely held belief that lunar light is the cause of the tides.</meta>

<page-num>304</page-num>
<header>NATURAL PHILOSOPHY</header>

...for them, the tide flows from the Moon most imprudently; he trifles, not without great laughter from Astronomers, Sailors, and even the fishermen who work in the rivers. Johannes Hagius <note>Johannes Hagius (Johann Hayn, 1533–1575) was a German scholar who wrote on meteorological and astronomical phenomena.</note> seeks the cause from the horizon <term>finitore: the horizon, or the circle that limits our sight</term>, arguing that because the lunar rays behold the seas obliquely, the heated sea breaks up and expands the mixed-up vapors <note>Original: "exhalationes" — in Aristotelian physics, these were dry or moist gases rising from the earth thought to cause weather and tides.</note>. By these expanded vapors, the sea itself is increased and swells up when it wishes to break forth, being stirred by the Moon; he also foolishly thinks that at the new moon, the seas are moved little or not at all. But that useless dream of the man is easily refuted when the Moon has declined toward the Tropic of Capricorn. For at a latitude of 60 degrees, the Moon sometimes does not emerge from the horizon, but remains hidden for as long as three days, and yet the tides of the sea occur twice in a twenty-four-hour period. Therefore, setting aside such great carelessness and ignorance of writers, we establish the true place of the sea's continuous approach <note>the flood tide</note> as the Meridian circle <note>the imaginary line passing through the celestial poles and the observer's zenith</note>; and for the change and retreat <note>the ebb tide</note>, the Meridian passing through the common intersection of the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note> and the horizon of the region in question.

## CHAPTER XIV.

->*The Moon does not move the seas through its light, neither its own,*<-
->*nor that borrowed from the Sun.*<-

Let it be permitted here, contrary to the opinion and perception of everyone until now, to demonstrate certain things, so that we may investigate by what forces the Moon moves the seas. The common opinion, accepted by all, is that the waters are drawn out, raised, and subsided by the power of Light, as they see that great tides occur during full moons, when she shines with a full orb. Therefore, neither the approach nor the retreat of the sea <note>Original: "accessus, nec recessus"—the flood and ebb tides.</note> comes from light.

Regardless of the tilt of the celestial sphere <term>Obliquity of the sphere: the angle of the Earth's axis relative to the ecliptic, which affects how celestial bodies appear to move depending on one’s latitude</term>, these movements are distinguished only by the right ascensions of the meridians <term>Right Ascension: the celestial equivalent of longitude, measured along the equator</term>, which pass through the poles and equal intervals of the equator. Every six hours the waters arrive, and every six hours they recede, with the addition of that slight difference arising from the Moon’s own eastward motion. There is no correspondence with the horizon; for in our "oblique sphere" <note>This refers to latitudes between the equator and the poles where the stars and planets rise at an angle.</note>, the Moon may reach the meridian circle only three hours after rising from the horizon, while at other times it may require nine hours to move from the horizon to the meridian. Similarly, in the other quarters and angles of the sky, great difficulties and inequalities arise. Therefore, neither the horizon nor the "circles of position"—which are constructed relative to the circles of the zenith and the horizon—can contribute to the demonstration of these matters. Only the Meridians, distinguished by equal spaces of the equator, are useful. 

As an example: high tide occurs on a given shore when the Moon is above the horizon on the meridian of that region. The greatest recession and an empty shore occur when the Moon reaches the "western meridian" (so to speak), which is 90 degrees distant from the true meridian on the equator. When it reaches the lowest point of the sky <note>The "Imum Coeli" or the meridian point directly underneath the Earth.</note>, which is the other side of the same meridian, the sea fills up again. It is exhausted once more when it falls into the "eastern angle"—not of the horizon, but of the meridian distinguished by 90 degrees.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### *The cause of variations in the flow and ebb of the sea from the Moon at the meridian.*

Dissimilarities arise in many ways and in many places concerning the fixed time of high tide and low tide; for so we call the highest flow <term>fluxus<gloss>high tide</gloss></term> and the lowest ebb <term>refluxus<gloss>low tide</gloss></term>. ## CHAPTER XIX.

### Why greater tides occur during the Full Moon and New Moon than during the quarters.

The waters rise highest during the <term>full moons<gloss>original: "pleniluniis"</gloss></term>, as well as during the <term>new moons<gloss>original: "noviluniis"</gloss></term>; our countrymen call these **spring tides** <gloss>original: "springtydes"</gloss>; they rise more gently in the <term>quarters<gloss>the first and third quarter phases of the lunar cycle</gloss></term>, which are called **neap tides** <gloss>original: "neape-tydes"</gloss>. In those places where the sea tides are naturally smaller, there are absolutely no tides at all during the quarters, as is the case in many parts of the **Mediterranean Sea**. If the tide were caused by light, it would be no greater during the new moon than during the quarters; indeed, it would be less, because the face of the Earth is illuminated by the <note>reflected</note> light of the middle phases. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that this is caused by the **Sun**; for although the Sun by itself is not able to stir our seas, it nevertheless possesses the greatest power in agitating and calming storms, and in summoning spirits <note>vapors or atmospheric forces</note> and winds from the earth when it is at the cardinal points of the heaven. ## C H A P T E R  X X I I.

### *That stones are formed in a short time, and on the rapid transformation of things into stone.*

In our Britain, in the forest of Knaresborough <note>A town in North Yorkshire famous for its "Dropping Well," a spring that deposits high mineral content on objects, giving them a stone-like shell.</note>, there is a spring whose water changes wood, leaves, and meat into stone after they have rested in it for some time. Near the stream there are waters that drip from hanging rocks, in which whatever is placed becomes stone over an interval of time. In Germany, in Saxony, there are various springs into which objects are cast and then petrify.

In the mountains near Alderley close to Kingswood in England, stones are frequently found that have the shape of snails and oysters <note>original: "cochlearum & Ostreorum"</note>; yet the common folk believe they have been there ever since the Flood <note>Referring to the biblical Deluge of Noah.</note>. I myself, among my many rarities, have at home a very hard fern <note>original: "filicem"</note>, on the side of which is a large snail; one half of it stands out, converted into the hardest stone, while the other half is hidden within the rock. I also have the stone heart of an animal, as well as the head of a duck; also a viper, or another serpent similar to a viper, changed into stone; of which I have now seen three, which are found on a certain mountain in northern England. These are stones grown to double the size of a fist; when the locals break them open, in the middle, as if in a belly, a coiled stone serpent is seen, complete in all the features of its limbs <note>These "serpent stones" are actually ammonites—the fossilized shells of extinct marine mollusks which were often mistaken for coiled snakes in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>. They say the people there were once plagued by such pests, and all those serpents were turned into stones by a certain holy Saint <note>original: "Diva." The author is likely referring to the legend of Saint Hilda of Whitby, who was said to have turned a plague of snakes into stone.</note>; although this story may be a fable invented for the sake of piety, it is nonetheless manifest that they have been changed into stones. Perhaps they were killed by cold and remained frozen until the nearby parts of the earth solidified, and so they were entombed in the rocks and themselves turned into stone.

<header>P H Y S I O L O G Y  B O O K  V.</header>

In a certain village of Gloucestershire in England, there are many trees, such as oaks and others, whose roots take on a stony nature; and yet that place is most fertile for trees. Near Stony Stratford <note>A historic market town in Buckinghamshire, situated on the Roman road of Watling Street.</note> in England, there is a spring in which wood becomes stone. Also in Newnham <note>Likely Newnham Regis in Warwickshire, which was famous in the 16th and 17th centuries for its mineral springs and "petrifying" waters.</note> in the county of Warwickshire, pieces of wood that have remained in the spring for a long time are clothed in stone, as if by a layer of bark. Therefore, it is manifest that their generation is rapid, and that they did not come into being many centuries ago, nor do they always grow together over such very long periods of time; rather, they take on their forms no differently than how stones <note>original: "calculi"</note> <term>calculi</term> <note>The author is referring to kidney or bladder stones. In early modern medicine, these were often compared to geological stones to explain how minerals could precipitate and solidify quickly within a body or environment.</note> are suddenly generated in the human body to the ruin of mortals.
